**Reading.**
* The cs baseline keeps its guarantee with a wide margin: at most 0.27% false alarms per day against a proved 5%, and the confidence bound itself failed on at most 0.08% of paths against an allowed 1%. Figure: `e08_false_alarms.png`.
* With 10,000 paths, the plug-in at 390 steps is at 4.5% (Gaussian and jumps) and 4.9% (t5) on the increase side, and 5.07% (t5) for either side, so it sits at the bound without exceeding it beyond Monte Carlo error. E4d's 5.4% (2000 paths, standard error about 0.5 points) is about 1.6 combined standard errors above our Gaussian value, so the "break" it reported was not confirmed. Over the 500 pre-change steps of Q8b (bound 500 / 7800 = 6.4%), the plug-in increase side at 390 steps under t5 alarmed on 7.0% to 7.5% of 2000 paths in three rows that share their calibration windows (`e08b_change.csv`), 1 to 2 standard errors above the bound. So the plug-in is close to its bound at short calibration, with no proof either way.
* margin_z = 1 brings every rate to 1.5% or less, but it is on the wrong side of the truth on 17% to 19% of paths: it is a heuristic safety margin, not a guarantee.
* Sitting at the bound within one day does not make the plug-in safe over longer runs. E14 (Q14a, Q14h) finds 41% to 43% false alarms within five days after 390 calibration steps (bound 25%) and 0.084 to 0.094 false alarms per day over 30-day streams, and proves that no bound of the form C m / A can hold for the plug-in at a fixed calibration length (Proposition A.6 in `docs/theory_running_tau.md`).

The spread of lengths is narrow (the 10% and 90% quantiles lie within 13% below and 17% above the median), so in these i.i.d. settings the rule behaves almost like a fixed length chosen for the target width. Its value is that the user states the precision they want instead of a length, and the proof covers the data-dependent stop (`docs/math.md`, 6.6).

### Q8d. Is the width the bound's fault? [SYNTHETIC]

Upper and lower bound divided by the true mean of X, at the end of a fixed window, δ = 0.01: a normal-approximation interval (no finite-sample guarantee), the best bound any constant bet can give for the true law ("best constant bet", a benchmark that knows the distribution, not a strict limit for every betting bound), and our empirical Bernstein bound (median of 500 paths).

| Returns | Calibration (sequence length) | Upper: normal approx. | best constant bet | ours | Lower: normal approx. | best constant bet | ours |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | 390 (292) | 1.189 | 1.290 | 1.368 | 0.811 | 0.785 | 0.741 |
| Gaussian | 1440 (1080) | 1.098 | 1.139 | 1.171 | 0.902 | 0.881 | 0.869 |
| Gaussian | 5000 (3750) | 1.053 | 1.072 | 1.078 | 0.947 | 0.934 | 0.931 |
| Jumps | 390 (292) | 1.194 | 1.301 | 1.377 | 0.806 | 0.780 | 0.731 |
| Student t5 | 390 (292) | 1.211 | 1.320 | 1.426 | 0.789 | 0.761 | 0.704 |
| Student t5 | 5000 (3750) | 1.059 | 1.080 | 1.082 | 0.941 | 0.926 | 0.920 |

**Reading.** At 1440 steps and above our upper bound is within 3.5 points of the best constant bet; at 390 steps the upper bound gives away 7.6 to 10.6 points. Most of the width is intrinsic: the truncated squared return has a standard deviation 1.4 to 1.6 times its mean and a range of 4.7 to 6.5 standard deviations, and even the best constant bet needs a bound 29% to 32% above the mean from 292 observations. A tighter construction (the "hedged capital" betting sequence) could recover roughly the gap to that benchmark.

### Q8f. Volatility clustering [SYNTHETIC]

GARCH(1,1) with α = 0.05, β = 0.94 (persistence 0.99, unit unconditional variance), 1440-step windows, 4000 paths. Inside one window the conditional truncated variance varies by a median factor of 2.6 between its 10% and 90% quantiles. Each bound is checked against its own target (`docs/math.md`, Theorem 6.2): the cs bounds against the bet-weighted average of the conditional means, the i.i.d. standard-error intervals against their plain average.

| Interval | Nominal miss | Upper bound misses | Lower bound misses |
|---|---|---|---|
| cs, δ = 0.01 (checked at every step) | 1% | 0.05% | 0.18% |
| cs, δ = 0.05 (checked at every step) | 5% | 0.85% | 1.50% |
| plug-in + 1.00 i.i.d. SE | 15.9% | 18.9% | 10.9% |
| plug-in + 1.64 i.i.d. SE | 5% | 6.7% | 2.1% |
| plug-in + 2.33 i.i.d. SE | 1% | 1.6% | 0.2% |

**Reading.** The confidence sequence stays valid under clustering, as the theorem says. The i.i.d. standard error is too small for the upper bound (1.6% misses at a nominal 1%), which is the side that protects the increase detector. The effect is moderate here, but it has no bound. The bigger issue is elsewhere: with conditional variance moving by a factor of 2.6 inside a window, the monitoring null "never above the calibration average" is simply false under clustering, whatever the baseline (E9 Q9c). The confidence sequence protects against estimation error, not against this.

### Q8e. Real data: Bitstamp BTC/USD, July to December 2025 [REAL]

Configuration of E5c: deseasonalised one-minute returns, c = 3, 1440-minute calibration, recalibrate after each alarm. cs uses δ = 0.01 and A = 1440 / 0.04 = 36,000. The validation is E5c's: robust volatility in the 1440 minutes after each alarm divided by the robust volatility of its calibration window. Unlike E5c, missing returns are passed to the monitor as missing (it skips them) instead of being set to 0, as the independent review (M6) recommends. In this file only the first return is missing, and a run with E5c's zero filling gave the same alarms and the same table to two decimals. The plug-in rows reproduce E5c's alarm counts and hit rates exactly.

| Baseline | Band | A | Alarms (per day) | Up / down | Median post / baseline, up | Up followed by higher vol | Median post / baseline, down | Down followed by lower vol | Median null / plug-in (up / down) | Median calibration | Share of time monitored |

| cs | 0 | 36000 | 131 (0.71) | 75 / 56 | 1.42 | 77% | 0.71 | 82% | 1.16 / 0.82 | 1440 | 29% |
| plugin | 0.25 | 28800 | 126 (0.68) | 73 / 53 | 1.43 | 81% | 0.65 | 90% | 1.25 / 0.75 | 1440 | 32% |
| plugin (control) | 0.25 | 36000 | 126 (0.68) | 74 / 52 | 1.43 | 77% | 0.64 | 92% | 1.25 / 0.75 | 1440 | 32% |
| margin_z=1 | 0.25 | 28800 | 118 (0.64) | 71 / 47 | 1.43 | 77% | 0.60 | 89% | 1.30 / 0.72 | 1440 | 36% |
| cs | 0.25 | 36000 | 101 (0.55) | 66 / 35 | 1.39 | 80% | 0.45 | 97% | 1.48 / 0.61 | 1440 | 45% |

| plugin | 0.5 | 28800 | 92 (0.50) | 59 / 33 | 1.49 | 83% | 0.41 | 97% | 1.50 / 0.50 | 1440 | 50% |
| cs | 0.5 | 36000 | 76 (0.41) | 54 / 22 | 1.52 | 83% | 0.31 | 100% | 1.77 / 0.41 | 1440 | 58% |

**Reading.**
* The cs baseline cuts alarms by 16% to 20% at every band (156 to 131, 126 to 101, 92 to 76). Almost all of the cut is in decrease alarms (86 to 56, 53 to 35, 33 to 22); increase alarms change little. The control row shows that the larger A alone changes almost nothing (126 alarms at both A values; the split moves from 73/53 to 74/52 and the increase hit rate from 81% to 77%), so the cut comes from the baseline.
* Hit rates of decrease alarms rise (67% to 82% with no band, 90% to 97% with band 0.25, 97% to 100% with band 0.5), and the remaining decrease alarms are followed by larger drops (median 0.45 against 0.65 at band 0.25). Hit rates of increase alarms stay at 77% to 83%. All variants beat random times (about 50%, E5c control). A rate-matched ratio rule does about as well (E6e), so this check shows that the alarms are not noise, not that they add precision.
* On this data the cs baseline acts like an extra, data-driven band: at band 0 its null values sit 16% above and 18% below the plug-in, close to a fixed band of 0.16 to 0.18, and its alarm count and decrease hit rate fall between those of the plug-in with band 0 and with band 0.25. Its value is the proof, not better alarms.
* A side effect worth knowing: with recalibration after every alarm, the monitor spends most of the time calibrating (it monitors only 15% of the minutes with the plug-in and no band). Fewer alarms mean more monitored time (29% for cs). The adaptive rule needed longer windows here (median 2455 minutes for w = 0.3, against 1233 steps for synthetic Gaussian data with a slightly different split), so it monitors only 25% of the time. We did not check why; a likely reason is that the truncated squared deseasonalised returns are more dispersed relative to their mean than in the synthetic laws, or drift within the window.

**Caveats.**
* The synthetic studies are i.i.d. within each regime, where the theorem's null holds exactly. Under clustering the null itself is false (Q8f, E9), and no baseline fixes that.
* The guarantee is conservative: about 0.3% or less against 5%. Part of that is Ville's inequality (with the true baseline the plug-in is already at about 1% to 2%, E9 Q9a), part is the width of the bound. The proved budget cannot be spent more aggressively without losing the proof.
* One asset, one venue, six months for the real run; "followed by higher volatility" is a sanity check, not ground truth (see E5c). The adaptive rule's target w = 0.3 was fixed from the synthetic design before the real run, not tuned on it.
* The betting (hedged capital) confidence sequence, a union bound over a grid of truncation levels, and a running τ (`docs/math.md`, 6.4) were not implemented.

## E9. How tight is the guarantee, and when does it stop applying?

Script `e09_stress_guarantee.py`. All results **[SYNTHETIC]**, fixed seeds.

**Q9a and Q9b. Tightness and distribution-free validity.** Two-sided monitor with the *true* baseline (τ = 3 times the scaled MAD of the distribution, m₀ = E[min(r², τ²)] from 20 million draws), alarm level A = 7800 per side pair (each side at 2A), 4000 independent paths per row. Theorem B says P(false alarm within m steps) ≤ m / A.

| Horizon m (steps) | Bound m / A | Gaussian | Student t3 (infinite fourth moment) | Jumps (0.5% per step, 10 sd) | Price ticks (tick = 0.5 sd, 20% zero returns) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 98 (a quarter of a 390-step day) | 1.3% | 0.00% | 0.18% | 0.12% | 0.05% |
| 390 (one day) | 5.0% | 1.1% | 1.4% | 1.3% | 1.4% |
| 1950 (one week) | 25% | 12.8% | 14.3% | 13.2% | 13.7% |
| 3900 | 50% | 29.6% | 30.6% | 29.7% | 31.2% |
| 7800 (= A) | 100% | 55.9% | 55.9% | 56.4% | 56.9% |

95% Wilson intervals for the one-day row are about ±0.3 points (for example 0.8% to 1.5% for the Gaussian case).

**Reading.** The guarantee holds in every case, and the four distributions give almost the same false alarm rates, which is what "nonparametric" should mean: once returns are truncated, the bound depends only on the mean of the bounded statistic (the observed rates could in principle differ more than they do). The bound is conservative by a factor of about 4 at one day (1.1% to 1.4% against 5%) and by about 2 at the scale of A. Part of the slack is structural (the two-sided split at 2A each, and Ville's inequality ignores the overshoot), part is the betting grid. We expect (from the other horizons in the table; we did not run it) that a user could lower A by a factor of up to about 3 and still see about 5% per day *in this i.i.d. setting*, but that would no longer be backed by a proof, so the default keeps the proven level. The theory track (E11) studies where the slack comes from.

**Q9c. Volatility clustering, where the null is false.** GARCH(1,1) returns with unit unconditional variance, τ and m₀ set to their unconditional values, 2000 paths of one 1440-step day, A = 28,800 (5% budget per day). Here E[X_t] = m₀ on average, but the *conditional* mean E[X_t | past] moves above and below m₀, so Theorem B does not apply. Share of days with a false alarm:

| Null band b | α + β = 0.95 (half-life 14 steps) | 0.99 (69 steps) | 0.999 (693 steps) | 0.9999 (6931 steps) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 78% | 100% | 100% | 100% |
| 0.10 | 41% | 97% | 99% | 98% |
| 0.25 | 16% | 77% | 93% | 92% |
| 0.50 | 3.6% | 34% | 60% | 69% |
| 1.00 (increase side only) | 0% | 12% | 16% | 20% |

**Reading.** Short-lived clustering (half-life 14 steps, the shortest case in the table) is absorbed by a band of 0.5. Persistent clustering is not absorbed by any reasonable static band: with a half-life of an hour or more, even b = 1 (alarm only if variance more than doubles) leaves 12% to 20% of days with an alarm. This is not a failure of the proof; it says what the monitor detects. Persistent GARCH clusters *are* changes in conditional volatility, and the monitor reports them. If the goal is to flag breaks *relative to a volatility model* rather than ordinary clustering, the null has to be stated relative to a forecast: monitor returns divided by a predictable volatility forecast. E10 tests that idea.

**Q9d. Runtime** (`e09d_profile.csv`; one shared 4-core machine, so timings are indicative). The streaming monitor processes about 100,000 returns per second for one series (10 µs per step), so a year of one-minute crypto bars takes about 5 seconds. The vectorised detector costs 0.04 µs per path-step at 10,000 paths, so a Monte Carlo study of 10,000 paths of one week takes about 1 second. The normalised robust kernel IQ costs about 0.15 µs per return. Nothing in the prototype needs compiled code at these sizes; numba was considered and not added.

## E10. Monitoring relative to a volatility forecast

Script `e10_forecast_relative.py`. Parts a, b, b2 and d are **[SYNTHETIC]** with fixed seeds; part c is **[REAL]** (Binance one-minute data from the GitHub mirror, see `data/MANIFEST.csv`).

**Why.** E9 showed that the false alarm guarantee stops applying under persistent volatility clustering, because the conditional mean of the monitored statistic wanders even when the unconditional variance never changes. A natural fix is to monitor standardised returns z_t = r_t / σ̂_t, where σ̂_t² is a volatility forecast that uses data up to t - 1 only (`forecast.py`). The null then reads "the forecast is right up to a constant", and under that null the guarantee applies again. E10 asks what this fix costs.

**Setup.** GARCH(1,1) returns with unit unconditional variance and three persistences: (α, β) = (0.05, 0.90), (0.05, 0.94) and (0.03, 0.969), that is α + β = 0.95, 0.99 and 0.999 (half-lives of 14, 69 and 693 steps). A "day" has 1440 steps and the alarm level is A = 28,800 (5% per day by Theorem B). Each path has 2000 warm-up steps for the forecasts, one calibration day (plug-in baseline, as in the streaming monitor) and then monitoring. Monitor inputs: raw returns; the oracle (returns divided by the true conditional volatility, or in Q10b by the pre-break model's filter); EWMA forecasts with half-lives 60 and 360 steps; and a GARCH(1,1) forecast whose parameters were fitted by quasi maximum likelihood with variance targeting on a separate 30,000-step training path and then frozen. The fitted parameters were close to the truth: (ω, α, β) = (0.050, 0.049, 0.901), (0.0092, 0.049, 0.942) and (0.0009, 0.029, 0.970).

**Q10a. Validity under a GARCH null with no break.** Share of 600 paths with a false alarm in the one monitored day (95% Wilson intervals are about ±1.8 points near 5%):

| Monitor input | Band b | α + β = 0.95 | 0.99 | 0.999 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| raw returns | 0 | 81.7% | 100% | 99.7% |
| raw returns | 0.25 | 20.7% | 79.8% | 92.0% |
| EWMA, half-life 360 | 0 | 72.2% | 99.8% | 99.5% |
| EWMA, half-life 360 | 0.25 | 14.0% | 72.7% | 83.0% |
| EWMA, half-life 60 | 0 | 24.5% | 82.3% | 75.5% |
| EWMA, half-life 60 | 0.25 | 1.7% | 10.0% | 4.8% |
| fitted GARCH | 0 | 5.8% | 3.0% | 6.2% |
| fitted GARCH | 0.25 | 0% | 0% | 0% |
| oracle | 0 | 5.3% | 4.7% | 5.3% |
| oracle | 0.25 | 0% | 0% | 0% |

**Reading.** With the fitted GARCH forecast the one-day false alarm rate falls to the oracle's level: 3% to 6% (5.8%, 3.0% and 6.2%; the 6.2% has a 95% Wilson interval of about 4.5% to 8.4%), against 4.7% to 5.3% with the true volatility. Both use a plug-in baseline, which the theorem does not cover; the proof needs the true or the confidence-sequence baseline and a correct forecast model. The level is about 5% rather than the 1% to 1.4% of E9 because the baseline is a plug-in estimate from one calibration day (E4d and E8 deal with this; it is not caused by the forecast). An EWMA forecast is only as good as its match to the clustering: half-life 60 steps nearly works at band 0.25, half-life 360 is too slow and behaves almost like raw returns. So "monitor relative to a forecast" is only as valid as the forecast.

**Q10b. Power: a break that doubles the long-run variance.** Persistence 0.99, break 200 steps after calibration, five days of monitoring, 300 paths per row. Two kinds of break: "scale" multiplies every later return by √2 (the variance doubles at once), "omega" doubles the GARCH intercept (the variance moves to twice its old level gradually). Band 0 shown; band 0.25 is in `results/e10b_power.csv`.

| Break | Monitor input | Alarm before the break | Detected within 1 day | Within 5 days | Median delay (steps) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| scale | raw returns | 39% | 61% | 61% | 69 |
| scale | EWMA, half-life 60 | 15% | 73% | 85% | 226 |
| scale | fitted GARCH | 0.3% | 34% | 93% | 1791 |
| scale | oracle (pre-break model) | 0.3% | 42% | 94% | 1603 |
| omega | raw returns | 43% | 57% | 57% | 125 |
| omega | EWMA, half-life 60 | 10% | 81% | 90% | 264 |
| omega | fitted GARCH | 0% | 36% | 93% | 1790 |
| omega | oracle (pre-break model) | 0% | 43% | 94% | 1523 |

"Alarm before the break" covers only the 200 steps between calibration and the break. At band 0.25 the forecast-relative monitors (oracle and fitted GARCH) never alarmed in five days, for either kind of break.

**Q10b2. Control: the same monitors with no break, and a larger break.** Same design and seeds for the model fit, 300 new paths per row, band 0. "Alarm" here means any alarm after the time at which Q10b put the break.

| Paths | Monitor input | Alarm within 1 day | Within 5 days | Median time to alarm (steps) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| no break | raw returns | 57% | 57% | 167 |
| no break | EWMA, half-life 60 | 74% | 87% | 482 |
| no break | fitted GARCH | 4.0% | 38% | 4075 |
| no break | oracle | 6.0% | 44% | 3519 |
| variance times 4 | raw returns | 60% | 60% | 65 |
| variance times 4 | EWMA, half-life 60 | 85% | 87% | 94 |
| variance times 4 | fitted GARCH | 89% | 100% | 712 |
| variance times 4 | oracle | 90% | 100% | 612 |

(For raw returns and the EWMA forecasts about 13% to 43% of paths had already alarmed in the 200 steps before the break time, which is why their "within" shares look capped.)

**Reading.** Two corrections to a naive reading of Q10b follow.

1. *Part of the "detection within five days" is not detection.* Without any break, the oracle monitor alarms within five days on 44% of paths and the fitted GARCH monitor on 38%. Against those, a doubling of the variance raises the rates to 94% and 93%; within one day the lift is from 4% to 6% (no break) to 34% to 43% (break). The break is clearly detected, but slowly.
2. *The plug-in baseline breaks the bound at long horizons.* For the oracle the standardised returns are exactly i.i.d. N(0, 1), so Theorem B with the true baseline guarantees at most 7200 / 28,800 = 25% false alarms over the five monitored days. With a baseline estimated from one calibration day the rate is 44% (95% interval 39% to 50%). At one day the plug-in error already raises the rate from about 1.4% (true baseline, E9) to about 5% (Q10a); that it lands near the 5% budget reflects the slack in Ville's inequality, not a guarantee. Its effect grows with the horizon, because a baseline that is a little too low makes the e-process drift upward at a small constant rate. This is a strong reason to use the confidence-sequence baseline (E8) whenever a monitor runs for days without recalibration.

With a 4-fold increase in the long-run variance the forecast-relative monitors detect within a day on 89% to 90% of paths (median 612 to 712 steps), against 4% to 6% without a break.

**Q10d. Why the forecast hides the break: a signal cap.** Two exact facts explain Q10b.

1. If x_t is GARCH(ω, α, β) then c·x_t is GARCH(c²ω, α, β): its conditional variance is c²σ_t² = c²ω + α(c x_{t-1})² + β c²σ_{t-1}². So a scale break and an intercept break lead to the same model; they differ only in the transient right after the break.
2. Run the pre-break filter s_t = ω + α r²_{t-1} + β s_{t-1} on post-break returns whose true conditional variance follows the same recursion with kω. The difference of the two recursions is d_t = (k - 1)ω + β d_{t-1}, so after the transient the forecast is off by the constant (k - 1)ω / (1 - β), and the filter absorbs the rest of the break through its α r² term. With unit pre-break variance (ω = 1 - α - β), the ratio of the mean squared return to the mean forecast is

   ρ(k) = k (1 - β) / (1 - α - β + α k),

   which increases in k but never exceeds (1 - β) / α, however large the break.

The monitor sees the mean of the ratio, E[r_t² / s_t], which is a little larger than the ratio of means (Jensen) but is bounded too. Simulation, 200 paths of 18,000 post-break steps per row. The simulated ratio of means is pooled over paths (the sum of the path means of the true variance divided by the sum of the path means of the forecast), with a bootstrap standard error over paths in brackets. The mean of the ratio has standard errors below 0.002 (`mean_of_ratio_se` in the CSV).

| α + β | Variance factor k | ρ(k) formula | Ratio of means, simulated (pooled) | Mean of ratio (what the monitor sees) | KL rate per step (nats) | ln A / KL, days |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.95 | 2 | 1.333 | 1.333 (0.0003) | 1.361 | 0.0276 | 0.26 |
| 0.95 | 1000 | 1.998 | 2.000 (0.0015) | 2.204 | 0.2200 | 0.03 |
| 0.99 | 1.5 | 1.059 | 1.058 (0.0003) | 1.074 | 0.0015 | 4.7 |
| 0.99 | 2 | 1.091 | 1.091 (0.0005) | 1.116 | 0.0037 | 1.9 |
| 0.99 | 4 | 1.143 | 1.142 (0.0007) | 1.187 | 0.0093 | 0.77 |
| 0.99 | 1000 | 1.200 | 1.200 (0.0010) | 1.271 | 0.0187 | 0.38 |
| 0.999 | 2 | 1.016 | 1.016 (0.0006) | 1.031 | 0.0003 | 21 |
| 0.999 | 1000 | 1.033 | 1.034 (0.0010) | 1.065 | 0.0015 | 4.8 |

The pooled ratio agrees with the formula within two standard errors in every row of the CSV. An earlier version of this table showed the average of per-path ratios instead; a mean of ratios is biased upward when the per-path means are noisy, which at persistence 0.999 put it at 1.034 and 1.038, above the proved cap of 1.033. Both columns are in `results/e10d_signal_cap.csv` (`ratio_of_means_sim` is the per-path average).

The KL column is the per-step Kullback-Leibler divergence between the post-break and pre-break conditional laws of r_t, averaged over the post-break path, I = E[½(q_t - 1 - ln q_t)] with q_t the ratio of the two conditional variances. By Lai (1998), any detector whose average run length to a false alarm is at least A needs, asymptotically as A grows, an expected delay of at least about ln A / I. At A = 28,800 this is only an order-of-magnitude guide, not an exact bound.

**Reading.** At persistence 0.99 a doubling of the long-run variance looks, after standardisation, like an increase of about 9% to 12%, and the information bound suggests delays of the order of two days for any detector with the same false alarm budget (an asymptotic statement, as A grows, about the worst-case delay); at this A the observed delays are about 0.6 times that, as explained next. The 1500 to 1800 step median delays of the oracle and fitted GARCH monitors in Q10b are of this order, though somewhat shorter. E11 explains the gap: at this alarm level the Shiryaev-Roberts statistic pools evidence over many candidate change times, and this memory term is worth 54% to 62% of ln A. In an i.i.d. version of the same steady state the detector alarms at 0.41 to 0.58 times ln A / KL with the true baseline (`results/e11e2_e10_crosscheck.csv`), so a ratio of about 0.6 is expected and the Lai figure is an asymptotic guide, not a prediction at A = 28,800.

**Q10e. Where in time is the evidence?** Persistence 0.99, 400 paths, the pre-break filter s0 run on post-break returns with true conditional variance s1. Mean of s1/s0 at t steps after the break, and the step at which the average cumulative KL divergence reaches ln A = 10.3 (`results/e10e_transient.csv`):

| Break | t = 0 | t = 10 | t = 30 | t = 100 | t = 1000 | Cumulative KL reaches ln A at step | Observed median delay (Q10b, Q10b2; oracle) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| scale, k = 2 | 2.00 | 1.47 | 1.20 | 1.11 | 1.12 | 2409 | 1603 |
| intercept, k = 2 | 1.00 | 1.09 | 1.15 | 1.13 | 1.12 | 2709 | 1523 |
| scale, k = 4 | 4.00 | 1.96 | 1.34 | 1.18 | 1.20 | 553 | not run |
| intercept, k = 4 | 1.00 | 1.26 | 1.36 | 1.24 | 1.20 | 945 | 612 |

A scale break is fully visible at first and then fades with the filter's half-life of about 11 steps; an intercept break builds up to a small peak after about 30 steps (the forecast error has converged at rate β while the true variance still converges at rate α + β). Both then settle at the steady-state level of Q10d. The transient is short, so it matters most for large breaks (for k = 4 a scale break delivers 6.2 nats in the first 100 steps, an intercept break 2.1). The observed median delays are about 0.6 times the "cumulative KL reaches ln A" step in all three cases that were run. We think the main reason is the plug-in baseline of Q10b2, which makes the monitor anti-conservative (and therefore faster) over several days; the asymptotic nature of the bound and the difference between a median and a mean also contribute. We did not separate these effects; rerunning Q10b with the true baseline or with the confidence-sequence baseline of E8 would.

At persistence 0.999 a doubling is practically invisible for weeks. This is a property of the question, not a weakness of the monitor: a highly persistent volatility model can explain a level shift as its own slow wandering. It is the mirror image of the known finding that unmodelled level shifts make fitted GARCH models look almost integrated (Diebold 1986; Lamoureux and Lastrapes 1990; Mikosch and Starica 2004).

**Practical consequence.** Under persistent clustering, only the forecast-relative monitors separate breaks from ordinary clustering at all. Compare Q10b with Q10b2: raw returns alarm on 57% to 61% of paths with or without a doubling, and the EWMA monitors alarm about as often without a break as with one (half-life 60, band 0: 74% within a day without a break, 73% to 81% with one; band 0.25: 47% within five days without, 48% to 51% with). So there are two different questions, and the user has to choose. *Raw returns* answer "has volatility moved, for whatever reason?", and under persistent clustering the answer is "yes" most days. *Forecast-relative* returns answer "has volatility moved away from what my model predicted?", with a guarantee under the model, but a break in the long-run level is seen only as a small, capped signal, at a speed set by α and β through ρ(k). A forecast that adapts quickly does not escape the trade-off: it absorbs breaks as well as clustering.

**Q10c. Real data: five Binance coins, July to December 2025.** One-minute log returns, deseasonalised as in E5 (rolling 20-day intraday profile; June 2025 is a warm-up and is not monitored), band 0.25, A = 28,800, recalibration after each alarm. For each alarm we compare realised variance over the next day with an EWMA forecast (half-life one day) made at the alarm, and compare with 2000 random times. 95% Wilson intervals in brackets.

| Coin | Monitor input | Alarms per day | "Up" alarms: next day above forecast | "Down" alarms: next day below forecast | Random times: above forecast |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | deseasonalised only | 0.69 | 67% (55 to 77) | 72% (59 to 82) | 45% |
| BTC | divided by EWMA, half-life 360 min | 0.62 | 66% (54 to 76) | 80% (66 to 90) | 45% |
| ETH | deseasonalised only | 0.66 | 71% (60 to 80) | 83% (69 to 91) | 45% |
| ETH | divided by EWMA, half-life 360 min | 0.59 | 65% (53 to 75) | 85% (70 to 93) | 45% |
| XRP | deseasonalised only | 0.70 | 69% (57 to 78) | 86% (75 to 93) | 37% |
| XRP | divided by EWMA, half-life 360 min | 0.62 | 60% (49 to 70) | 82% (67 to 91) | 37% |
| SOL | deseasonalised only | 0.67 | 64% (53 to 74) | 87% (74 to 94) | 45% |
| SOL | divided by EWMA, half-life 360 min | 0.57 | 62% (51 to 72) | 81% (63 to 92) | 45% |
| DOGE | deseasonalised only | 0.68 | 60% (48 to 70) | 72% (58 to 82) | 42% |
| DOGE | divided by EWMA, half-life 360 min | 0.57 | 65% (53 to 75) | 80% (65 to 90) | 42% |

The half-life 1440 variant and all event times are in `results/e10c_real_forecast_relative.csv` and `results/e10c_events.csv`.

**Reading.** Dividing by an EWMA forecast changes the alarm rate by between +2% and -17% (0.57 to 0.71 alarms per day in every variant), far above the at most 0.05 per day that a correct forecast would give. One-minute crypto volatility therefore moves much more than an hours-scale EWMA forecast tracks, so in practice the real-data alarms are mostly genuine departures from such a forecast, not false alarms in the sense of the theorem. The alarms carry information beyond the forecast: after "up" alarms the next day's realised variance exceeded the forecast 60% to 71% of the time in the variants of the table (57.5% to 71% including the half-life 1440 variant in the CSV), against 37% to 45% at random times; after "down" alarms it fell short 72% to 87% of the time, against 55% to 63% at random times. The 95% intervals of the alarm groups exclude the random-time rate for every coin and variant on the "up" side, and for all but one case on the "down" side (DOGE, deseasonalised only, where the lower end of the interval equals the random-time rate of 58%). The comparison forecast is deliberately simple; part of the effect is ordinary persistence (an alarm reflects the last few hours, which the one-day EWMA has not yet absorbed).

**Relation to E6 (Q6e).** E6 asks the same question with a robust volatility measure (median of |u|) instead of realised variance, adds a HAR forecast and a rate-matched ratio rule, and also runs out of sample. The two agree: alarms are followed by volatility on the flagged side of a forecast far more often than random times (E6: 71% to 83% against 48% to 52%). The random-time rates differ (about 50% in E6, 37% to 45% here) because realised variance is a mean of squares, whose distribution is skewed, so at a random time it falls below its own forecast more often than above. E6 also shows the limit of this kind of evidence: a ratio rule tuned with hindsight to the same number of alarms is about as precise, so the e-detector's contribution on real data is the guarantee with fixed settings, not extra precision. What E10 adds is the forecast-relative *monitor input*: dividing returns by an EWMA forecast changes the alarm rate little on real data, unlike the synthetic GARCH case.

## E11. How fast does the detector react? Delay theory, price of robustness, bet design and the slack in the false alarm bound

Script `experiments/e11_delay_theory.py` (parts A, B, C, C2, C3, C4, C4V, D, D2, E, E2, FIG), helpers `src/avmonitor/design.py`, tests `tests/test_delay_theory.py`, full theory with proofs in `docs/theory_delay.md`. All results are **[SYNTHETIC]** (numerical integration and simulation, fixed seeds). Unless stated otherwise: true baseline, truncation c = 3, alarm level A = 7800 per side, change at the first monitored step (ν = 1), Gaussian, jump (probability 0.005, size 8 sd) and Student t returns.

**Why.** `docs/math.md` proves that false alarms are rare. E4 measured median delays of 87, 35 and 17 steps for sd ratios 1.25, 1.5 and 2 (mean delays 99.7, 39.6 and 18.0, which are what the theory tables below compare with) and a 10% to 70% penalty against the Gaussian likelihood ratio detector; E9 found the false alarm bound conservative by about 4. E11 explains these numbers, asks how the bets should be chosen, and (tracker B73) whether the detector is optimal as false alarms become rare.

### Q11a. Predicting the delay

**Method.** For a bet λ the log wealth grows at `g(λ) = E log(1 + λ(Y - 1))` per step after the change, `Y = min(r², τ²) / m₀`. Three predictions: first order `log(A) / g`; a proved bound for every A, change time and history, `min_k (log(A / w_k) + overshoot_k) / g_k` (Theorem 1); and a second-order Shiryaev-Roberts formula `(log A + κ - ζ) / g`, where ζ ≈ `log(1/g) + 0.58` is the statistic's memory of earlier start times (closed form from Dufresne's identity) and κ the overshoot. Compared with 3000 simulated paths per case (`results/e11a_growth.csv`, `e11a_delay.csv`).

| Case | first order | proved bound | simulated, default grid | second order, best single bet | simulated, best single bet |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian, sd 1.25 | 179 | 233 | 122 | 109 | 107 |
| Gaussian, sd 2 | 22 | 30 | 23 | 18.4 | 18.7 |
| Student t5, sd 1.25 | 280 | 362 | 178 | 158 | 159 |
| Gaussian, sd 0.67 | 150 | 179 | 124 | 99 | 99 |

**Reading.** The second-order formula is within 3% of the simulation in all 20 cases. The first-order formula overstates small-change delays by up to 112% (its error decays only like `1 / log A`). The proved bound is 1.3 to 2.7 times the truth. The default grid costs 9% to 26% against the best single bet. With the change at step 501 (as in E4) delays are 17% to 34% shorter (head start of the statistic) and match E4 within about 10%. The plug-in quadratic bet of the adaptive bettor is 1.4 to 4.4 times too small for increases and keeps only 49% to 94% of the growth.

### Q11b. The price of robustness

**Method.** A proved information ladder, `KL(raw returns) ≥ KL(truncated) ≥ KL_inf ≥ g_grid`, where `KL_inf = max_λ g(λ)` is the best growth of any detector valid for every return distribution with the same truncated mean (proved duality). The three ratios are the truncation, nonparametric and grid losses (`e11b_information.csv`, `e11b_price_simulated.csv`, `e11b_c_curve.csv`, `e11b_jump_burst.csv`).

| Gaussian data, c = 3 | sd 1.25 | sd 1.5 | sd 2 | sd 0.8 | sd 0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| truncation / nonparametric / grid loss | 1.03 / 1.10 / 1.02 | 1.08 / 1.23 / 1.02 | 1.27 / 1.48 / 1.04 | 1.00 / 1.24 / 1.02 | 1.00 / 3.61 / 1.05 |
| predicted penalty `KL / g_grid` | 1.16 | 1.37 | 1.95 | 1.27 | 3.79 |
| simulated penalty against the E4 Gaussian LR mixture | 1.14 | 1.35 | 1.73 | 1.48 | 3.45 |

**Reading.** The information ratio explains E4's penalty (about 1.12, 1.35, 1.7). On a log scale the predicted gap `KL / g_grid` at sd 1.25 to 2 splits into 59% to 68% for making no distributional assumption, 19% to 35% for truncation and 6% to 16% for the finite grid (this splits the first-order prediction, not the simulated penalty). For decreases truncation caps the evidence per step at `log(B / (B - 1))`, about `1/c²`, and this cap applies to every bet that is valid over the whole null. With c = 3 and A = 7800, even a total collapse of volatility takes any Shiryaev-Roberts e-detector built from valid bets at least 58 steps (64 at the two-sided level 2A), and the default five-bet grid 73 (79); the floors for c = 2, 4 and 5 are 29, 96 and 141 steps for any valid bets and 36, 122 and 180 for the default grid (`docs/theory_delay.md`, Corollary 4). **Truncation constant:** c = 3 to 4 for increases (with jumps, growth peaks at c = 3.25 to 4.25; without truncation a jump burst looks like 39% of a real 25% volatility rise, against 3.5% at c = 3); c = 1.5 to 2 for decreases (with the true baseline and Gaussian data, mean decrease delays fall by 26% to 49% at c = 2). The two sides may use different c; the guarantee then needs a known or confidence-sequence baseline for each side, and E11f below shows that with prices rounded to a coarse tick the gain depends on the tick size.

### Q11c. Which bets?

**Method.** Minimise the worst-case ratio of the mixture's delay to the best single bet's delay over a prior range (sd ratio 1.2 to 2 up, 0.5 to 0.85 down), designed on formulas, selected and validated by simulation on separate seeds. A first design used Gaussian data only; after it failed under fat tails, a second design pooled Gaussian, jump, t5 and t3 laws with a selection rule fixed in advance (`e11c*.csv`).

| Worst ratio to the best single bet (in range, 4 tail shapes, ν = 1 and 501, 2000 paths) | default grid | Gaussian-tuned | robust (pooled) |
|---|---|---|---|
| increase bets | 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5 | 0.25, 0.5 | 0.16, 0.39 |
| decrease bets (fraction of the largest admissible bet) | 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95 | 0.9, 0.99 | 0.5, 0.85 |
| Gaussian, increase / decrease | 1.25 / 1.26 | 1.13 / 1.04 | 1.24 / 1.25 |
| Student t3, increase / decrease | 1.19 / 1.17 | 1.39 / 1.78 | 1.17 / 1.13 |

**Reading.** The Gaussian-tuned bets are up to 18% faster than the default on Gaussian or jump data but up to 55% slower under t3 data (one decrease case has negative growth). The robust bets are at least as fast as the default in all 48 in-range validation cases, by 0.4% to 10.5% (median 5%), but up to 17% slower for small increases (sd 1.1) under fat tails. The formula-based design predicted a larger gain (worst ratio 1.54 to 1.27) than the simulation shows (1.25 to 1.24): it overstates the cost of many-bet grids. **Recommendation:** robust bets (0.16, 0.39) up and (0.5, 0.85) × largest bet down, equal weights, for A around `10^4`; keep the default if small increases matter or A is much larger.

### Q11d. Why the false alarm bound looks loose

**Method.** An exact optional-stopping identity splits `P(false alarm within m) / (m / A)` into stopping (F1), the share of expected wealth on paths that crossed A (F2) and overshoot (F3). For single bets, dynamic programming over the whole nonparametric null gives a lower bound on the worst case, reached by an explicit adversary (`e11d_*.csv`).

| One day (m = 390), Gaussian null | false alarms | rate / bound | F2 | F3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| two-sided default (E9), 10,000 paths | 0.88% | 0.18 | 0.24 | 0.80 |
| two-sided default (E9), 40,000 paths (factors not computed) | 1.03% | 0.21 | | |
| increase side, single bet 0.5 | 3.52% | 0.70 | 0.92 | 0.67 |
| worst null law found for a single bet 0.5 (dynamic programming; a lower bound on the worst case) | 4.73% | 0.95 | | |

**Reading.** The factor of about 5 (E9: about 4) is overshoot (1.25) times wealth stranded on paths that never alarm (about 4): 60% of it is held by the decrease side and 31% by the three smallest increase bets, which cannot build wealth within a day. The two-sided split is tight (both sides alarm on the same day in 0.00% of days). The bound itself is nearly attained by an adversarial null for single bets, and exactly at m = A for each side alone or a one-sided detector at level A (the two-sided rule alarms at 2A per side), so no much sharper threshold is provable for single bets; for the default mixture the best i.i.d. adversary found reaches 42% of the bound for the increase grid, an adaptive adversary reaches 52% for the two-sided detector (E16), and a certified sharper bound is open. Provable gains: an uneven split of the budget between the sides, and dropping bets that cannot use it.

### Q11e. Optimality as false alarms become rare (tracker B73)

**Theorem (proved in `docs/theory_delay.md`, section 9).** The worst-case delay of the Shiryaev-Roberts mixture equals its delay with the change at step 1. As `A → ∞`: for a fixed grid, the delay divided by `log A / KL_inf` tends to `KL_inf / g_grid` (1.00 to 1.08 for the default grid in the cases below), so a fixed grid is first-order optimal only when the best bet is one of its bets; a grid refined with about `√(log A)` bets has delay at most `(log A + ½ log log A + O(1)) / KL_inf`; a continuous mixture over the bet has delay at most `(log A + log log A + O(1)) / KL_inf` (`½ log log A` by a Laplace heuristic). These are upper bounds. `log A / KL_inf` is, to first order, the lower bound for every detector valid over the nonparametric null (Lorden 1971 at the least favourable null law; Ram and Ramdas 2026). First-order optimality for bounded means is already known (Ram and Ramdas 2026 prove the lower bound in general and show that it is attained for bounded means); what E11 adds is the refinement rate and the constants for this detector, with no claim of priority. Lai (1998) gives the simple-law bound `log A / I`; Shin, Ramdas and Rinaldo (2024) give matching upper bounds for mixtures of exponential e-detectors.

| delay / (log A / KL_inf), Gaussian, A = 10^4 / 10^8 | sd 1.25 | sd 2 | sd 0.8 | sd 0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| best single bet (simulated) | 0.66 / 0.83 | 0.90 / 0.94 | 0.62 / 0.82 | 0.74 / 0.87 |
| same, second-order formula | 0.63 / 0.82 | 0.89 / 0.95 | 0.62 / 0.81 | 0.74 / 0.87 |
| fine mixture (100 bets) | 0.71 / 0.90 | 0.96 / 0.97 | 0.80 / 0.94 | 0.96 / 1.03 |
| default grid (limit `KL_inf / g_grid`) | 0.73 / 0.90 (1.02) | 1.11 / 1.08 (1.04) | 0.77 / 0.91 (1.02) | 0.92 / 1.00 (1.05) |

**Reading.** The asymptotic regime arrives very slowly: at A = 10^8 even the best bet is 5% to 24% faster than `log A / KL_inf` (15 cases, Gaussian, t3 and jumps), and the second-order formula explains the gap to within 0.024 for every A ≥ 10^4. Fixed grids approach their predicted limits; the fine mixture is 4% to 19% slower than the best bet at A = 10^8 and slowly closing in. The robust detector keeps `KL_inf / KL` = 53% to 88% of the Gaussian likelihood ratio detector's asymptotic speed for increases (sd 2 to 1.25) and 28% to 80% for decreases; under t3 data 94% to 98% of the correctly specified detector's speed for increases. **E10 cross-check:** in an i.i.d. version of E10's steady state (A = 28,800) the memory term is 54% to 62% of `ln A`, and the detector alarms at 0.41 to 0.58 times `ln A / KL` with the true baseline, so the memory term alone can produce E10's factor of about 0.6.

**Caveats.** All results are synthetic, with i.i.d. post-change data and the true baseline (E8 and E10 treat estimated baselines and clustering). The second-order formula is a heuristic whose regularity conditions were not checked. The bet designs were tuned at A = 7800 and change sizes 1.2 to 2 (up), 0.5 to 0.85 (down). The dynamic programming gives rigorous lower bounds for the worst case only. The real-data tail shape, which decides between the bet designs, was not studied here.

Figures: `results/figures/e11_delay_predictions.png`, `e11_price_of_robustness.png`, `e11_false_alarm_slack.png`, `e11_asymptotic_optimality.png`.

## E11f. A tighter clip for decreases, tested

**Question.** Section 6.3 of `docs/theory_delay.md` predicts that clipping at c = 1.5 to 2 on the decrease side, while keeping c = 3 for increases, cuts decrease delays by a quarter to a half. Does it, with an estimated baseline, with ties and zeros, and on real data? The monitor has this as an option, `VolatilityMonitor(c_down=...)`; the default keeps c_down = c.

**What is guaranteed.** Each side is an e-detector for its own clipped statistic, and the two-sided rule needs only each side's guarantee. So the false alarm bound holds with c_down ≠ c when each side's baseline is known, or with the confidence-sequence baseline of `docs/math.md` section 6, which `VolatilityMonitor(baseline="cs", c_down=...)` now supports: the lower confidence sequence runs on `min(r², τ_dn²)` and the upper one on `min(r², τ²)`, each at level δ/2, so Theorem 6.4 of `docs/math.md` applies to each side with the same total δ (tested in `tests/test_monitor_cs.py`: coverage of both bounds, alarm counts on long null streams, and c_down = c reproducing the default exactly). The decrease side's null then reads "the mean of `min(r², τ_dn²)` has not fallen". For a fixed shape of the return distribution this follows from "volatility has not fallen", but a smaller clip is more sensitive to changes of shape at constant volatility, for example a larger share of zero returns. **The runs below use the plug-in baseline, which has no proof** (E4e), so their false alarm rates are empirical only.

**Method.** `experiments/e11f_split_c.py`. Part a [SYNTHETIC]: plug-in baseline from a 1440-step calibration window, band 0, A = 28,800 (each side at 2A, so at most 5% per 1440-step day if the baseline were the true one); 2000 no-change paths per law; decreases (sd × 0.8, 0.67, 0.5 at the first monitored step) with the same paths for the three values of c_down. Two kinds of return law:

* continuous: Gaussian, Student t4, Gaussian with jumps (0.5% per step, 8 sd); 600 paths per decrease;
* rounded prices ("ticks"): a Gaussian return is multiplied by its standard deviation and then rounded to a tick that is fixed in units of the pre-change standard deviation (0.25, 0.5 or 0.75 sd), as on a real price grid; 2000 paths per decrease, with the same normal draws for every tick size. Because the tick is fixed, more returns are zero after a fall: at a tick of 0.5 sd, 19.7% before the change and 24.5%, 29.1% and 38.3% after falls to 0.8, 0.67 and 0.5.

The first version of this experiment rounded the returns before multiplying them by the change ratio, so the tick shrank with volatility and the share of zeros stayed at 19.7% (independent review round 2b, C2). That law is kept in the CSV only for comparison (`ticks_0.5_scaled`), on the same normal draws. The vectorised code is checked alarm for alarm against the class on 216 runs in `tests/test_e11f_split_c.py` (four laws, sd ratios 1, 0.8 and 0.5, c_down 3, 2 and 1.5, six paths each, with a shorter calibration and a lower A so that paths with an increase alarm, a decrease alarm and no alarm all occur). Part b [REAL]: the five Binance coins, July to December 2025, deseasonalised with the past-only intraday profile, band 0.25; an alarm counts as confirmed when the robust scale of the next 1440 minutes is on the flagged side of the calibration scale. Files: `results/e11f_split_c_synthetic.csv`, `results/e11f_split_c_real.csv`.

**Results [SYNTHETIC], continuous laws.** Median decrease delay in steps (rounded to whole steps; every path detected):

| Law | sd × 0.8: c_down 3 / 2 / 1.5 | sd × 0.67 | sd × 0.5 | No change: false alarm within one day, both sides (decrease side), c_down 3 / 2 / 1.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gaussian | 247 / 176 / 185 | 158 / 85 / 73 | 118 / 58 / 40 | 5.7% (2.1%) / 5.65% (2.1%) / 6.1% (2.5%) |
| Student t4 | 334 / 289 / 277 | 160 / 117 / 106 | 100 / 62 / 48 | 5.4% (2.65%) / 5.65% (2.9%) / 5.95% (3.2%) |
| jumps | 273 / 196 / 206 | 161 / 88 / 74 | 119 / 59 / 40 | 6.05% (2.45%) / 6.15% (2.55%) / 6.7% (3.1%) |

**Results [SYNTHETIC], rounded prices.** Same layout, 2000 paths per cell. "Scale" is the median over paths of the calibration scale (scaled MAD) in units of the true pre-change standard deviation. With rounded returns the median absolute return is a whole number of ticks on almost every path, so the scale moves in steps of 1.4826 ticks and the clip c × scale, in units of the true standard deviation, depends on the tick.

| Tick (scale) | sd × 0.8: c_down 3 / 2 / 1.5 | sd × 0.67 | sd × 0.5 | No change, both sides (decrease side) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 sd (scale 1.11) | 292 / 185 / 188 | 191 / 98 / 77 | 144 / 69 / 45 | 5.0% (2.45%) / 5.6% (3.05%) / 5.0% (2.45%) |
| 0.5 sd (scale 0.74) | **188 / 211 / 251** | 99 / 80 / 86 | 70 / 39 / 35 | 5.7% (2.9%) / 5.7% (2.9%) / 5.4% (2.6%) |
| 0.75 sd (scale 1.11) | 295 / 201 / 207 | 192 / 100 / 81 | 144 / 69 / 47 | 5.4% (2.45%) / 6.0% (3.05%) / 5.9% (2.95%) |
| for comparison: 0.5 sd, tick shrinking with volatility (old law) | 185 / 173 / 244 | 96 / 69 / 80 | 68 / 38 / 33 | as for 0.5 sd |

**Reading.**

* **Continuous laws: c_down = 2 is faster in all nine cells,** by 13% to 51% in median delay. For Gaussian data the mean delay falls by 25%, 44% and 50% at sd × 0.8, 0.67 and 0.5, against 26%, 43% and 49% predicted by the theory with the true baseline (`e11b_price_simulated.csv`, mean delays, c = 2 against c = 3). c_down = 1.5 is faster still for falls to 0.67 and 0.5, but for a 20% fall it is slower than c_down = 2 for Gaussian and jump data (185 against 176 and 206 against 196 steps) and slightly faster for Student t4 data (277 against 289).
* **Rounded prices: the answer depends on the tick size.** With ticks of 0.25 and 0.75 sd, c_down = 2 is faster in all six cells, by 32% to 52%. With a tick of 0.5 sd it is **12% slower for a 20% fall** (median 211 against 188 steps; mean 234 against 205; paired difference +29 steps with standard error 1.7; slower on 66% of paths), and faster for larger falls (by 19% and 44%). c_down = 1.5 at a tick of 0.5 sd is 34% slower than c = 3 for a 20% fall (251 against 188 steps).
* **Why the tick of 0.5 sd is different.** With rounded returns the calibration scale is, on almost every path, a whole number of ticks times 1.4826. At a tick of 0.5 sd the median absolute return is one tick, so the scale is 0.74 sd and c = 3, 2 and 1.5 clip at 2.2, 1.5 and 1.1 true standard deviations; at ticks of 0.25 and 0.75 sd the scale is 1.11 sd and the clips are at 3.3, 2.2 and 1.7. So at a tick of 0.5 sd the default c = 3 already clips near the value that section 6.3 of `docs/theory_delay.md` finds best for a 20% fall (c = 2 for Gaussian data), and the tighter clips go past it, while the growing share of zero returns after the fall adds to the effect. This is our reading of the numbers, not a proof.
* **The old tick law overstated the case.** On the same normal draws, the law with a tick that shrinks with volatility gives c_down = 2 faster at a 20% fall (173 against 185 steps), the conclusion of the first version of this experiment. With a fixed tick of the same size it is slower.
* **False alarms are plug-in rates.** With no change, the one-day rate is 5.0% to 6.7% over all 18 cells, and 5.0% to 6.05% with c_down = c (= 3) in the same CSV, so the excess over 5% is there without the split and comes from the estimated baseline (E4e); 5% is the bound that holds with the true baseline. With 2000 paths the standard error of a 5% rate is about 0.5 points. The decrease side's share rises by at most 0.65 percentage points when c_down is lowered, probably because its larger bets react more to errors in the estimated baseline.

**Results [REAL].** Decrease and increase alarms per coin, and the share confirmed by the next day. The share is computed over the alarms with more than 720 observed returns in the next 1440 minutes (an alarm near the end of the sample or just before a gap in the data may have fewer), so its denominator is given:

| Coin | Decrease alarms, c_down 3 / 2 / 1.5 | Confirmed decreases | Increase alarms, c_down 3 / 2 / 1.5 | Confirmed increases |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | 55 / 50 / 47 | 46 of 54 (85%) / 45 of 50 (90%) / 44 of 47 (94%) | 72 / 76 / 75 | 57 of 72 (79%) / 59 of 76 (78%) / 59 of 75 (79%) |
| ETH | 46 / 43 / 40 | 41 of 46 (89%) / 39 of 43 (91%) / 37 of 40 (93%) | 76 / 80 / 80 | 60 of 76 (79%) / 63 of 80 (79%) / 63 of 80 (79%) |
| XRP | 58 / 58 / 54 | 52 of 58 (90%) / 49 of 58 (84%) / 47 of 54 (87%) | 71 / 69 / 70 | 59 of 70 (84%) / 55 of 69 (80%) / 56 of 70 (80%) |
| SOL | 46 / 46 / 39 | 43 of 46 (93%) / 44 of 46 (96%) / 36 of 38 (95%) | 77 / 77 / 79 | 61 of 77 (79%) / 62 of 77 (81%) / 62 of 79 (78%) |
| DOGE | 53 / 49 / 42 | 45 of 53 (85%) / 44 of 49 (90%) / 39 of 42 (93%) | 73 / 77 / 81 | 55 of 72 (76%) / 61 of 76 (80%) / 60 of 81 (74%) |

On real data the tighter clip gives the same number or slightly fewer decrease alarms and, for four of five coins at c_down = 2, a higher confirmed share, but with 38 to 58 checked alarms per coin these differences are within sampling noise (a 95% Wilson interval for 46 of 54 runs from 73% to 92%). Increase alarms are unaffected, as they should be. The coins have few ties (1.0% to 4.3% of the deseasonalised returns are zero). The monitor still spends about two thirds of the time calibrating, whatever c_down.

**Conclusion.** c_down = 2 is faster than c = 3 in all nine cells of the three continuous laws and in all six cells with ticks of 0.25 and 0.75 sd, and neutral to slightly positive on the five coins, which have few ties. With rounded prices the result depends on the tick size and can reverse for small falls: at a tick of 0.5 sd, c_down = 2 is 12% slower for a 20% fall. c_down = 1.5 is no better than c_down = 2 for a 20% fall except under Student t4 data, and is much slower at the tick of 0.5 sd. The guarantee of the split holds with a known baseline or with `baseline="cs"`; the plug-in runs above have no guarantee, with or without the split. We kept c_down = c as the package default so that every earlier experiment stays reproducible. We recommend `c_down=2` for new runs on data with few ties. On data with a coarse tick, where zero returns are common, compare c_down = 2 with c = 3 at that tick first, for example by a simulation like this one.

## E12. Event study: do crypto alarms line up with scheduled US macro news?

Script `experiments/e12_crypto_events.py`, outputs `results/e12_*.csv`, figure `results/figures/e12_event_profiles.png`. All results **[REAL]**.

**Headline numbers [REAL].** Robust monitor (band 0.25), number of releases followed by an "up" alarm (a detected rise in volatility) at most 1 hour and at most 6 hours after the release. The *matched control rate* is the share of ordinary days with an up alarm in the same window, where each release is compared only with days of the same weekday at the same US Eastern clock time, averaged over the releases. p is the one-sided stratified permutation test for the 6-hour window, which was fixed in advance; the 1-hour window was added after review round 2a and is secondary. Sources: `e12_delay.csv` and `e12_tests.csv`.

| Design | Releases | | BTC | ETH | SOL |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Streaming (primary) | FOMC, 16 | flagged within 1 hour | 9 | 6 | 8 |
| | | flagged within 6 hours | 9 | 8 | 9 |
| | | matched control rate, 1 hour / 6 hours | 2% / 14% | 2% / 11% | 2% / 17% |
| | | p, 6 hours | 0.0001 (Holm 0.0002) | 0.0002 | 0.0005 |
| | CPI, 22 | flagged within 1 hour | 2 | 5 | 8 |
| | | flagged within 6 hours | 5 | 7 | 9 |
| | | matched control rate, 1 hour / 6 hours | 3% / 12% | 2% / 9% | 1% / 8% |
| | | p, 6 hours | 0.11 (Holm 0.11) | 0.003 | 0.00004 |
| Fresh calibration (secondary) | FOMC, 16 | flagged within 1 hour | 14 | 13 | 11 |
| | | flagged within 6 hours | 14 | 14 | 15 |
| | | matched control rate, 1 hour / 6 hours | 2% / 29% | 8% / 32% | 5% / 32% |
| | | p, 6 hours | 0.000003 | 0.00001 | 0.0000006 |
| | CPI, 22 | flagged within 1 hour | 8 | 11 | 11 |
| | | flagged within 6 hours | 13 | 16 | 14 |
| | | matched control rate, 1 hour / 6 hours | 5% / 23% | 4% / 28% | 5% / 23% |
| | | p, 6 hours | 0.0004 | 0.00002 | 0.00006 |

The streaming monitor was monitoring (not recalibrating after an earlier alarm) at 9, 8 and 9 of the 16 FOMC statements. It flagged every one of those within 6 hours (9 of 9, 8 of 8, 9 of 9) and most of them within 1 hour (9 of 9, 6 of 8, 8 of 9). For CPI it was monitoring at 9, 8 and 12 of 22 releases and flagged 4, 6 and 9 of them within 6 hours. In the primary family (BTC, streaming, Holm), FOMC passes and CPI does not. The 1-hour p-values are below 0.001 in every cell except BTC CPI streaming (0.12). A sentence that can be quoted: "The streaming monitor flagged 8 to 9 of 16 FOMC statements within six hours, every statement at which it was monitoring, against 11% to 17% of matched control times; a monitor calibrated on the day before each statement flagged 14 to 15 of 16 within six hours (11 to 14 within one hour), against about 30% (2% to 8% within one hour) of matched control times."

**Question.** Scheduled US macro releases are known to move crypto volatility. If the monitor is doing its job, an "up" alarm (volatility increase) should be much more likely in the hours after a release than at the same time of day on ordinary days, it should come after the release rather than before it, and it should not simply be the one big minute at the release. Four questions: (a) is an up alarm more likely in the 6 hours after a release than in matched control windows; (b) how many minutes after the release does the first up alarm come, and does the monitor alarm before the release; (c) do "down" alarms (volatility normalising) follow in the next 1 to 2 days; (d) does the Gaussian likelihood-ratio benchmark alarm around releases for the wrong reason, that is one jump rather than a regime change.

**Events [REAL].** `data/events/us_macro_events.csv`: the 16 FOMC rate decisions of 2024 and 2025 (statement released at 14:00 US Eastern, second day of each scheduled meeting) and the 23 US CPI releases of 2024 and 2025 (08:30 US Eastern). Every date was checked by web search on 2026-11-02 against the Federal Reserve meeting calendar and the BLS release schedule or the archived BLS news release, and the URL is in the file (the official hosts could not be fetched directly from this environment, so verification used search results that index the official pages; one CPI date, 11 June 2025, rests on the BLS schedule listing only, the other 38 on an individual official page). No date was left out for lack of verification. The late-2025 federal shutdown (1 October to 12 November 2025) changed the CPI calendar and the file records what happened, with sources: the September 2025 CPI was moved from 15 to 24 October 2025 (a Friday), the October 2025 CPI, due on 13 November 2025, was cancelled (BLS could not collect October data), and the November 2025 CPI was moved from 10 to 18 December 2025. The December 2025 CPI kept its date, 13 January 2026, which is outside the sample. Eastern times were converted to UTC with the IANA time zone database, so the switch between EST (UTC-5) and EDT (UTC-4) on 10 March 2024, 3 November 2024, 9 March 2025 and 2 November 2025 is handled by the library; the script recomputes the UTC column and stops if the file disagrees. 15 of the 16 FOMC statements fall on a Wednesday (7 November 2024 is a Thursday, after the US election); the 22 CPI releases used fall on Tuesdays (5), Wednesdays (11), Thursdays (5) and one Friday. The first CPI release of 2024 (11 January) falls inside the 20-day warm-up of the intraday profile (next paragraph) and is excluded (`e12_events_excluded.csv`), so **38 events are used: 16 FOMC and 22 CPI**.

**Data [REAL].** Binance spot one-minute bars for BTCUSDT, ETHUSDT and SOLUSDT, 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2025 (no missing minutes in the mirror). Returns are divided by the predictable intraday profile (`intraday_scale`, 20-day rolling median of |r| per minute of day, past days only; returns are passed with their NaN, never filled with zeros). The first 20 days warm up the profile and the monitored stream runs from 21 January 2024 to 31 December 2025 (711 days, 1,023,840 minutes per coin).

**Method.** Settings frozen from E5c, not tuned here: A = 28,800, each side alarming at 2A (together at most a 5% chance of any false alarm per day under the null), c = 3, calibration 1440 minutes, null band 0.25. Benchmark: the Gaussian likelihood-ratio monitor (band 0, as in E5c), which does not truncate returns. The band alone changes how often a monitor alarms, so for a like-for-like comparison with the benchmark the robust monitor was also run with band 0 (added after review round 2a; secondary). Two designs:

* *Streaming*: the monitor runs over the whole stream exactly as in E5c and E6 (calibrate 1440 minutes, monitor, alarm, recalibrate). This is what a user of the monitor would have seen.
* *Fresh calibration* (added in iteration 2, see `docs/iterations/EV1.md`, after the streaming run showed that the monitor was still recalibrating after an earlier alarm at about half of the releases, 44% to 64% by coin and release type): for every release and every control time a new monitor is calibrated on the 1440 minutes before that time and then monitors the next 48 hours; for the pre-release window a monitor calibrated on the 1440 minutes ending 6 hours before the release monitors those 6 hours. Both detectors are awake at every anchor, so this design measures what the detector can do, not where the stream left it.

*Control windows*: for each event, every day in the monitored period with the same weekday, at the same US Eastern clock time, at least 2 days away from any event day: 65 to 94 control windows per event, 134 distinct ones for the FOMC statements and 299 for the CPI releases. Because weekday and clock time match, an event and its controls also agree on whether a window reaches into the weekend: the 6-to-48-hour window of a Thursday or Friday anchor does, that of a Tuesday or Wednesday anchor does not (the script checks this for every event, `e12_events_checked.csv`). Outcomes per window: an up alarm within [0, 6 h) of the anchor, an up alarm at most 60 minutes after the anchor, an up alarm within [-6 h, 0), a down alarm within [6 h, 48 h), any alarm within 6 hours.

*Matched control rate*: for each event, the share of its own control windows with the outcome, averaged over the events. Each weekday therefore counts as often as it has events. Earlier versions of this section printed the rate over the union of all events' control windows, and a pooled Fisher test on it. That union gave the Thursday windows half the weight for FOMC (65 Wednesdays and 69 Thursdays, for 15 Wednesday statements and one Thursday statement) and gave Thursdays and Fridays 163 of the 299 CPI windows (for 6 of 22 releases). It matters for the down-alarm outcome (Q12c), because a 6-to-48-hour window that starts on a Thursday or Friday runs into the weekend. The union rates and the pooled Fisher test are superseded; they remain in `e12_tests.csv` only in columns ending in `_superseded`.

*Test*: a stratified permutation test, computed exactly. Within each event's stratum (its window plus its matched control windows) the event label is exchangeable under the null, so the number of event windows with an alarm is a sum of independent Bernoulli draws with p_i = (windows with an alarm in stratum i) / (windows in stratum i); the one-sided p-value is P(T >= observed). This test compares each event only with its own matched controls, so the weekday mix of the union never entered it; the rerun gives the same p-values as before to the last digit. Cross-check (`p_stratified_fisher`): an exact stratified Fisher test, which is the exact form of the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, with one stratum per weekday and clock time; the events of a stratum share its control windows, and strata share none. *Multiple comparisons*: the primary family, fixed before the first run, is {FOMC, CPI} x {up alarm within 6 hours} on BTC with the robust detector in the streaming design, Holm-corrected at 5%. ETH and SOL are replications with raw p-values (the three coins move together, so they are not three independent tests). Everything else (the Gaussian benchmark, the band-0 robust monitor, the fresh-calibration design, the 1-hour, pre-release and down-alarm outcomes) is secondary and reported raw; a Holm correction over the six robust "up within 6 hours" tests (3 coins x 2 types) is also given within each design (`e12_tests.csv`, column `p_holm_six_coins_types`).

**Q12a. Up alarm within 6 hours of the release (robust detector).** Event rate against the matched control rate; p from the stratified permutation test.

| Coin | Design | FOMC: events with alarm | matched control rate | p | CPI: events with alarm | matched control rate | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | streaming (primary) | 9 / 16 (56%) | 14% | 0.0001 (Holm 0.0002) | 5 / 22 (23%) | 12% | 0.11 (Holm 0.11) |
| ETH | streaming | 8 / 16 (50%) | 11% | 0.0002 | 7 / 22 (32%) | 9% | 0.003 |
| SOL | streaming | 9 / 16 (56%) | 17% | 0.0005 | 9 / 22 (41%) | 8% | 0.00004 |
| BTC | fresh calibration | 14 / 16 (88%) | 29% | 0.000003 | 13 / 22 (59%) | 23% | 0.0004 |
| ETH | fresh calibration | 14 / 16 (88%) | 32% | 0.00001 | 16 / 22 (73%) | 28% | 0.00002 |
| SOL | fresh calibration | 15 / 16 (94%) | 32% | 0.0000006 | 14 / 22 (64%) | 23% | 0.00006 |

Holm over the six robust tests: streaming 0.0006, 0.0007, 0.001 (FOMC) and 0.11, 0.006, 0.0002 (CPI); fresh calibration all at most 0.0004. The exact stratified Fisher test agrees (at most 0.007 in every cell except BTC CPI streaming, 0.13). For this outcome the matched control rates are close to the superseded union rates (at most 4.2 points apart), so the conclusions of Q12a do not change. Why the streaming rates are lower: the streaming robust monitor spends about 70% of the time (67% to 70% by coin) recalibrating after its own alarms (0.7 alarms per day, each followed by a 1440-minute calibration; `e12_monitor_summary.csv`), and it was in monitoring mode at only 9 of 16 FOMC and 9 of 22 CPI releases on BTC (8/16 and 8/22 on ETH, 9/16 and 12/22 on SOL), against 33% to 43% of matched control windows. Restricted to releases at which it was awake, it alarmed within 6 hours at 9 of 9 FOMC statements on BTC (matched controls 26%, p = 0.00001), 8 of 8 on ETH (29%, p = 0.0001) and 9 of 9 on SOL (39%, p = 0.0004), and at 4 of 9 (BTC, p = 0.27), 6 of 8 (ETH, p = 0.005) and 9 of 12 (SOL, p = 0.0001) CPI releases (`sample = monitoring at start`).

The streaming Gaussian monitor is in monitoring mode only 8% to 10% of the time (0.9 alarms per day), so it was awake at 0 to 3 of the releases per coin and its event rates say little; the same holds for the streaming robust monitor at band 0 (monitoring 15% to 17% of the time, 0.8 alarms per day; rows in `e12_tests.csv`). With a fresh calibration the Gaussian monitor alarms at almost every release, but also in 62% to 76% of the matched control windows: an ordinary 6-hour window usually contains a return large enough to trip it. Event rate divided by matched control rate, fresh calibration:

* Gaussian LR (band 0): 1.4 to 1.6 for FOMC, 1.3 to 1.5 for CPI;
* robust, band 0.25 (the frozen setting): 2.7 to 3.0 for FOMC, 2.5 to 2.8 for CPI;
* robust, band 0 (same band as the Gaussian monitor): 1.7 to 2.4 for FOMC, 1.8 to 2.0 for CPI.

So the earlier comparison of the frozen settings mixed two things. Averaged over the six cells, the matched control rate is 28% for the robust monitor at band 0.25, 42% at band 0 and 69% for the Gaussian monitor: about a third of the gap comes from the band and two thirds from the detector itself (no truncation in the Gaussian monitor, and a different betting rule). At the same band the robust monitor still alarms in fewer control windows and has the higher ratio in all six cells. Within the first hour the Gaussian monitor alarms in 20% to 34% of matched control windows, the robust monitor in 6% to 16% at band 0 and 2% to 8% at band 0.25 (`e12_delay.csv`).

**Q12b. Delay and anticipation (fresh calibration, robust detector).** Minutes from the release to the first up alarm, among events with an alarm within 6 hours. Control columns are matched control rates.

| Coin | Type | with alarm | median delay (IQR) | min to max | within 30 min | within 60 min | control windows, within 60 min | up alarm in the 6 h before (events) | same, control windows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | FOMC | 14 / 16 | 33 (16 to 40) | 14 to 45 | 6 | 14 | 2% | 1 / 16 | 20% |
| BTC | CPI | 13 / 22 | 32 (22 to 104) | 14 to 356 | 6 | 8 | 5% | 2 / 22 | 22% |
| ETH | FOMC | 14 / 16 | 34 (18 to 43) | 15 to 67 | 6 | 13 | 8% | 3 / 16 | 32% |
| ETH | CPI | 16 / 22 | 23 (20 to 98) | 10 to 352 | 9 | 11 | 4% | 2 / 22 | 20% |
| SOL | FOMC | 15 / 16 | 32 (19 to 57) | 14 to 145 | 7 | 11 | 5% | 3 / 16 | 20% |
| SOL | CPI | 14 / 22 | 28 (19 to 36) | 15 to 282 | 7 | 11 | 5% | 2 / 22 | 16% |

The Gaussian LR monitor (fresh calibration) has a median delay of 0 to 2 minutes (BTC FOMC: 2, IQR 0 to 3; CPI: 0, IQR 0 to 0; 15 of 15 FOMC and 20 of 21 CPI alarms within 30 minutes): the first minute after the release is enough for it. The robust monitor at band 0 is faster than at band 0.25 (median 18 to 22 minutes, minimum 8 to 11) but, like it, never alarms in the first minutes, so the speed of the Gaussian monitor comes from the missing truncation, not from the band. In the streaming design the robust delays are shorter (BTC FOMC median 15 minutes, IQR 12 to 39; SOL 10; ETH 33) because a Shiryaev-Roberts statistic that has been running for hours starts the release with a head start (it adds 1 per step under the null), whereas a fresh monitor starts at 0.

Alarms *before* the release (robust detector): 6% to 19% of events had an up alarm in the 6 hours before the release, against 16% to 32% of matched control windows (fresh design); in the streaming design 0 to 1 of 16 FOMC and 0 to 1 of 22 CPI releases per coin, against 5% to 12% of matched control windows. So there is no sign of more alarms before releases. Event days had fewer pre-release alarms than their matched control days in all twelve cells (3 coins x 2 release types x 2 designs), but no single cell's one-sided test for "fewer" reaches p = 0.10 (p = 0.11 to 0.65, column `p_stratified_permutation_fewer`, a test added after the review), and the cells are not independent, so we do not claim that the hours before a release are quieter than usual. Of the 13 pre-release up alarms across the three coins (fresh design), the three on 12 June 2024 came 312 to 320 minutes before the FOMC statement, which is the CPI release of that morning, and only two came within 10 minutes of the release (ETH, 10 December 2025, 6 minutes before; SOL, 11 September 2025, 4 minutes before). The Gaussian LR monitor alarms in 41% to 75% of the pre-release windows and in 52% to 74% of the matched control windows, again a base rate rather than anticipation.

**Q12c. Down alarms in the next 1 to 2 days (window 6 to 48 hours after the anchor, robust detector, fresh calibration).** Control columns are matched control rates.

| Coin | Type | events with a down alarm | control windows | p (one-sided, more on event days) | among events with an up alarm within 6 h: later down alarm | same for control windows with an up alarm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTC | FOMC | 10 / 16 (63%) | 49% | 0.20 | 8 / 14 (57%) | 45% |
| BTC | CPI | 16 / 22 (73%) | 64% | 0.26 | 8 / 13 (62%) | 59% |
| ETH | FOMC | 9 / 16 (56%) | 43% | 0.21 | 7 / 14 (50%) | 42% |
| ETH | CPI | 9 / 22 (41%) | 62% | 0.99 | 6 / 16 (38%) | 65% |
| SOL | FOMC | 9 / 16 (56%) | 42% | 0.17 | 8 / 15 (53%) | 38% |
| SOL | CPI | 13 / 22 (59%) | 55% | 0.44 | 9 / 14 (64%) | 54% |

Not clearly. After FOMC statements a down alarm in the following 6 to 48 hours is more common than on matched control days in all three coins and in both designs, by 13 to 27 percentage points: with a fresh calibration 63%, 56% and 56% against 49%, 43% and 42% (p = 0.20, 0.21, 0.17), in the streaming design 69%, 63% and 69% against 45%, 43% and 41% (p = 0.04, 0.09, 0.02). These are secondary, uncorrected tests; a Holm correction over the six down-alarm tests of the streaming design (3 coins x 2 release types) leaves none below 0.15. Among the releases at which the streaming monitor was awake the excess is smaller and far from significant (5/9, 4/8 and 4/9 against 48%, 38% and 39%; p = 0.37 to 0.50). After CPI releases the differences are small and go both ways (fresh: 73%, 41%, 59% against 64%, 62%, 55%; streaming: 64%, 59%, 59% against 55%, 54%, 53%; p = 0.26 to 0.99 for "more"; on ETH with a fresh calibration there are fewer, one-sided p for "fewer" 0.03, not a planned test). Conditional on an up alarm, a later down alarm is somewhat more common after FOMC statements than in control windows with an up alarm (57%, 50%, 53% against 45%, 42%, 38%), not after CPI releases, and the numbers are too small to call.

The earlier version of this answer said that a down alarm is about as common after a release as in control windows "because the base rate is high". That was largely an artefact of comparing with control days of the wrong weekday: a window that starts on a Thursday or Friday runs into the weekend, when crypto volatility falls, and contains a down alarm in 70% to 94% of cases (by coin, weekday and design), against 38% to 57% for windows starting on a Tuesday or Wednesday (BTC, fresh calibration: 94% of Thursday 14:00 windows against 46% of Wednesday 14:00 windows). Matched on weekday, the FOMC base rate is 41% to 49%, not the 63% to 71% of the superseded union. The base rate is still substantial (0.3 down alarms per day), which limits the size of any excess. When a down alarm does follow, its median time is 32 to 35 hours after the release, which is as early as the protocol allows (the up alarm at about 30 minutes is followed by a 1440-minute recalibration that absorbs the burst, and the decrease side then needs a few hundred quiet minutes, E4).

**Q12d, second part. Is the Gaussian alarm driven by one jump?** For the first up alarm within 6 hours of an anchor (fresh calibration): the largest |deseasonalised return| in the 5 minutes up to the alarm in units of the baseline scale (the robust monitor clips at 3), the robust volatility of the next 1440 minutes relative to the baseline (1 = no persistent change), and the share of alarms that had both a return above 3 scale units and no persistent increase ("jump only"). The "controls" rows pool the control windows of both release types (433 per coin); they describe ordinary alarms and are not used in any test.

| Coin | Detector | windows | n alarms | median largest recent return (scale units) | share above 5 | median post / baseline | share post > 1 | share jump only |

| BTC | robust | controls | 124 | 4.0 | 27% | 1.08 | 60% | 34% |
