| BTC | robust, band 0 | controls | 181 | 3.7 | 21% | 1.06 | 57% | 30% |
| BTC | Gaussian LR | releases | 36 | 8.1 | 78% | 1.11 | 67% | 33% |
| BTC | Gaussian LR | controls | 314 | 4.5 | 39% | 0.97 | 47% | 45% |
| ETH | robust | releases | 30 | 4.4 | 33% | 1.05 | 53% | 40% |
| ETH | robust | controls | 122 | 4.1 | 31% | 1.11 | 68% | 25% |
| ETH | robust, band 0 | releases | 31 | 3.9 | 29% | 1.08 | 58% | 35% |
| ETH | robust, band 0 | controls | 194 | 3.7 | 26% | 1.06 | 60% | 24% |
| ETH | Gaussian LR | releases | 37 | 8.3 | 78% | 1.05 | 57% | 41% |
| ETH | Gaussian LR | controls | 322 | 4.8 | 42% | 0.99 | 48% | 48% |
| SOL | robust | releases | 29 | 3.9 | 34% | 1.06 | 62% | 34% |
| SOL | robust | controls | 115 | 3.9 | 30% | 1.08 | 62% | 28% |
| SOL | robust, band 0 | releases | 33 | 3.9 | 24% | 1.05 | 61% | 24% |
| SOL | robust, band 0 | controls | 180 | 3.6 | 21% | 1.05 | 59% | 33% |
| SOL | Gaussian LR | releases | 37 | 8.9 | 84% | 1.05 | 68% | 30% |
| SOL | Gaussian LR | controls | 291 | 4.2 | 33% | 1.02 | 53% | 39% |

The Gaussian alarm at a release sits on a return of 8 to 9 scale units (median; above 5 in 78% to 84% of cases) and comes in the first minute or two: a single return of 8 standard deviations multiplies its statistic by more than 10^9, far above the alarm level of 57,600, so one minute decides. The robust detector cannot be moved by one minute: returns are clipped at 3 scale units, so one minute multiplies its statistic by at most about 4 (about 5 at band 0). It needs a run of elevated minutes, which is why its minimum delay with a fresh calibration is 14 minutes (10 on ETH) at band 0.25 and 8 to 11 minutes at band 0, and why the median largest recent return of its alarms at releases is 3.7 to 4.4 scale units at either band. These two facts, the size of the triggering return and the delay, are what support reading a robust alarm at a release as a short burst of volatility rather than a single jump.

The "jump only" column does not support that reading on its own. At releases the robust shares (19%, 40%, 34% at band 0.25; 19%, 35%, 24% at band 0) are not clearly below the Gaussian shares (33%, 41%, 30%). What the column can show: how often an alarm sat on a return above 3 scale units and was not followed by higher volatility over the next day. What it cannot show: whether that return caused the alarm (for the robust detector it cannot have done so alone), or whether volatility stayed high for a few hours after the alarm, because it compares the next full 1440 minutes with the baseline, and a release burst of 1 to 3 hours that is over by the evening counts as "no persistent increase". With 27 to 37 alarms per cell, differences of 10 points are also within noise. In control windows, the Gaussian alarms are a coin flip on persistence (47% to 53% followed by higher volatility, median post / baseline 0.97 to 1.02), against 57% to 60% for the robust detector at band 0 and 60% to 68% at band 0.25: the false alarms that E4 predicted for untruncated detectors on heavy-tailed data. Over all streaming up alarms, the robust detector's median post / baseline is 1.30, 1.22 and 1.22 (BTC, ETH, SOL; 76% to 80% above 1), and 1.25, 1.16 and 1.15 at band 0 (74% to 80%), against 1.12, 1.09 and 1.08 for the Gaussian monitor (64% to 66%), as in E5c and E6.

**What the releases do to volatility.** Median over events of the mean |deseasonalised return| in the first hour after the release divided by the mean over the 6 hours before: FOMC 2.5 (BTC), 2.5 (ETH), 2.3 (SOL); CPI 2.0, 2.0, 2.1. Over the whole 6-hour window: FOMC 1.8, 1.6, 1.5; CPI 1.4, 1.3, 1.3. The figure (`e12_event_profiles.png`) shows the average profile from 6 hours before to 12 hours after each release type and coin, with the control average and the alarm times: a CPI release is a spike that is back to normal within about 2 hours, an FOMC statement starts a burst that lasts 2 to 3 hours (the press conference starts half an hour after the statement), and the robust alarms cluster 15 to 60 minutes after the release. The control curve in the figure averages all control windows of a release type with equal weight (it is descriptive and enters no rate or test).

**Events the robust detector missed (fresh calibration, no up alarm within 6 hours on any of the three coins):** the FOMC statement of 7 November 2024 (first-hour |return| 1.7 to 2.0 times the pre-release level, a burst too short for the detector) and the CPI releases of 11 December 2024, 13 May 2025, 15 July 2025 and 24 October 2025 (the rescheduled September CPI, released during the shutdown; first-hour ratio 1.8 to 2.5). The FOMC statement of 20 March 2024 was caught only on SOL (67 minutes). Per-event rows are in `e12_event_windows.csv`.

**Reading.**
* Yes, the alarms line up with the news. In the primary streaming design the robust monitor flagged 9, 8 and 9 of the 16 FOMC statements within 6 hours (BTC, ETH, SOL), against 11% to 17% of matched control windows. These are exactly the statements at which it was monitoring rather than recalibrating (9 of 9, 8 of 8, 9 of 9), and it flagged most of them within the first hour (9 of 9, 6 of 8, 8 of 9). With a fresh calibration before every statement it flagged 14, 14 and 15 of 16 within 6 hours and 14, 13 and 11 within the first hour, against 29% to 32% (6 hours) and 2% to 8% (1 hour) of matched control windows; within 6 hours that is 2.7 to 3.0 times the rate at the same clock time on the same weekday of ordinary weeks. CPI releases are caught in 59% to 73% of cases within 6 hours (fresh calibration), 2.5 to 2.8 times the matched control rate; their volatility spike is shorter, and the 08:30 ET control windows contain other scheduled releases (see caveats), which works against the contrast.
* The primary family (streaming design, BTC): FOMC passes Holm (p = 0.0002); CPI does not (p = 0.11), because the streaming monitor was asleep at 13 of the 22 CPI releases. ETH and SOL replicate the FOMC result and both replicate CPI (p = 0.003 and 0.00004); with a fresh calibration all six tests are at p <= 0.0004 after Holm.
* The alarms come after the release, not before: median 23 to 34 minutes with a fresh calibration (10 to 33 minutes for a running monitor at FOMC statements), never earlier than 14 minutes with a fresh calibration on BTC and SOL (10 on ETH). There is no sign of more alarms in the hours before a release.
* Down alarms within two days: after FOMC statements they are 13 to 27 points more common than on matched control days, in every coin and both designs, but no test is significant after correction (fresh calibration p = 0.17 to 0.21; streaming p = 0.02 to 0.09 raw, Holm at least 0.15). After CPI releases there is no clear excess. The earlier explanation, that a high base rate hides any effect, came from comparing with control days of the wrong weekday. The protocol itself limits this question: the recalibration after the up alarm absorbs the burst.
* The Gaussian benchmark "detects" releases by reacting to the first big minute (median delay 0 to 2 minutes, on a return of 8 to 9 scale units), and with a fresh calibration it also alarms in 62% to 76% of ordinary 6-hour windows. Compared like for like, both at band 0, the robust monitor alarms in 39% to 51% of those windows, needs at least 8 minutes, and has a higher event-to-control ratio in every cell (1.7 to 2.4 against 1.3 to 1.6). About a third of the difference between the frozen settings comes from the band and two thirds from the detector. The Gaussian monitor's detection is detection for the wrong reason: the same mechanism gives its false alarms in E4 and E6.
* A practical finding about the protocol, not about the news: a monitor that recalibrates for a full day after every alarm is blind about 70% of the time when alarms come every 1.4 days. A shorter recalibration, or a warm restart from the last baseline, would be the first thing to change for live use. E14 (Q14g) reruns this design with monitors that have no blind period and a proof: they watch all 114 releases instead of 55, and the BTC CPI cell gives p = 0.003 and 0.0003 instead of 0.11. That rerun was designed after seeing these results, so it is a check of the protocol, not a new pre-registered test.

**Caveats.**
* Small numbers of events: 16 FOMC statements and 22 CPI releases. Rates per coin have Wilson 95% intervals of roughly plus or minus 20 points (`e12_tests.csv`), and the three coins are not independent replications.
* Overlapping windows: the CPI release and the FOMC statement of 12 June 2024 are 5.5 hours apart, so the FOMC fresh baseline for that day includes the CPI spike and the CPI 6-hour window contains the statement; the pre-release FOMC alarms of that day are the CPI. Events of the same type are at least four weeks apart, so event windows do not overlap each other; control windows of the same weekday are shared by all events of that type, which the stratified permutation test allows for by construction but which makes its strata dependent through their shared controls. The exact stratified Fisher test, with one stratum per weekday and clock time, has no shared controls and agrees.
* "Non-event" control windows are only free of FOMC and CPI releases. Other scheduled US releases (weekly jobless claims every Thursday at 08:30 ET, producer prices, payrolls, retail sales) and crypto-specific events fall inside some control windows, which raises the control rate and makes the CPI contrast conservative. These dates were not verified here, so they were not excluded.
* The 2025 calendar disruptions: one CPI release moved by 9 days and delivered on a Friday (24 October 2025; no alarm on any coin), one cancelled (October 2025 data), one moved by 8 days (18 December 2025; alarms at 30, 20 and 238 minutes). The CPI list is therefore 22 releases rather than 24, and one of them is on an unusual weekday.
* Verification used web search results that index the official Federal Reserve and BLS pages rather than a direct fetch of those pages (blocked in this environment).
* Settings were chosen in E5c on Bitstamp BTC, July to December 2025, which overlaps the last six months of this sample; the fresh-calibration design was added after seeing the streaming results (it is marked secondary for that reason). The band-0 robust monitor, the 1-hour outcome, the matched control rates, the stratified Fisher test and the test for fewer pre-release alarms were added after review round 2a, with the results already known; they are secondary.
* The Gaussian monitor runs with band 0 and the robust monitor with band 0.25, as in E5c. The like-for-like comparison uses the robust monitor at band 0; the remaining difference still mixes truncation with the different betting rule of the two detectors.
* Binance data come from a third-party mirror (checked for gaps and duplicates, none found).

**Revision after review round 2a.** (1) The counts "within the hour" were the 6-hour counts; the 1-hour counts are now given separately (streaming 9/9, 6/8, 8/9 among the FOMC statements at which the monitor was awake; fresh calibration 14, 13 and 11 of 16). (2) Control rates are now matched on weekday and clock time, and the pooled Fisher test is replaced by an exact stratified one; the old union rates (for example 71%, 66%, 65% for FOMC down alarms) are superseded, and with them the Q12c explanation "because the base rate is high". The stratified permutation p-values are unchanged. (3) The Gaussian against robust comparison is now also made at equal band. (4) Two sentences that the data did not support were replaced ("the pre-release hours are quieter than usual" and the reliance on the "jump only" column). Three rounding errors were corrected (BTC FOMC down-alarm p 0.20, not 0.21; SOL jump-only and above-5 shares at releases 34%, not 35%; BTC Gaussian control alarms followed by higher volatility 47%, not 48%), and the share of releases at which the streaming monitor was recalibrating is 44% to 64%, not 40% to 60%.

## E13. Benchmarks against strong published competitors

Script `experiments/e13_benchmarks.py`; code `src/avmonitor/competitors.py` (tests in `tests/test_competitors.py`); outputs `results/e13*.csv` and `results/figures/e13_*.png`. Seeds are fixed in the script. Every tuning constant was fixed before the reported runs (a Gaussian pilot with its own seed, `docs/iterations/E13.md`, iteration 2). Three methods, marked below as our modifications or as the CS baseline, were added after the first runs (the studentised BJV and the CS-baseline e-detector in iteration 3, BOCPD on truncated returns in iteration 5); no constant was tuned on the reported runs. Review round 3 added longer competitor windows (iterations 9 and 10): BJV with windows of 250 and 500 returns on simulated data, and on real data BJV with 480 and 1440 minutes and BOCPD with 720 and 1440 minutes (one session, 375 bars, for both on Nifty). These lengths were fixed before those runs, as simple fractions of the window or the day, and nothing else was changed.

**Question.** Until now the e-detector was compared only with weak or non-robust benchmarks (a Gaussian likelihood ratio detector, Page's CUSUM, a repeated z-test, raw r²), and the independent review (point M3) showed that a naive trailing-window rule matches its real-data validation score. How does it compare with the two strongest relevant published methods: the nonparametric volatility jump test of Bibinger, Jirak and Vetter (2017), the reference *offline* (after-the-fact) method for this question in high-frequency econometrics, and Bayesian online change-point detection (Adams and MacKay 2007), the reference *online* method in machine learning?

### The competitors and how they were made comparable

**BJV (adjacent-window volatility jump test).** For each candidate change point, compare the realised variance (mean squared return) of the k returns before it with that of the k returns after it, standardise the difference so that it is approximately standard normal when volatility does not jump, and take the maximum over the sample. Under no change, the maximum follows an extreme value (Gumbel) law, which gives the critical value. The jump-robust version drops returns larger than 4 times a local bipower scale (bipower variation, (π/2) mean |r_i||r_{i-1}|, is a variance estimate that a single price jump cannot inflate much), and the location of the maximum estimates the change point. Two versions: non-overlapping blocks (the paper's main statistic) and overlapping windows (the paper's second statistic, reported as more powerful). We also add a *studentised* version (our modification, not in the paper) that standardises with the sample variance of the squared returns instead of the Gaussian value 2σ⁴.

*Verification gap, stated plainly.* The paper text could not be opened from this environment (arxiv.org, its ar5iv mirror and the authors' university repository were blocked by the network policy). Web search verified the paper's metadata and its structure (rescaled differences of local spot volatility estimates on adjacent windows, a non-overlapping and an overlapping statistic, a Gumbel-type limit, k_n = 125 in its simulations), but not its exact normalisation or equation numbers. Our Gumbel constants come from standard extreme value theory for maxima of Gaussian sequences (Leadbetter, Lindgren and Rootzén 1983) and, for overlapping windows, from the moving-sum limit as coded in the CRAN package `mosum` (Eichinger and Kirch 2018). To make the conclusions independent of these constants, **every comparison below also uses critical values calibrated by simulation**. The implementation should be checked against the paper's equations before it is cited as "the BJV test".

**BOCPD.** Inside a regime, returns are N(0, σ²) with an inverse gamma prior on σ² (a conjugate prior, so the posterior and the predictive Student t density are exact). With a constant hazard H (the prior probability of a change at each step), Algorithm 1 of Adams and MacKay updates the posterior of the *run length* (time since the last change) exactly. We cap run lengths at 512. This is an approximation: runs of 511 steps or more share one bucket, which keeps the statistics of the heavier run. One unit test checks the recursion before the cap is reached; a second one, in which the cap binds, checks the merge rule and shows that the alarm statistic then departs from the exact recursion. Against the exact recursion in the E13 setting (`results/e13_bocpd_cap_check.csv`, one simulated path per case), the posterior probability of a short run differs by at most 0.0003 when nothing changes, and the first crossing of the alarm level is at the same step after a change of sd × 1.25 or × 0.8; later on that path the two differ by up to 0.56. So the first alarm in simulation is not affected in these checks, but on real data, where the filter runs on through many changes, BOCPD here is the capped approximation. We alarm when the posterior probability of a run shorter than w = 250 steps exceeds a threshold. Settings: α₀ = 2, prior mean of σ² from the calibration window, H = 1 / A (one change per 20 days a priori). We also run BOCPD on returns clipped at the e-detector's truncation level τ = 3 × scaled MAD ("BOCPD on truncated returns", our modification), to separate what truncation buys from what betting buys.

**Our method.** The two-sided robust e-detector of E4 (each side at level 2A, c = 3), in two versions that must be kept apart:
* the **plug-in e-detector**, the default: the baseline is estimated from the calibration window and then treated as known. Its false alarm bound is proved only for a known baseline. With an estimated baseline it has **no proved bound** (E14, Proposition A.6, shows that at a fixed calibration length no bound of the form C m / A holds for it), so all its false alarm rates below are measured, not guaranteed;
* the **CS-baseline e-detector**: the confidence-sequence baseline of E8 (δ = 0.01), whose false alarm bound (δ + m / A) is **proved** with an estimated baseline.

**Fair comparisons.**
* *Offline (Q13a).* A fixed window of 2000 steps, change (if any) at step 1000. BJV uses the whole window. BOCPD and the e-detector use the first 500 steps as a change-free calibration window and monitor the remaining 1500, so they get one piece of information BJV does not use: where a clean stretch is. Each method's statistic is its maximum over the window. Critical values are set to give exactly 5% rejections on 2000 clean Gaussian windows ("matched size"); we also report the nominal levels (Gumbel for BJV; A = 1500 / 0.05 for the plug-in e-detector, a level that would hold only with a known baseline; A = 1500 / 0.04 for the CS-baseline e-detector, so that its proved bound δ + m / A is 5%). Review round 3 adds the overlapping BJV statistic with k = 250 and k = 500 on exactly the same windows (`offline-long` in the script).
* *Online (Q13b, Q13c).* The E4 design: 2000 calibration steps, then monitoring; A = 7800 (a bound of 5% false alarms per 390-step "day", proved for the CS-baseline e-detector and for the plug-in only if its baseline were known). BJV becomes a rolling test: at each step, compare the last k = 120 returns with the 120 before them and alarm when |statistic| exceeds a threshold. BOCPD alarms on its posterior rule. The competitor thresholds are set so that their false alarm rate per 390-step day on 4000 clean Gaussian paths equals the plug-in e-detector's (1.55% on that calibration set). Neither competitor has an anytime guarantee, so their false alarm rates are measured, not assumed. We also report BJV with its nominal daily Gumbel level and BOCPD with the natural rule "probability above one half". The nominal level uses the MOSUM formula for a series of 390 + 2k - 1 returns, the returns that 390 window positions span (the first runs used 390 by mistake; review round 3, m16, and the rows were rerun). On clean Gaussian data, review round 3 adds the rolling BJV with k = 250 and k = 500, matched in the same way (`online-long`).

All simulated results are [SYNTHETIC]. "Jumps": probability 0.005 per step, size N(0, 8²). "Student t5": unit-variance t innovations with 5 degrees of freedom. "Price noise": i.i.d. N(0, 0.5²) noise on log prices. "Ticks": returns rounded to 0.5 sd (about 20% zeros). "Slow SV": log-volatility AR(1) with sd 0.15 and half-life 390. "GARCH 0.99": GARCH(1,1), α = 0.05, β = 0.94. Under slow SV and GARCH the e-detector's null is false by design (E4c, E9c): volatility does move.

### Q13d. Real data [REAL]

**Set-up.** One-minute returns divided by a predictable intraday volatility profile (E6b for crypto, E7's session profile for Nifty). The e-detector uses its frozen real-data settings: crypto A = 28,800 per day, cal 1440, c = 3; Nifty A = 7500 per session, cal 750 (E7's primary). The competitors run continuously: BOCPD with a predictable prior (robust variance of the previous day) and H = 1 / A; BOCPD on returns clipped at 3 times the robust sd of the previous day; rolling BJV with k = 120 (truncated, Gaussian-normalised and studentised). After every alarm each method pauses for as long as the e-detector recalibrates (1440 or 750 steps). Gaussian-matched thresholds come from 2000 simulated Gaussian paths with the same day length, calibration length and A (`results/e13d_real_thresholds.csv`; the e-detector's simulated rate there is 3.95% per 1440-step day and 1.45% per 375-step session). Lag-one autocorrelation of the deseasonalised returns is -0.016 to 0.027 for BTC, ETH, XRP and SOL, 0.013 for Nifty and 0.132 for DOGE, so microstructure noise is small at one minute except for DOGE (coarse price ticks); this is why plain, not pre-averaged, realised variance is used.

**Validation.** As in E6e: after an up alarm, is the robust volatility of the next day (1440 minutes or 375 bars) above an EWMA forecast made with past data only; after a down alarm, is it below? At random times the next day is above the forecast 46.5% to 50.1% of the time and below it 49.9% to 53.5% (each coin, both half-years), and 50.3% and 49.7% for Nifty. "Rate-matched": each competitor's up and down thresholds are set, per series, so that it raises the same numbers of up and down alarms as the e-detector (this uses the real data, but not the outcome). p-values: two-proportion z-test against the e-detector, which treats every alarm as an independent trial. They are not: alarms of one method cluster in time (volatility clusters, and the five coins move together), and the methods often alarm on the same days. The section "Longer competitor windows" below adds a test that allows for both.

**What the outcome measures.** The outcome asks whether the next *day* stays beyond a *one-day* forecast. That is the time scale of the e-detector, whose baseline is calibrated on a window of 1440 minutes (750 bars for Nifty) before it starts monitoring, so its alarms mark shifts against a day-long reference level by construction. The first-run competitors compare much shorter stretches: rolling BJV two windows of 120 minutes, BOCPD runs shorter than 250 minutes. Their alarms flag changes over 2 to 4 hours, which can be real and still not last a day. The tables below therefore show how often alarms are followed by a day beyond the forecast *at these window lengths*; they do not by themselves show that the published methods are less precise. Longer windows are tried further down.

#### Longer competitor windows, a four-hour outcome and clustered tests (review round 3)

**Set-up.** Same data, same e-detector, same matching of up and down alarm counts per series (band 0.25 below; band 0 in `results/e13d_real_long_windows_pooled.csv`). Only the competitor windows were made longer, with lengths fixed before the run: BJV with k = 480 (a third of a day) and k = 1440 minutes (one day), computed with the returns before the monitored period so that it exists from the first possible alarm; BOCPD with short-run windows w = 720 (half a day) and w = 1440 (one day) and run-length caps of 2w; on Nifty k = w = 375 (one session; the first-run windows of 120 and 250 bars are already a third and two thirds of a session). Hazard, priors, clipping and the pause after each alarm are unchanged. The e-detector's alarms and the first-run Gaussian-matched BJV alarms were reproduced exactly (checked in the script). Every alarm is also scored on a **four-hour outcome**: is the robust volatility of the next 240 minutes (bars) above (up alarm) or below (down alarm) a forecast built in the same way at that scale (an EWMA with a half-life of 240 steps, rescaled by the median ratio over the previous 30 four-hour blocks)? At random times the next four hours are above that forecast 48.7% to 52.4% of the time for the coins and 53.3% for Nifty (`results/e13d_real_long_windows_*_random_4h.csv`).

**Tests.** "z-test" is the two-proportion test of the first run. "Week-clustered" replaces its standard error by a cluster-robust ("sandwich") one in which all alarms of the same calendar week, on any coin and of either method, may be dependent, and different weeks are taken as independent (`cluster_z` in the script; clustering by calendar day gives similar values and is in the CSV). Clustering can move a p-value either way: dependence within a method widens the standard error, but two methods that alarm in the same weeks have positively correlated outcomes, which narrows the standard error of their difference. A more conservative version that treats the two methods as independent samples, each clustered by week, is in the CSV as `p_week_clustered_unpaired`. The share is over the alarms whose outcome can be scored (a few alarms near the end of a period cannot).

* **First-run windows, with clustering.** The first-run comparisons hold with the clustered test: week-clustered p ≤ 0.006 in Jul to Dec 2025 and p ≤ 0.010 in Jan to Jun 2025, except the truncated BOCPD's held-out down alarms (p = 0.42). With the conservative unpaired version the p-values are larger, ≤ 0.043 and ≤ 0.035, except the held-out down alarms of rolling BJV (p = 0.062) and of the truncated BOCPD (p = 0.63).
* **Down alarms: day-long windows close the gap.** With windows of a day (BJV and studentised BJV with k = 1440, BOCPD on truncated returns with w = 720 or 1440), the competitors' down alarms are as informative as the e-detector's: 77.7% to 81.7% against 80.5% in Jul to Dec 2025 (p ≥ 0.45) and 69.3% to 73.7% against 69.7% held out (p ≥ 0.28); three of these are above the e-detector in the held-out half-year and one in the other. Plain BOCPD stays lower (59.5% to 69.9%).
* **Up alarms: the gap shrinks but stays.** No competitor configuration reaches the e-detector's up alarms in either half-year: the eight longer-window ones score 66.3% to 72.6% against 78.5%, and 69.3% to 75.7% against 82.0% held out. The best of them, picked after seeing the results (which favours the competitors), are about 6 points lower: BOCPD on truncated returns with w = 720, 72.6% (z-test p = 0.065, week-clustered 0.047, unpaired 0.21), and BJV with k = 480, 75.7% held out (p = 0.054, 0.028 and 0.19). So the remaining up-alarm advantage is borderline, not clear. Matched to band 0 (more alarms), the up-alarm gap to the best longer-window competitor is 5.6 and 3.7 points (p = 0.10 and 0.29), and on down alarms the best one equals the e-detector (68.2% against 68.3%; 66.6% against 66.3%).
* **At four hours the order changes.** On the four-hour outcome, the first-run (short-window) competitors do as well as the e-detector or better: 72.6% to 85.4% (up) and 69.1% to 74.4% (down) against 77.9% and 66.9% in Jul to Dec 2025, where BOCPD's up alarms are significantly higher (85.4%, p = 0.009), and 73.7% to 87.9% and 65.7% to 71.1% against 84.4% and 67.4% held out, where the only significant difference is a lower score for the studentised BJV's up alarms (73.7%, p = 0.001). The day-long BJV windows score near chance on this horizon (46.1% to 51.6%).
* **Nifty.** Longer windows do not help on Nifty: BJV with k = 375 scores lower than with k = 120 (68.4% and 62.3%, against 81.0% and 82.6% for the e-detector; down alarms p = 0.008), and BOCPD with w = 375 is not significantly different from the e-detector (p ≥ 0.07).
* **What this means.** Much of the first-run crypto gap was a matter of time scale: the outcome asks about the next day, the e-detector's own scale, and competitors with day-long windows match its down alarms. Its up alarms keep a borderline advantage of about 6 points, and at a four-hour scale the short-window competitors do at least as well. What the comparison does not take away is that the e-detector reaches its score without a window to choose, with settings frozen in advance; but on real data it runs with the plug-in baseline, which has no proved false alarm bound either.

Figure: `results/figures/e13_real_long_windows.png` (share by competitor window, with the e-detector as a horizontal line).

**Alarm rates at the Gaussian-matched thresholds.** Real volatility moves far more than the Gaussian null, so every method alarms much more often than its Gaussian rate (about 0.04 per day). Crypto, Jul to Dec 2025: e-detector 0.83 alarms per day (band 0) and 0.68 (band 0.25); BOCPD 0.95; BOCPD on truncated returns 0.91; rolling BJV 0.87 (0.825 at its nominal 5% per day, with the corrected critical value of m16; 0.83 before); studentised BJV 0.72. Nifty, per session: 0.38 and 0.30; 0.46; 0.41; 0.39 (0.37); 0.29. At these unmatched rates the competitors' forecast scores are 52.9% to 66.2% on crypto and 58.0% to 74.7% on Nifty (`results/e13d_real_pooled.csv`).

### Q13e. Cost per step

One series, 20,000 steps, Python and numpy on the shared 4-core machine (`results/e13e_cost.csv`; indicative): e-detector (`VolatilityMonitor.update`, two sides, 11 bets) 10.8 µs per step; BOCPD 300 µs (run-length cap 256) and 317 µs (cap 512), dominated by numpy call overhead on a few hundred run lengths; rolling BJV 211 µs per step if one truncated window pair is recomputed at each step, 27 µs per step vectorised over a whole series, 0.19 µs per step without truncation (running sums). The e-detector is the cheapest of the robust online methods by a factor of about 2.5 to 30; all are far below one minute per step.

### Reading

* **Where the competitors win.** On clean Gaussian data BOCPD detects large decreases two to three times faster than the plug-in e-detector (26 against 81 steps for a halving of the sd, 51 against 109 for sd × 0.67); for sd × 0.8, and with ticks or price noise, it is 1.0 to 1.9 times faster (for example 137 against 169 steps for sd × 0.8 on Gaussian data, 132 against 132 with ticks, 66 against 122 for a halving with price noise), and in the cells with sd × 0.8 it detects fewer of the changes (86.5%, 85.5% and 64.5% against 97.5% to 98.5%). It also detects large increases faster (13 against 20 steps for a doubling), at the same false alarm rate. Clipping the returns first (our "BOCPD on truncated returns") keeps most of the speed for decreases under jumps (25 against 81 steps) with 1.6% false alarms per day. On real crypto data, with day-long windows, the competitors' down alarms were as informative as the e-detector's in both half-years, and in the held-out half-year even the first-run truncated BOCPD's down alarms were not significantly different (67.0% against 69.7%, p = 0.47). These are real advantages, and a practitioner who trusts the Gaussian shape of returns, or cares mostly about decreases, could prefer BOCPD on truncated returns.
* **Where they lose.** Plain BOCPD is not usable on returns with jumps or fat tails: false alarms on 73% (jumps) and 53% (Student t5) of days at a threshold that gives 1% on Gaussian data. Truncation fixes jumps but not fat tails: 7.5% per day under t5, against 1.2% for the plug-in e-detector, which has no proved bound (measured), and 0.0% for the CS-baseline e-detector, whose 5% bound is a theorem. Neither BOCPD version detects small increases as reliably: 81% to 90% of 25% increases with Gaussian returns or jumps and 46.5% to 84.5% with ticks or price noise, against 97% to 99% for the plug-in e-detector.
* **BJV.** Truncation makes it robust to price jumps (as designed); Gaussian normalisation does not survive fat tails (24% to 53% size under t5 for the truncated versions at every window length, 87% for the plain one) unless the statistic is studentised. With the short windows of the first runs its power is much lower: offline, a 25% change is found in 6% to 8% of windows with k = 50 and 30% with k = 125, against 100% for the e-detector at the same size. **The gap is window length**, not the lack of betting: with windows of 250 returns the same truncated statistic finds 76% of 25% increases and 77% of 20% decreases, and with windows of 500 returns, as long as the e-detector's calibration window, 99% and 100%, at matched size on Gaussian data. Long windows have costs. The statistic needs k returns on both sides of the change and is centred on it, which a monitor is not; another change within k steps would blur it. It locates small changes less precisely among its rejections (within 25 steps in 49% to 54% of rejections with k = 500 against 63% to 65% with k = 125). Run online as a rolling test with k = 500, it detects 96% of 25% increases and 20% decreases on Gaussian data (k = 120: 30% and 32%), but with median delays of 277 and 326.5 steps against 104 and 169 for the plug-in e-detector, and 67.5 against 20 steps for a doubling. The e-detector's real advantages over BJV are that it does not have to choose a window or know where the change is, and that it is online and fast. This is not a flaw of the paper: BJV is built to find *local* volatility jumps inside smoothly moving volatility, so its windows are meant to be short, and it has no reference period. Its asymptotic Gumbel critical values were very conservative here (0.2% to 1.5% for a nominal 5% on Gaussian data). As an online rolling test with k = 120 it is a Shewhart-type chart and misses most small changes (9% to 35% detected for sd ratios 1.25 and 0.8, of which 77% to 95% in the right direction for the matched version).
* **Real data, rate-matched (first review, point M3; review round 3, point M4).** With the first-run windows (2 to 4 hours), the e-detector's alarms on crypto were followed by a day beyond an EWMA forecast more often than the competitors' (78.5% and 80.5% against 58.7% to 71.7% in Jul to Dec 2025; 82.0% and 69.7% against 56.7% to 71.5% in the held-out Jan to Jun 2025), and this holds with tests clustered by week. But the outcome asks whether the next day stays beyond a one-day forecast, the time scale of the e-detector's 1440-minute baseline, and the first-run competitor windows were not chosen for it. With windows of half a day to a day, the competitors' down alarms are as informative as the e-detector's in both half-years, the e-detector's up-alarm advantage shrinks to about 6 points against the best competitor (p = 0.065 and 0.054 with the z-test, 0.047 and 0.028 week-clustered), and on a four-hour outcome the short-window competitors do as well or better. So the e-detector is not more precise on crypto in general; its alarms are better aligned with day-long shifts than those of competitors with short windows. On Nifty all methods score 62% to 83% at band 0.25 and longer windows do not help the competitors (BJV with k = 375 is worse). A plausible reason for the remaining up-alarm gap, not tested here: the e-detector compares against a fixed calibrated baseline and alarms only after evidence has accumulated against it.
* **The guarantee needs the CS baseline.** With only 500 calibration steps, the plug-in e-detector's nominal offline size was 11.4% to 18.6% instead of 5% (review point M4 of the first review again). The CS baseline restores it (0.0%) at a cost of 1.25 to 2.6 times the median delay in Q13c with Gaussian returns, jumps or Student t5 (up to 2.6 with price noise, and 3.7 to 3.9 for decreases with ticks).

### Caveats

* The BJV implementation follows the published idea, not the published equations, which could not be read here (see above). Results with simulation-calibrated critical values do not depend on the asymptotic constants, but the exact standardisation might differ from the paper's.
* BOCPD settings (w = 250, run-length cap 512, α₀ = 2, H = 1 / A) were chosen on a Gaussian pilot to help BOCPD; a Student t likelihood or a learned hazard might do better under fat tails and was not tried. On real data, w = 720 and 1440 (375 on Nifty) were also run; no other setting was varied. The run-length cap makes BOCPD here an approximation of Adams and MacKay's exact recursion once runs reach the cap (see "BOCPD" above).
* Competitor thresholds matched "per day" rest on about 60 false alarms in 4000 Gaussian paths; online change cells have 200 paths (standard error of a detection share up to 3.5 points; medians are noisy).
* The real-data validation is a proxy (next-day robust volatility against an EWMA forecast) on the e-detector's own time scale of one day. Alarms are not independent (volatility clusters); the clustered tests allow for dependence within a day or a week but take different weeks as independent. The matching of alarm counts uses the same data, but not the outcome. The e-detector's settings were frozen in E5 on Bitstamp BTC in Jul to Dec 2025, so only the Jan to Jun 2025 crypto run is fully held out for it.
* Under slow stochastic volatility and GARCH clustering every method alarms often; for the e-detector this is the stated behaviour (its null is false there, E4c and E9c), for the others it shows that none of them separates "regime change" from ordinary clustering either.

## E14. A running truncation level with a guarantee, and a monitor with no blind period

Script `experiments/e14_running_tau.py`; outputs `results/e14*.csv` and `results/figures/e14_*.png`. Theory in `docs/theory_running_tau.md`. Code: `src/avmonitor/running.py` (`RunningTauMonitor`, `ConformalMonitor`, `AwakeRunningTauMonitor`); tests `tests/test_running.py`. Seeds are fixed in the script; all settings were fixed before the reported runs (`docs/iterations/TH2.md`).

**Question.** The e-detector bets on `X_t = min(r_t², τ²)` against the null mean `m(τ)`. E8 keeps a proved false alarm bound with an estimated mean, but only for one τ fixed before monitoring. Real data want τ_t to follow the current scale, and E12 found that the 1440-step recalibration after every alarm leaves the streaming monitor blind about 70% of the time. Can τ_t be any predictable rule with a proof, can monitoring resume right after an alarm with a proof, and what do the proofs cost?

**Method.** Three constructions, all proved in `docs/theory_running_tau.md`:

* **Route A (band).** A band `L(s) ≤ m_F(s) ≤ U(s)` that holds for all truncation levels s at once with probability 1 - δ; the increase side bets against `U(τ_t)`, the decrease side against `L(τ_t)`, for any predictable τ_t. Bound: P(false alarm within m) ≤ δ + m / A (Theorem A.1). Two bands: the time-uniform DKW band of Howard and Ramdas (2022), integrated (`A-dkw-run`), and empirical Bernstein confidence sequences on a grid of 13 levels (`A-grid-*`). τ_t = 3 × scaled MAD of the last 120 returns, refreshed every 10 steps and snapped to the grid (`A-grid-run`), or the grid centre (`A-grid-fixed`).
* **Route B (ranks).** Smoothed conformal p-values of |r_t| among all earlier values are i.i.d. uniform under exchangeability (Vovk, Nouretdinov and Gammerman 2003), so betting on them gives P(false alarm within m) ≤ m / A exactly, with no baseline, no δ and no τ (Theorem B.2). Bets: a clipped Gaussian likelihood ratio in rank space (`B-lr`) or indicators of running quantiles (`B-ind`). `B-freeze` freezes the reference set when a statistic reaches 20 (a heuristic with no proof).
* **No blind period.** `awake-A`: after an alarm the grid band is learned from the post-alarm returns while monitoring; the Shiryaev-Roberts chain started at step j bets against the band snapshot taken before j; each chain is multiplied by the indicator that the band has not failed by its snapshot time, an event known when the chain starts, which keeps it a supermartingale without conditioning on the unobservable event "the band never fails" (Theorem A.4, the structure of `docs/math.md` Theorem 6.4). `awake-B`: route B with the reference set restarted empty and betting from the first post-alarm return (Remark B.3). Both resume at once; only the very first segment needs 120 returns.

Comparators: `plugin` (the default monitor: fixed τ, plug-in mean; no proof), `plugin-run` (plug-in mean at the running level; no proof), `cs` (E8), `oracle` (true τ and true m(τ)). A = 7800 for methods with bound m / A and 390 / (0.05 - 0.01) = 9750 for methods with bound δ + m / A (δ = 0.01), so every proved bound is 5% per 390-step day. Two-sided rule as in the monitor (each side at 2A).

**Summary.**
* **The default plug-in monitor has no false alarm guarantee, and it fails in the long run.** Within one day it stays under the nominal 5%, but within five days it alarms on 41% to 43% of null paths after 390 calibration steps, where a known baseline would guarantee at most 25%. In 30-day streams it raises 0.084 to 0.094 false alarms per day against a nominal 0.05. Proposition A.6 gives the mechanism: for a fixed calibration length, the plug-in drifts upward under the null on a share of calibration windows that does not depend on A, so no bound of the form C m / A can hold for it. Lemma A.7 proves that this share is positive; its size (77% to 83% of windows at 390 steps) is a numerical estimate. The proposition does not account for the size of the failure: its own lower bound on the five-day rate is below 1% (0.5% to 0.8% at 390 steps).
* **Route B is exact, and fast.** The rank detector has a proved m / A bound with no baseline, no δ and no truncation level. It uses its budget (1.7% to 3.2% per day) without exceeding it. It is faster than the unproved plug-in on every decrease (x0.5: 25 to 34 steps against 69 to 77) and comparable on increases, except under Student t3 tails. Part of this speed comes from its likelihood-ratio bets.
* **Route A allows any predictable τ_t with a proof.** It integrates a band that holds at all truncation levels at once. On 13 levels, the grid band is as tight as E8's single-level bound at 1440 calibration steps (1.20 / 0.85 against 1.19 / 0.86 times the truth). It is valid with a wide margin but slow after short calibration. The integrated DKW band of Howard and Ramdas is too wide to be useful.
* **No blind period.** The awake rank monitor (awake-B) keeps its guarantee from the first return after an alarm. In streams where volatility moves about once a day, it detects 98% to 99.6% of the changes, with median delays of 34 to 60 steps. The standard 1440-step recalibration protocol is blind 57% to 71% of the time and catches 56% to 66% of the changes (65% to 66% for the default plug-in monitor, 56% to 58% for cs, 65% to 66% for B-lr). Route A with a learning band (awake-A) is also proved, but it cannot detect a change that comes within the first few dozen returns after a restart.
* **Real data.** In E12's design (BTC, ETH, SOL, 2024 to 2025), the awake monitors watch all 114 macro releases, against 55 for the plug-in. Up alarms within 6 hours rise from 21 to 24 (awake-A) and 31 (awake-B) of 66 CPI releases, and from 26 to 30 and 35 of 48 FOMC statements. The BTC CPI cell, not significant in E12 (p = 0.11), gives p = 0.003 and 0.0003.
* **Cost.** Well under a millisecond per return on a shared machine: plug-in 13 µs, route A 16 µs, rank monitor 44 µs, awake-A 47 µs (97 to 182 µs on real data, where it restarts its learning phase after every alarm; measured on a more heavily loaded machine, see Q14e).

[SYNTHETIC] Unit-scale returns: Gaussian, Student t3 (unit variance), jumps (probability 0.005 per step, size N(0, 10²)), price ticks (Gaussian rounded to 0.5, about 20% zeros: P(|Z| < 0.25) = 0.197), as in E9.

The band of route A failed (true m outside the band at some grid level) on at most 0.02% of paths in every cell, against an allowed 1%; the E8 confidence sequence failed on at most 0.04% (`band_failed` in the CSV files). Figure: `e14_validity.png`.

**Reading.**
* **The plug-in breaks at longer horizons.** Within one day it stays below 5% (4.0% to 4.9% at 390 calibration steps), as E8 found, but within five days it alarms on 40.6% to 42.9% of null paths at 390 calibration steps, far above the 25% that a known baseline would guarantee (the plug-in itself has no bound); at 1440 steps it is at 23% against 25%. A running τ does not change this (`plugin-run`). This is not a Monte Carlo accident: Proposition A.6 and Lemma A.7 of the theory note prove that at a fixed calibration length the plug-in has a positive drift under the null on a share of calibration windows that does not shrink as A grows, so its run length there grows only like log A; Q14w estimates the share.
* **Route B is valid at its nominal level and uses its budget.** 1.7% to 3.2% per day, 14% to 18% over five days, close to the oracle (0.8% to 1.7%, 12% to 14%). `B-freeze` exceeds the bound (6.4% to 7.0% per day at 390 calibration steps; 31% to 34% over five days), which is what the theory predicts for a frozen reference.
* **Route A and E8 are valid with a very wide margin**: at most 0.26% over five days. They spend almost none of the budget, which is the price of the band: see the delays in Q14b.

**Reading.**
* **B-lr, a proved and exact detector, beats the unproved plug-in on every decrease**, by a factor of two to three for the larger ones (x0.5: 25 to 34 steps against 69 to 77; x0.67: 51 to 80 against 97 to 118), and on x1.5 and x2 under Gaussian and jump returns. It is about as fast on x1.25 under Gaussian and jump returns (99 to 125 steps against 99 to 108) and slower on increases under Student t3 (x1.25: 260 and 243 against 182 and 194; x1.5: 78 and 73 against 68 and 67), where the heavy tails make the Gaussian-tuned rank bets inefficient. Part of the speed comes from the bets, not from the ranks: the rank bets are likelihood ratios for a normal scale change (λ = 1 for increases, 0.95 for decreases), clipped only at u_0 = P(|Z| > 3) so that one extreme return can multiply the wealth by a bounded factor, while the bets on X are linear with λ at most 0.5. The clip lowers the increase growth rate below the Kullback-Leibler divergence (0.573 against 0.807 at ρ = 2; docs/theory_running_tau.md, section 4.3). B-ind, the rank detector with simple indicator bets, is slower than the plug-in on increases (Gaussian x1.5: 44 to 45 against 39) and still faster on decreases (x0.5: 35 to 44 against 69 to 77).
* **Route A pays for its band.** At 1440 calibration steps the grid band is close to E8 on increases and faster on decreases with a running τ (Gaussian x0.5: 71 steps against 105 for cs; Student t3: 81 against 103). At 390 calibration steps it misses most small changes (x1.25: 4% to 37% detected). The running τ helps decreases. On small increases it costs a little for Gaussian returns (1440 calibration steps, x1.25: 336 against 326 steps with τ fixed) and more under Student t3 tails (937 against 783 steps, 76% against 88% detected), because after an increase τ_t moves up to a level where the band is wider.
* **The integrated DKW band is too wide to be useful**: it detects none of the x1.25 changes and at most 19% of the x1.5 changes within 2500 steps. It is kept as the simplest band that is uniform over all levels, and as a negative result.
* **B-freeze** is the fastest but has no proof and exceeds the pre-change bound (up to 11.8%).

### Q14c. Seasonality and drift (the null is false) [SYNTHETIC]

Share of paths with an alarm within one day (390 steps) and five days (1950) after 1440 calibration steps; in brackets the share with an increase alarm. 1000 paths. No monitor here has a guarantee: the returns are not identically distributed.

The null band b (0 or 0.25) means two different things here and in Q14d and Q14g. For the monitors that bet on X (plugin, cs, route A) it widens the baseline: the increase side bets against 1 + b times the baseline (or its upper bound), the decrease side against 1 - b times the baseline (or its lower bound), so b = 0.25 tolerates a change of the truncated second moment of up to 25%. For the rank monitors (B-lr, B-ind, awake-B) the same number divides each rank payoff by 1 + b (theory note 4.2), which tolerates a conditional mean payoff of up to 1.25 and has no direct meaning in units of volatility. E12's frozen setting, 0.25, is used for both kinds.

The grid band costs almost nothing against E8's single level at 1440 steps (1.20 / 0.85 against 1.19 / 0.86, Gaussian) and a little at 390 (1.46 / 0.68 against 1.40 / 0.72), while it covers 13 levels and needs no sample split. It is tight at low levels (what the decrease side needs) and loose at the highest levels, where an upper bound for a [0, 1] variable with mostly tiny values cannot be sharp (theory note 3.5). The integrated DKW band is much wider: at the centre its upper bound exceeds the truth by 1.5 to 3.1 times as much as the grid band's, and at high levels by far more; its time-uniform radius is 0.131 at 390 and 0.068 at 1440 observations (constant C = 9.28 for α = 0.01, solved numerically as in the authors' code; the closed form 0.8 log(1612 / α) gives 9.59), against 0.082 and 0.043 for Massart's fixed-n DKW radius (`e14w_constants.csv`).

**Plug-in drift (Proposition A.6).** For each calibration window, the expected log growth of every bet given the window, computed by quadrature on 20,000 quantile points of 4 million draws from the true law; "positive drift" means some bet on that side has `E log f > 0`, so that the detector reaches any threshold in finite expected time, bounded by `(log(2AK) + log f_max) / g` (`e14w_plugin_drift.csv`).

At 390 calibration steps 77% to 83% of calibration windows give the plug-in detector a positive drift under the null, at 1440 steps 56% to 68% (estimates from 2000 windows per cell; Lemma A.7 of the theory note proves only that the share is positive). The bound on the expected run length grows only from about 13,000 to about 19,000 steps when A grows 128-fold (7800 to 10⁶), which is the log A behaviour of the proposition. At A = 10⁶ the bound m / A for 7800 steps (20 days of 390 steps) would be 0.78%; Markov's inequality applied to the run length bound gives an estimated lower bound of 7.6% to 8.0% on the false alarm probability at 390 calibration steps (a Monte Carlo estimate over 2000 windows, with quadrature for the expectations, not a proved value). This crude lower bound uses only the chain started at the first step; the simulated rates of Q14a are much higher.

**Dilution of the rank detector after a change** (`e14w_dilution.csv`). Expected log growth per step of the matching rank bet k steps after a normal scale change by ρ, with 1940 pre-change values in the reference set (1440 calibration + 500 monitored, as in Q14b), from the formula of theory note 4.3 by numerical integration; and the number of steps a chain started at the change needs to gain log(2A) = log(15600) with and without dilution.

| 1.25 | 0.055 | 0.029 | -0.001 | -0.019 | 175 | 199 |
| 1.5 | 0.194 | 0.086 | -0.008 | -0.057 | 50 | 53 |

| 0.8 | 0.043 | 0.028 | 0.005 | -0.016 | 225 | 249 |
| 0.667 | 0.126 | 0.085 | 0.013 | -0.054 | 76 | 79 |
| 0.5 | 0.313 | 0.206 | 0.010 | -0.173 | 31 | 32 |


The growth falls to about zero once the post-change values are as many as the pre-change values (k ≈ 1940: -0.028 to 0.013 per step, against 0.043 to 0.573 at k = 0). This is a numerical finding: the theory gives only the limit ≤ 0 as k / n₀ → ∞. Within the time a chain needs to gain log(2A), dilution costs 3% to 14% (for example 199 steps against 175 for ρ = 1.25). These numbers are for one chain started at the change; the Shiryaev-Roberts statistic also carries the evidence of earlier chains, which is why the medians of Q14b are shorter.

**Reading.**
* **Both awake monitors keep their guarantee from the first step after a restart.** awake-B uses its budget (2.70% to 3.35% per day, 15.7% to 17.0% over five days), awake-A almost none (0.03% at most).
* **awake-B detects changes that the standard protocol cannot see.** A change 120 steps after a restart is found in 20 to 70 steps (Gaussian) and 42 to 115 steps (Student t3), on 65% to 99% of paths; the standard protocol is still calibrating and finds at most 61% of them within 2000 steps, 1660 to 1830 steps after the change. Even a change 30 steps after the restart is often caught (x0.5: 91% Gaussian, 70% t3), although with 30 reference values the p-values are coarse and the post-change values soon dominate the reference set (dilution, theory note 4.3).
* **awake-A is valid but slow early in a segment, a real limitation of the learning band.** With a change 30 steps after a restart it detects nothing: the band from fewer than 30 returns is very wide, and every later snapshot contains post-change returns, so the band learns the new level instead of testing against the old one. With a change after 120 steps it detects the halving of the standard deviation (x0.5: 100% Gaussian, 81% t3) but at most 34% of the other changes; after 360 steps it detects 58% to 100%. Where awake-A detects, awake-B is about 3 to 10 times faster (median delays). The rank route is the one to use for the no-blind-period monitor.

"Blind" is the share of steps not monitored (calibrating, or the first 120 steps of a path for the awake monitors).

**No change** (i.i.d. Gaussian or Student t3 returns). False alarms per day with a 95% upper confidence limit (Poisson), and the per-day bound of Corollary A.5 (for E8 Corollary 6.6 of `docs/math.md`; for the rank monitors Remark B.3), (δ + m / A) / (1 - δ) with m = 30 days, or m / A:

* **Blind time.** With volatility moving about once a day, the standard protocol is blind 57% to 71% of the time (E12 measured about 70% on crypto) and is awake at only 31% to 49% of the changes. The awake monitors are blind 0.28% of the time (the first 120 steps of each path).
* **False alarms per day under a true null.** The proved monitors stay within their bounds: awake-B 0.029 and 0.035 per day (bound 0.050), B-lr 0.028 and 0.033, awake-A, cs essentially 0. **The plug-in does not: 0.094 and 0.084 false alarms per day, about twice the nominal 0.05, with 95% lower limits above 0.05** (113 and 101 alarms in 1200 days; per monitored day the excess is larger). Streaming monitors are plain Python with NumPy, one return at a time, with an infinite threshold so that no alarm resets them. Vectorised rows are the experiment engine (many paths at once).

| RunningTauMonitor grid (route A), one series, no alarm | 200,000 | 15.83 |

| AwakeRunningTauMonitor (route A, no blind period), one series, no alarm | 200,000 | 47.44 |
| AwakeRunningTauMonitor, learning phase (first 1560 steps) | 1,560 | 76.99 |
| vectorised plugin (calibration + monitoring), 1000 paths x 3390 steps | 3,390,000 | 0.17 |
| vectorised cs (calibration + monitoring), 1000 paths x 3390 steps | 3,390,000 | 0.26 |
| vectorised A-grid-run (calibration + monitoring), 1000 paths x 3390 steps | 3,390,000 | 1.35 |
| vectorised A-dkw-run (calibration + monitoring), 1000 paths x 3390 steps | 3,390,000 | 0.28 |

**Reading.** Every monitor costs well under a millisecond per return, so cost is not a constraint for minute or second data. The running level costs about 20% over the plug-in (route A: 15 to 16 µs against 13); the awake route A monitor costs about 4 times the plug-in (47 µs; 77 µs in its learning phase, which updates 13 confidence sequences per return). The rank monitor costs 44 µs per return on this 200,000-step series because its sorted reference set grows without bound when there is no alarm and each insertion moves O(n) entries; on the real series of Q14d, where restarts keep the reference set short, the measured cost was 5.8 to 45.6 µs per return for the monitors that recalibrate (band 0.25; `us_per_step` in `e14d_real_summary.csv`; their blind steps are cheap and included), 45 to 70 µs for awake-B and 97 to 182 µs for awake-A, which restarts its learning phase after every alarm. Q14d was rerun after review round 3 (see the caveats) while other jobs kept the four cores busier (load average about 6) than during Q14e, so these real-data costs are more inflated than the rows of the table above; the first run of Q14d (the previous version of the CSV) had measured 3.4 to 28.7, 34 to 55 and 81 to 115 µs. A balanced tree or a blocked sorted list would make the rank monitor O(log n) per return; we did not need it.

### Caveats and open issues

* Every guarantee here is for its stated null: i.i.d. calibration (route A), exchangeable returns within a segment (route B, awake monitors). Volatility clustering violates all of them, so the real-data alarm rates are statements about the data, not false alarm rates (Q14c, Q14d).
* The speed of B-lr against the X-based detectors mixes two effects, ranks and likelihood-ratio bets; we did not run an X-based detector with likelihood-ratio bets.
* awake-A is valid but weak right after a restart (Q14f). For a no-blind-period monitor, the rank route is the one we recommend.
* Without a null band, awake-B alarms 3.6 to 4.3 times per crypto day (Q14d). It needs the band, or a larger A, on real data.
* Proposition A.6's numerical lower bound (Q14w) uses Markov's inequality on a single chain and quadrature for the expectations. It demonstrates the failure clearly at A = 10⁶ and 390 calibration steps (an estimated lower bound of 7.6% to 8.0% against 0.78%), but not at 1440 steps, nor in the five-day setting of Q14a (0.5% to 0.8% against the 41% to 43% simulated); the simulated rates (Q14a, Q14h) are the direct evidence. Lemma A.7 proves only that the share of windows with positive drift is positive; the shares of Q14w are estimates.
* The rank monitor's sorted reference set costs O(n) per insertion when there are no alarms for a long time (Q14e).
* The decrease-side convention was changed after review round 3. At a step where the decrease side has no admissible bet (a lower bound of 0, or a squared truncation level τ_t² at or below the lower bound), the decrease statistic is now left unchanged; before, it grew by 1 per step, so a side that stayed off for 2A steps would have alarmed for certain. The new convention is the one of `docs/math.md` 6.3 (theory note, section 1), and every proof holds with either. Every cell that uses the changed code was rerun or recomputed with the new code. The plug-in, cs and route A results are identical: no path of Q14a or Q14c had such a step, and 46 paths of one Q14b cell (jumps, 390 calibration steps, x2, A-grid-run) had one without any effect. awake-A changed a little, because its first snapshot (no data yet, lower bound 0) used to add a constant 16 to its decrease statistic. Its null rates in Q14f are unchanged; Q14d, the delay part of Q14f, Q14g and Q14h were rerun, and the tables above are from the rerun. What changed: one median delay in Q14f (966 to 967 steps), the Student t3 row of Q14h (77.9% to 77.8% detected; x0.67 median 324 to 314, x1.5 343 to 348), one awake-A alarm per day figure and a few confirmation counts in Q14d, and in Q14g one CPI release fewer with an awake-A up alarm (SOL 8 to 7, so 25 to 24 of 66; SOL p 0.0013 to 0.0059, BTC p 0.0032 to 0.0026). No other monitor's numbers changed.
* Some alarms are left out of the E5c check in Q14d: alarms in the last day of a series, which have no next-day window, and awake-B alarms raised with fewer than 30 reference values, for which no baseline scale is defined. That is at most 6 per series and monitor (`e14d_real_alarms.csv`).
* In the Q14g windows, some alarms had a zero baseline scale (a reference set with a median absolute return of 0), which gives infinite diagnostic ratios in E12's alarm frame (a warning in the log). The release counts and tests do not use those ratios.
