## E15. Monitoring a panel of assets with false discovery control

Script `e15_panel.py`, code `src/avmonitor/panel.py`, theory and proofs `docs/theory_panel.md`. Q15a to Q15c are **[SYNTHETIC]** with fixed seeds (15 onwards, 151, 1500); Q15d and Q15e are **[REAL]** (Binance one-minute data and Nifty 50 one-minute data, see `data/MANIFEST.csv`; control draws use seed 152). Every number below is in `results/e15*.csv`.

**Why.** A user rarely watches one asset. With K single-asset monitors, each at false alarm level α per day, the chance that some monitor raises a false alarm on a quiet day grows with K (up to about Kα). Raising every level to K/α (Bonferroni) fixes that but makes every monitor slower. In fixed-sample testing the standard compromise is the false discovery rate (FDR): the expected share of false alarms among the alarms raised. Its version for e-values, e-BH (Wang and Ramdas 2022), works under any dependence between assets, which matters because asset volatilities move together. But e-BH needs e-values, and the Shiryaev-Roberts statistic of the single-asset monitor is not one at a data-dependent time (`docs/theory_panel.md`, Proposition 1). E15 tests the fix proposed in the theory note: turn each asset's bet chains into a mixture e-process for "no change since the block started", run e-BH on these e-processes at every step, and keep an asset discovered once it is discovered ("sticky e-BH").

**What is proved (`docs/theory_panel.md`, Theorem 1).** Within one block, whatever the dependence between assets: the FDR is at most α at every stopping time; the expected worst false discovery proportion over the block is at most α(1 + log(1/α)), about 20% for α = 5%; and if nothing changes, the probability of any discovery is at most α. Not controlled: the probability of at least one false discovery once some assets change, the expected number of false discoveries (up to αK), and the FDR of all discoveries pooled over many blocks.

**Methods compared.** All use the same truncated squared returns and the same bet grids as the single-asset monitor (c = 3, both directions).

* *naive SR (A)*: one Shiryaev-Roberts e-detector per asset at the single-asset level A = m/α (m = block length), no multiplicity correction.
* *Bonferroni SR (A × K)*: the same detectors at A·K.
* *panel Bonferroni*: the panel e-process (window weights over one block) with threshold K/α. By the window identity this is almost the same detector as Bonferroni SR.
* *panel e-BH*: the panel e-process with sticky e-BH at level α.

Path by path, for the three panel rules applied to the same e-values, naive flags an asset no later than e-BH, and e-BH no later than Bonferroni (`tests/test_panel.py`).

### Q15a. Validity [SYNTHETIC]

**Setup.** One block of m = 390 steps, α = 5% per block (A = 7,800). Unit-variance Gaussian returns plus jumps (probability 0.002 per step, jump sd 4), truncation at 3. "Independent": separate shocks and jumps per asset. "Factor + co-jumps": a common factor with correlation 0.7 between every pair of assets, and jumps that hit every asset at the same step. The baseline is the exact null mean of the truncated square (closed form), so that the multiple-testing layer is tested on its own. 2,000 paths when nothing changes, 600 otherwise (`results/e15a_synthetic.csv`).

Probability of any discovery when no asset changes (95% interval about ±0.3 points near 0.5%, ±1 point near 5%):

| Dependence | K | naive SR (A) | Bonferroni SR (A × K) | panel Bonferroni | panel e-BH |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| independent | 5 | 5.55% | 0.90% | 0.90% | 0.90% |
| independent | 10 | 9.20% | 0.70% | 0.70% | 0.70% |
| independent | 20 | 17.50% | 0.50% | 0.50% | 0.50% |
| independent | 50 | 37.20% | 0.50% | 0.50% | 0.50% |
| factor + co-jumps | 5 | 4.45% | 0.60% | 0.60% | 0.60% |
| factor + co-jumps | 10 | 7.15% | 0.55% | 0.55% | 0.55% |
| factor + co-jumps | 20 | 13.35% | 0.65% | 0.65% | 0.65% |
| factor + co-jumps | 50 | 22.35% | 0.30% | 0.30% | 0.35% |

When some assets change (48 designs: 20% or 60% of assets change by sd × 1.25, at a common step 100 or at steps drawn uniformly from 50 to 300, or by sd × 1.5 at step 100; four K; two dependence settings), the worst value over all 48 designs of each error measure:

| Error measure (worst design) | naive SR (A) | Bonferroni SR (A × K) | panel e-BH | proved bound for e-BH |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FDR at the end of the block | 4.57% | 0.58% | 0.96% | 5% |
| FDR at the first discovery | 7.83% | 0.67% | 0.67% | 5% |
| E[max over the block of the false discovery proportion] | 13.28% | 0.75% | 1.00% | about 20% |
| P(at least one false discovery) | 33.3% | 1.17% | 8.0% | not controlled |
| E[number of false discoveries] | 0.44 | 0.012 | 0.115 | not controlled (up to αK) |

The largest standard error of an e-BH FDR estimate is 0.29 points. The worst e-BH value of P(at least one false discovery), 8.0%, is at K = 50, independent assets, 60% changing together; the worst E[number of false discoveries], 0.115, is the same design with a common factor.

**Reading.** The naive rule fails as expected: with 50 independent assets, 37% of quiet blocks contain a false alarm. Bonferroni and e-BH keep this below 1% for every K, under strong dependence too. With changes, e-BH's FDR stays below 1% in every design, so the proved 5% bound is far from tight here. The slack is already there for one asset: from the naive column at K = 5 with independent assets (5.55% for five assets), a single monitor at level A raises a false alarm in about 1.1% of quiet blocks, against its bound of 5%. e-BH inherits that slack. The price of e-BH is visible where theory says it should be: the chance of at least one false discovery rises to 8% at K = 50, because once many assets are discovered, e-BH lowers the bar for the rest. Panel Bonferroni and Bonferroni SR agree to within 0.17 points of power in every design, as the window identity predicts.

### Q15b. Power and delay [SYNTHETIC]

Factor + co-jumps, sd × 1.25 at the change. Power is the share of changed assets discovered at or after their change within the block; delay is in steps, over detected changes only. Independent assets and sd × 1.5 are in `results/e15a_synthetic.csv`.

| Changed assets | K | Power: naive | Bonferroni SR | e-BH | Median delay: naive | Bonferroni SR | e-BH |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20%, together at step 100 | 5 | 97.7% | 92.7% | 92.7% | 110 | 139 | 139 |
| | 10 | 98.0% | 92.3% | 94.1% | 102.5 | 147.5 | 143 |
| | 20 | 98.0% | 88.8% | 93.3% | 107 | 161 | 148 |
| | 50 | 98.4% | 84.0% | 93.1% | 110 | 178 | 159 |
| 60%, together at step 100 | 5 | 97.4% | 94.0% | 96.2% | 107 | 136.5 | 127 |
| | 10 | 97.4% | 89.9% | 96.0% | 110 | 152 | 134 |
| | 20 | 97.9% | 88.9% | 96.3% | 110 | 162 | 137 |
| | 50 | 98.0% | 84.1% | 96.2% | 109 | 174 | 138 |
| 20%, staggered (steps 50 to 300) | 5 | 83.0% | 72.2% | 72.2% | 95.5 | 122 | 122 |
| | 10 | 85.0% | 68.2% | 71.4% | 96.5 | 127.5 | 125 |
| | 20 | 83.6% | 61.7% | 69.2% | 99 | 140 | 133 |
| | 50 | 83.2% | 55.5% | 67.5% | 96 | 150 | 137 |
| 60%, staggered (steps 50 to 300) | 5 | 83.6% | 74.1% | 78.6% | 97 | 123 | 117 |
| | 10 | 84.0% | 67.1% | 77.7% | 95 | 128 | 118 |
| | 20 | 82.5% | 62.4% | 76.6% | 96 | 139 | 122 |
| | 50 | 84.2% | 56.9% | 77.8% | 93 | 146 | 121 |

Over all 48 change designs, e-BH finds on average 5.0 percentage points more changed assets than Bonferroni SR (never fewer; at most 21.3 points more, independent assets, 60% staggered, K = 50: 77.7% against 56.4%). With sd × 1.5 all rules find essentially every change (power at least 99.88%), and the median delay is 47 to 57 steps for e-BH, 51 to 66 for Bonferroni SR and 41 to 42.5 for the naive rule.

**Reading.** e-BH recovers most of what Bonferroni loses as K grows. With 60% of 50 assets changing together, Bonferroni's power falls to 84% and its median delay rises to 174 steps; e-BH stays at 96% and 138 steps (96% and 127 steps at K = 5). The gain is largest when many assets change, which is when the e-BH bar drops furthest. Delays are measured on different sets (e-BH detects a superset of Bonferroni's detections, including harder ones), so the delay comparison, if anything, favours Bonferroni. The naive rule is faster still but, as Q15a shows, gives no multiplicity control.

**Estimated baselines (robustness).** With the confidence-sequence baseline (`docs/math.md`, section 6) estimated from 1,440 null steps per asset, δ = 0.01 split over K (so the proved bound is α + δ = 6%), K = 20, 20% of assets changing together by sd × 1.25, 400 paths (`results/e15a_cs_baseline.csv`):

| Dependence | Rule | P(any false discovery), no change | P(any false discovery), with changes | Power | Median delay |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| factor + co-jumps | e-BH | 0% | 0% | 41.0% | 213 |
| factor + co-jumps | Bonferroni | 0% | 0% | 35.5% | 212.5 |
| independent | e-BH | n/a | 0% | 36.0% | 234 |
| independent | Bonferroni | n/a | 0% | 33.0% | 224.5 |

With the oracle baseline the same designs give 93.3% (e-BH) and 88.8% (Bonferroni) power with a common factor, 94.1% and 88.4% with independent assets. **Negative result:** the provable baseline costs more than half the power at this small change, much more than the multiplicity correction does. The confidence-sequence bounds per asset are at level δ/K = 0.0005, so they are wide.

### Q15c. One guarantee per block against one for the whole horizon [SYNTHETIC]

K = 20 independent assets, ten blocks of 390 steps (3,900 steps). Either no change, or 6 assets change (sd × 1.5) at times drawn uniformly over the whole horizon. Baselines are the exact null mean throughout (no recalibration). 400 paths (`results/e15c_horizon.csv`). The block rules restart every 390 steps and the first discovery of each asset over the ten blocks is kept; the "since start" rules run one block of 3,900 steps.

| Rule | P(any discovery), no change | P(at least one false discovery), 6 change | FDR, 6 change | E[max FDP over the horizon] | E[false discoveries] | Power | Median delay |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| daily blocks, e-BH | 4.75% | 23.5% | 3.81% | 6.44% | 0.27 | 98.1% | 56 |
| daily blocks, Bonferroni | 4.75% | 4.25% | 0.63% | 1.80% | 0.04 | 98.0% | 63 |
| since start, Pareto weights (h = 390), e-BH | 1.75% | 5.75% | 0.86% | 2.26% | 0.06 | 97.4% | 72 |
| since start, window h = 3,900, e-BH | 2.00% | 5.75% | 0.88% | 1.56% | 0.06 | 97.9% | 67 |

Median delay by the time of the change (`results/e15c_delay_by_change_time.csv`; share of changes detected in brackets):

| Change at step | daily e-BH | daily Bonferroni | since start, Pareto | since start, window 3,900 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 to 389 | 62 (100%) | 64 (100%) | 63 (100%) | 74 (100%) |
| 390 to 1,299 | 59 (99.8%) | 65 (99.8%) | 71 (99.8%) | 71 (100%) |
| 1,300 to 2,599 | 54 (99.6%) | 62 (99.9%) | 72 (99.8%) | 65 (99.9%) |
| 2,600 to 3,899 | 53 (94.9%) | 63 (94.5%) | 76 (92.7%) | 64 (94.0%) |

**Reading.** Two lessons, both predicted by the theory note (section 6).

1. *A guarantee per block is not a guarantee for the horizon.* Under no change, ten daily blocks give 4.75% probability of any discovery, well inside the 10 × 5% that per-block control allows. With changes, daily e-BH has a 23.5% chance of at least one false discovery over the horizon, against 4.25% for daily Bonferroni. The reason: in this design baselines are never recalibrated, so a changed asset is discovered again in every later block; each time, e-BH lowers the bar for the other 19 assets, and the null assets get many chances at a low bar. In each block the FDR guarantee holds, but nothing bounds the pooled count over blocks. The pooled FDR here (3.8%) and worst FDP (6.4%) happen to stay moderate; they are not covered by any theorem.
2. *One e-process for the whole horizon keeps a single guarantee and pays with delay.* The Pareto rule keeps the any-false-discovery probability at 1.75% (no change) and 5.75% (with changes) for all 3,900 steps, but its median delay grows from 63 to 76 steps as the change comes later, the cost of the Pareto weights, log(1/w), which by Proposition 2 of the theory note cannot be avoided in order. The last row is censored (changes near the end are often not detected in time), so its medians are biased toward short delays. Daily e-BH and the window rule get *faster* for later changes because earlier discoveries stay in the e-BH set and lower the bar; daily Bonferroni has no such effect and is flat.

### Q15d. Five Binance coins [REAL]

**Setup.** BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL and DOGE against USDT, one-minute log returns divided by a past-only intraday volatility profile (`avmonitor.data.intraday_scale`, 20-day look-back). One block per UTC day (1,440 minutes), α = 5% per day, K = 5. At each UTC midnight each coin is calibrated on its previous 1,440 returns: plug-in baseline (as in E6), c = 3, null band b = 0.25 (the E5/E6 primary setting) or b = 0.5 (the other band of the E6 grid). Window weights over 1,440 returns. Periods: Jul to Dec 2025 (the E6 period) and Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 (the E6 out-of-sample period; blocks start on 22 Jan 2024 to leave room for the profile and calibration). No setting was chosen from E15 results (see `docs/iterations/PANEL.md` for when band 0.5 was added).

Four rules on the same e-value paths: sticky e-BH; Bonferroni (first time the e-value reaches K/α = 100); naive (first time it reaches 1/α = 20); and, as a hindsight benchmark, a per-asset constant threshold chosen after the fact so that it makes exactly as many discoveries as e-BH ("rate-matched"). The vectorised e-BH run was checked step by step against an offline e-BH on the first 40 blocks of every run.

**Validation (as in E6).** For each discovery, the robust sd (scaled MAD) of the coin's next 1,440 returns is divided by the calibration scale. An up discovery is "confirmed" if this ratio is above 1, a down discovery if it is below 1. Controls: for each e-BH discovery, 5 random days of the same asset at the same minute of the day.

| Coins, period | Band | Discoveries: e-BH / Bonferroni / naive | e-BH per day (of 5) | Up confirmed (95% CI), n | Control | Down confirmed (95% CI), n | Control |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jul to Dec 2025 (184 days) | 0.25 | 790 / 762 / 810 | 4.29 | 78.0% (74.2 to 81.4), 500 | 50.4% | 86.4% (81.9 to 89.9), 286 | 48.7% |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 (526 days) | 0.25 | 2,296 / 2,211 / 2,346 | 4.37 | 80.0% (77.8 to 82.1), 1,313 | 46.2% | 84.9% (82.5 to 87.0), 978 | 52.7% |
| Jul to Dec 2025 | 0.5 | 552 / 508 / 573 | 3.00 | 80.7% (76.6 to 84.1), 424 | 49.4% | 96.9% (92.2 to 98.8), 127 | 50.0% |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 | 0.5 | 1,527 / 1,446 / 1,614 | 2.90 | 82.6% (80.3 to 84.6), 1,176 | 47.0% | 96.2% (93.7 to 97.8), 346 | 55.4% |

What e-BH adds over Bonferroni, and what the naive rule adds over e-BH (`results/e15d_validation.csv`, `results/e15d_structure.csv`):

| Coins, period | Band | e-BH only (not Bonferroni): n; up confirmed; down confirmed | naive only (not e-BH): n; up; down | Median / mean minutes e-BH before Bonferroni | e-BH strictly earlier | e-BH discoveries with e-value below K/α |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jul to Dec 2025 | 0.25 | 28; 12 of 21; 5 of 7 | 20; 4 of 10; 9 of 10 | 4 / 32 | 76.8% | 613 of 790 |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 | 0.25 | 85; 20 of 39; 35 of 46 | 50; 10 of 28; 19 of 22 | 4 / 38 | 76.1% | 1,767 of 2,296 |
| Jul to Dec 2025 | 0.5 | 44; 15 of 30; 14 of 14 | 21; 10 of 13; 7 of 8 | 2 / 30 | 71.7% | 408 of 552 |
| Jan 2024 to Jun 2025 | 0.5 | 81; 22 of 52; 29 of 29 | 87; 33 of 58; 25 of 29 | 2 / 24 | 70.5% | 1,101 of 1,527 |

"Strictly earlier" is the share of coin-days found by both rules on which e-BH flagged first. The rate-matched hindsight threshold confirms at the same rate as e-BH in all 12 panel, period, band and direction cells (two-proportion tests, p-values 0.56 to 1.00, `results/e15d_rate_matched_tests.csv`; the two discovery sets overlap, so the tests are only indicative).

**Reading.**

1. *The strict daily null is false on most coin-days.* At band 0.25 e-BH discovers 86% to 87% of coin-days, at band 0.5 58% to 60%, and at band 0.25 there are at least two discoveries on 170 of 184 days. This repeats E9 and E10: under volatility clustering, "the truncated variance stays within 25% of yesterday's level all day" is rarely true for crypto. The FDR guarantee is then nearly empty in practice, because almost every hypothesis is false.
2. *The multiplicity rule changes the timing more than the set.* e-BH finds only 3.7% to 8.7% more coin-days than Bonferroni. But on the coin-days both find, e-BH flags first 71% to 77% of the time, by a median of 2 to 4 minutes and a mean of 24 to 38 minutes (the mean is pulled up by a long tail, see `results/figures/e15_real_discoveries.png`, panel c). 72% to 78% of e-BH discoveries were made while the e-value was still below the Bonferroni level K/α.
3. *Discoveries point the right way.* An e-BH up discovery is followed by a higher robust volatility over the next day 78% to 83% of the time, against 46% to 50% at matched random times; a down discovery by a lower one 85% to 97% of the time, against 49% to 55%.
4. *The marginal up discoveries are weak.* The up discoveries that only e-BH makes (not Bonferroni) are confirmed 42% to 57% of the time, which is near the control rate; marginal down discoveries are confirmed 71% to 100% of the time (small n). The up discoveries that only the naive rule makes are confirmed 36% to 77% of the time across cells, a wider range. So the extra discoveries add little information beyond what Bonferroni finds; the value of e-BH here is earlier alarms, not more alarms.
5. *e-BH is not better than a well chosen fixed threshold, in hindsight.* A per-asset threshold set after the fact to make as many discoveries confirms at the same rate. The difference is that e-BH's level is fixed in advance and carries the FDR guarantee; the rate-matched threshold (33 to 48 on the e-value scale) was read off the data.

### Q15e. Five coins and the Nifty 50 index on one clock [REAL]

**Setup.** The five coins plus the Nifty 50 index, Feb 2024 to Dec 2025 (700 UTC days, 472 Nifty sessions), K = 6, other settings as in Q15d. Nifty: regular sessions only, 09:15 to 15:30 IST (03:45 to 10:00 UTC), 374 one-minute returns per session; returns divided by a strictly past-only session profile (per-minute median of |r| over the previous 20 sessions, 5-minute smoothing within the session, normalised to median 1; E7's settings without its start-up look-ahead). Outside its session the Nifty return is missing: its e-process does not move and its clock does not advance. Nifty has its own clock throughout: window h = 374 returns (one session), calibration on its previous 750 returns (E7's primary setting). Each UTC day contains at most one Nifty session. Nifty stays in the panel on weekends and holidays with e-value 1, so K = 6 every day (a small, conservative cost).

Panel totals (`results/e15d_validation.csv`):

| Band | Discoveries: e-BH / Bonferroni / naive | e-BH per day (of 6) | Up confirmed (95% CI), n | Control | Down confirmed (95% CI), n | Control | Median / mean minutes e-BH before Bonferroni |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | 3,257 / 3,107 / 3,352 | 4.65 | 80.8% (79.0 to 82.5), 1,906 | 47.2% | 85.7% (83.7 to 87.4), 1,347 | 52.3% | 5 / 35 |
| 0.5 | 2,120 / 1,990 / 2,273 | 3.03 | 82.8% (80.9 to 84.6), 1,638 | 48.0% | 95.8% (93.7 to 97.3), 481 | 53.1% | 2 / 25 |

Nifty discoveries only (`results/e15e_nifty_discoveries.csv`; controls are pooled over assets in this design and are not reported separately for Nifty):

| Band | Rule | Up confirmed, n | Down confirmed, n | Discovered outside the Nifty session |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.25 | e-BH | 92.1% (116 of 126) | 87.0% (87 of 100) | 3 up, 1 down |
| 0.25 | Bonferroni | 91.0% (101 of 111) | 88.1% (74 of 84) | 0 |
| 0.25 | naive | 89.7% (122 of 136) | 89.4% (93 of 104) | 0 |
| 0.5 | e-BH | 90.4% (75 of 83) | 95.2% (20 of 21) | 1 up |
| 0.5 | Bonferroni | 89.7% (70 of 78) | 100% (16 of 16) | 0 |
| 0.5 | naive | 92.3% (84 of 91) | 83.3% (25 of 30) | 0 |

e-BH discovered Nifty on 226 of 472 sessions at band 0.25 (48%) and 104 at band 0.5 (22%). Which assets are discovered together on a day (`results/e15e_codiscoveries.csv`): at band 0.25, all six on 144 days and all five coins without Nifty on 329 of 700 days; Nifty alone on 4 days. At band 0.5: all six on 35 days, the five coins without Nifty on 212, Nifty alone on 28.

**Reading.**

1. *Trading hours are handled without any synchronisation.* Each asset runs on its own clock and its own calibration window, and the guarantee needs only that the trading calendar is known one step ahead. The Nifty discoveries confirm at about 87% to 95% in both directions.
2. *Borrowing strength across assets is real and visible.* Under e-BH, Nifty was discovered 4 times (band 0.25) and once (band 0.5) after its session had closed: its e-process was frozen, but crypto discoveries later in the UTC day lowered the e-BH bar below Nifty's frozen e-value. Bonferroni and naive rules cannot do this by construction. Such a discovery means "Nifty's session already looked different, and the market-wide picture makes it count" (`docs/theory_panel.md`, section 7).
3. *The coins move together, Nifty much less.* At band 0.25 the five coins are discovered together on 329 of 700 days without Nifty and on 144 more with it. At band 0.5 Nifty is discovered alone on 28 days, as often as XRP and more often than any other coin. Crypto and Indian equity volatility regimes overlap only partly.

### Caveats

* **Oracle baselines in Q15a to Q15c.** The synthetic validity results use the exact null mean. With the confidence-sequence baseline (proved bound α + δ) power falls from about 93% to 36% to 41% in the one design tested; with the plug-in baseline used on real data there is no proved bound (E4d, E8).
* **The real-data null.** The strict daily null with a band is false on most crypto days (point 1 of Q15d). A forecast-relative null (E10) would make the panel's discoveries mean "the forecast was wrong", which is closer to what a user wants; this was not tested in the panel.
* **Which past the null conditions on.** Theorem 1 needs each asset's null to hold given the whole panel's past. If volatility spills over from one asset to another with a lag, this is stronger than the asset's own-past null. E15 does not test for spillovers.
* **Validation is a proxy.** "Confirmed" compares the next day's robust volatility with the calibration scale. It measures persistence of the regime, not whether the null was false at the discovery time, and the controls are pooled over assets.
* **Nifty data cleaning.** E7 sets frozen-price runs (5 or more minutes of exact zero returns) to missing. E15 did not apply that filter, but E7's list of such runs (`results/e07a_frozen_runs.csv`) has none in 2024 or 2025, so it would not have changed the input.
* **Per-block guarantee only.** Q15c shows that per-block FDR control does not bound false discoveries pooled over many blocks.
* **Seeds and sample sizes.** Synthetic rows use 600 paths (2,000 under no change), so a power estimate near 90% has a standard error of at most about 1.2 points (one changed asset); differences between e-BH and Bonferroni of 2 points or less at K = 5 or 10 are within noise.

## E16. Adversarial null search: how close to the bound can a legitimate adversary get, and where does the guarantee break?

Script `experiments/e16_adversarial_null.py`; outputs `results/e16*.csv` and `results/figures/e16_*.png`; tests `tests/test_e16_adversarial.py`; iteration notes `docs/iterations/E16.md`. All results **[SYNTHETIC]**. Seeds are fixed in the script, and every reported rate comes from seeds that the search never saw.

**Question.** Theorem B says that the default two-sided detector raises a false alarm within m steps with probability at most m / A, whenever E[X_t | past] = m0 with the true m0. E9 found it about 4 times conservative for four natural laws (1.1% to 1.4% per day against 5%). How close to m / A can a legitimate adversary, one that satisfies every condition of the theorem, push the full default detector, including laws that depend on the past and on the detector's own state? And outside the theorem's conditions, where exactly does the bound fail, by how much, and does each failure match the condition that was broken?

**Set-up.** The full default detector: X_t = min(r_t², τ²), τ = 3 times the scaled MAD, six increase bets 0.02 to 0.5, five decrease bets 0.1 to 0.95 of 1 / (B - 1) with B = τ² / m0, Shiryaev-Roberts statistics, each side alarming at 2A, A = 7800. The bound is 5% for one 390-step day and 25% for five days (1950 steps). Inside the class only the law of Y_t = X_t / m0 matters: Y_t lies in [0, B] and must have conditional mean exactly 1. At each step both statistics are affine in Y_t, so a two-point law with mean 1 is as good as any law for the adversary (the concave envelope argument of Lemma 2a in `docs/theory_delay.md`), and the adversary's whole choice is a pair of points at each step, possibly depending on everything seen so far. With τ = 3 times the scaled MAD of the law itself and a positive median absolute return, B can only lie between 1.90 and 39.6 (half the returns are at least the median in size, so m0 is at least half the squared median; the other half are at most the median, so m0 is at most the average of the squared median and τ²; and τ² / median² = (3 × 1.4826)² = 19.78); the Gaussian value is 9.045. When more than half of the returns are zero, the monitor's fallback (the median of the nonzero absolute returns) allows larger B, up to 149 for the price ticks of Q16f; bold play at B = 100 to 1,000 stays below its rates at B = 2 (Q16b). Under the theorem τ may be any level fixed in advance, so any B above 1 is legitimate.

**Search and reporting.** Grid search, then Nelder-Mead, on common random numbers (the same uniforms for every candidate, so the objective is a fixed function of the parameters); 20,000 paths at one day and 6,000 to 8,000 at five days. The search maximum is biased upwards (iteration 2 of the notes; the in-sample values are kept in the CSV files as `train_rate`), so the best law of each family is re-run on fresh seeds: 200,000 paths at one day and 60,000 at five days (102,560 and 41,020 for shape switching), with 95% Wilson intervals. "Above the bound" means that the lower end of the interval is above it. The tests check that every searched law keeps the conditional mean at 1, that bold play lands on the threshold, that each return law uses its own true τ and m0, that the price-tick control keeps the values and removes the dependence, that the floor constant of Q16c is the smallest value of the statistic, and that the vectorised detector matches `VolatilityMonitor` alarm for alarm.

**Summary.**
* **Inside the class the bound always holds, with room to spare.** No law found, i.i.d., dependent or adaptive, uses much more than half of the bound at one day: the worst is bold play, an adversary that watches the detector and uses the widest legal spread, at 2.62% per day (95% interval 2.50% to 2.75%, B = 2) against 5%; at the Gaussian B it gives 2.40% (2.34% to 2.47%). Over five days the worst is 18.1% (17.8% to 18.5%) against 25%. Not one interval reaches the bound.
* **The adversary removes about half of E9's slack; under every law tried, the rest is wealth left on paths that never alarm.** The Gaussian null uses 0.19 of the bound in one day (0.97%); the worst legitimate law uses 0.52, so E9's factor of about 4 to 5 shrinks to about 2 (at five days from 2.0 to 1.4). Under bold play stopping and overshoot cost nothing; what is left is expected wealth held on paths that never alarm (about half of it), 60% of it by the decrease bets and 36% by the three smallest increase bets, which did not reach 2A within a day under any law tried while the same draws also serve the other bets; whether some null law can move this wealth onto alarmed paths is open. What is proved is much weaker: no null law can exceed 0.98 of the bound at one day (Q16c).
* **Outside the class the bound fails exactly where a stated condition fails.** GARCH clustering: above the bound in 43 of 64 cells at one day, ordered by the drift of the conditional mean (Spearman 0.99), from a mean drift of 3.9% at one day (1.6% over five days); betting against the true conditional mean on the same paths stays at or below 0.24 of the bound (0.56 at five days). Plug-in baseline: 41% to 42% over five days with i.i.d. returns after a 390-step calibration, up to 32.5% in one day under a shape change that keeps the conditional mean, while the same τ-hat with the true mean never exceeds 0.59 of the bound on fresh paths (0.63 in the search) and does not alarm at all under that shape change. Price-level ticks: above the bound only from a tick of 4 sd over five days (6 sd for one day), where the conditional mean after an unchanged price drops to 0.88 of m0; the same returns drawn independently, with the same τ and m0, stay at or below 0.32 of the bound at one day and 0.57 at five days (7.4% over five days at 4 sd, against 28.8%). None of these is a failure of Theorem B.

### Q16a. Inside the class: the worst laws found

Families: i.i.d. two-point and three-point laws for Y (B at the Gaussian 9.045, or free in [2, 40]); return laws with τ and m0 computed from the law itself (scale mixtures of two normals, Student t with ν from 2.1, returns rounded to a tick of up to 1.3 sd); exogenous switching between the shapes {0, B} and Gaussian by a hidden Markov chain, the conditional mean staying at 1 in both; and adaptive laws that see the detector's state. "Bold play" uses the widest spread {0, B} at every step, except that when one draw can take a side exactly to 2A it puts the point exactly there, so that no wealth is wasted as overshoot (the landing point is closed form because each side's statistic is affine in Y_t). The searched policy family makes the two points depend on both statistics and on the time left (8 parameters; bold play is one point of it), and "hold, then bold" sets Y = 1 for a number of steps first (every bet then gains wealth without risk) and then plays bold.

**Reading.** No law or policy comes near the bound: the largest ratio in the table is 0.48 at one day and 0.71 at five days, and the Monte Carlo intervals are narrow (about plus or minus 0.07 points at one day). Among i.i.d. laws the worst are two-point laws at the edges, {0, B} with a small B (2.14% at B = 2.05); the worst return law is a scale mixture with almost half the returns at 13 times the scale (2.07%), and heavy tails as such matter less (Student t with ν = 2.1: 1.66%; ticks: 1.49%). E11 (Q11d) found an i.i.d. law at 42% of the bound for the increase grid alone; for the full two-sided detector the best i.i.d. law reaches 43%. Seeing the detector's state adds about half a point at one day and about three points at five days (bold play 2.40% and 17.6% against 1.92% and 14.5% for the best i.i.d. two-point laws at the same B; the law {0, B} itself: 1.88% and 14.9%). The 8-parameter policy search did not beat bold play on fresh seeds (2.37% against 2.40% at one day, 17.2% against 17.6% at five days), although on its own training paths it looked clearly better (2.82% against 2.63%): with a small probability as the objective, a search over many policies finds paths, not policies. Holding Y = 1 first and then playing bold changes little (2.39% after a hold of 50 steps; 17.8% after a hold of 1000 steps at five days). Switching between shapes at random times, with the conditional mean held at 1, is no worse for the detector than the i.i.d. law {0, B} (1.89% and 15.0%).

B below 1.9 cannot arise when τ is 3 times the scaled MAD of the law itself (with a positive median absolute return), but it is legitimate for a τ fixed in advance, and it is no worse.

### Q16c. Where the remaining slack sits

**Method.** The exact optional-stopping identity of `docs/theory_delay.md` (8.1) for the two-sided statistic N = (M↑ + M↓) / 2: P(alarm within m) = (m / A) × F1 × F2 × F3, with F1 the stopping factor, F2 the share of expected wealth that sits on paths that alarmed (one minus the "stranded" wealth on paths that did not), and F3 = A / E[N at the alarm], the overshoot. 100,000 fresh paths of one day for each law (`e16a_slack.csv`). Then bold play on single bets at level A and on each side of the default grid alone at 2A (bound m / (2A)), against E11's dynamic programme (DP), whose values are lower bounds on the worst case over the whole null class (`e16a_single_bet_check.csv`, 41,020 fresh paths each). Entries are rate divided by the bound. Finally, what can be proved, and the same programme on finer wealth grids (`e16a_floor_and_dp.csv`, part a6, no random draws).

| Law (one day, 100,000 paths) | Rate (95% interval) | / bound | F1 stopping | F2 wealth on alarmed paths | F3 overshoot | F1 F2 F3 | Stranded wealth: decrease bets | increase 0.02, 0.05, 0.1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| adaptive: bold play | 2.39% (2.29 to 2.48) | 0.48 | 0.99 | 0.49 | 1.00 | 0.49 | 60% | 36% |
| Gaussian | 1.02% (0.96 to 1.08) | 0.20 | 1.00 | 0.25 | 0.79 | 0.19 | 61% | 31% |
| i.i.d. two-point {0, B} | 1.92% (1.84 to 2.01) | 0.38 | 0.99 | 0.49 | 0.79 | 0.38 | 60% | 36% |

The identity holds up to Monte Carlo noise: its two sides differ by 0.6% to 1.2%, which is why F1 F2 F3 and the measured ratio differ in the second digit.

| Detector (bold play, threshold) | Bound | 98 steps | 390 | 1950 | 3900 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| single bet, up 0.5, at A | m / A | 0.89 (DP 0.87) | 0.94 (DP 0.95) | 0.87 (DP 0.88) | 0.78 (DP 0.78) |
| single bet, up 0.2, at A | m / A | 0.56 (DP 0.52) | 0.86 (DP 0.85) | 0.87 (DP 0.88) | 0.78 (DP 0.79) |
| single bet, up 0.05, at A | m / A | 0.00 (DP 0.00) | 0.26 (DP 0.18) | 0.77 (DP 0.69) | 0.75 (DP 0.72) |
| single bet, down 0.95 λ_max = 0.118, at A | m / A | 0.38 (DP 0.46) | 0.82 (DP 0.85) | 0.86 (DP 0.87) | 0.77 (DP 0.78) |
| increase side alone, default grid, at 2A | m / (2A) |  | 0.61 | 0.79 |  |
| decrease side alone, default grid, at 2A | m / (2A) |  | 0.40 | 0.69 |  |

**Reading.** Bold play removes the overshoot completely (F3 rises from 0.79 to 1.00: at an alarm the two sides together hold 2A instead of about 1.27 times 2A) and doubles F2 relative to Gaussian data (0.25 to 0.49), which the i.i.d. law {0, B} already does. What is left is F2: half of the expected wealth at the end of the day sits on paths that did not alarm, 60% of it in the five decrease bets and 36% in the increase bets 0.02, 0.05 and 0.1. Every Y_t has to serve all eleven bets at once: a draw at B multiplies the increase wealth but cuts the decrease wealth, a draw at 0 does the opposite, and, as E11 found for Gaussian data, the small increase bets are held back by their size and the decrease bets by the cap 1 / (B - 1), so under the laws tried they keep their expected wealth without reaching 2A within a day. For a single bet the same policy is about as strong as the best adversary known: it matches E11's dynamic programme within 0.03 of the bound for the bets 0.5 and 0.2 and the decrease bet at one to ten days (at a quarter of a day it is 0.08 below it for the decrease bet), and for the bet 0.05 it does better than E11's values (0.26 against 0.18 at one day, 0.77 against 0.69 at five days). Those values are lower bounds computed on a 700-point log grid of wealth states, which rounds the step M → M + 1 (a draw at Y = 1, the way a small bet builds its wealth) back down to M once M exceeds about 77. On finer grids the programme's value for the bet 0.05 rises to 0.205, 0.220 and 0.232 of the bound at one day (1,400, 2,800 and 5,600 states), still below bold play's 0.26, and to 0.77 at five days and 0.81 at ten days (2,800 states), level with bold play at five days (0.77, interval 0.75 to 0.78) and above it at ten (0.75). So the bound is nearly sharp for the single bets 0.5 and 0.2 and the decrease bet at one day or more, while no law tried takes the mixture of eleven bets on two sides above about half of it within a day; a provably sharper threshold for the default grid would need a proof that F2 stays well below 1 for every null law, which we do not have (the smallest value the two-sided statistic can take on a day without an alarm, c = 8.3, proves only P(false alarm within m) ≤ (m - c) / (A - c), 4.90% at one day, 0.98 of the bound: on such a day every increase bet is at least where draws of 0 at every step would leave it and every decrease bet at least where draws of B would, and optional stopping gives A P + c (1 - P) ≤ m).

### Q16d. Outside the class: GARCH clustering (the conditional mean drifts)

**Method.** GARCH(1,1) returns with Gaussian innovations and unit unconditional variance, on a grid of 8 persistences α + β (0.5 to 0.999, half-lives of the volatility shocks 1 to 693 steps) and 8 values of α (0.002 to 0.3): 64 cells, 6,000 paths of five days each. τ and m0 are the true *unconditional* values (from 400 stationary paths of 10,000 steps per cell), as in E9. Here the conditional mean μ_t = E[X_t | past] = σ_t² h(τ / σ_t), with h(k) = E[min(Z², k²)] for a standard normal Z, is known exactly, which gives two things on the same paths: the size of the broken assumption, written as the mean absolute drift E|μ_t / m0 - 1|, and the false alarm rate of the same detector betting against the true μ_t (its decrease bets rescaled each step), which is back inside the class (`e16b_garch.csv`). Bold cells: the lower end of the 95% interval is above the bound.

**Reading.** The failure follows the drift of the conditional mean. At one day the bound is exceeded in every cell whose mean absolute drift is above 5.6% and in none whose drift is below 3.9%; at five days the cut lies between 1.6% and 2.5%. Persistence matters at a given drift: a drift of 5.6% that dies out within a step (α + β = 0.5, α = 0.05) gives 0.60 of the bound in one day, a drift of 3.9% with a half-life of 69 steps (α + β = 0.99, α = 0.005) gives 1.11, because the bets compound over a run of steps on the same side of m0. Across the 64 cells the drift alone orders the one-day ratio almost perfectly (Spearman correlation 0.99). Both sides raise alarms (the increase side gives 33% to 86% of the alarms in the failing cells at one day), because calm spells push μ_t below m0 just as bursts push it above. The control settles the attribution: betting against the true μ_t, the same detector on the same paths never exceeds 0.24 of the bound at one day (at most 1.2% of days) or 0.56 at five days (at most 14.1%), including in the cells where the unconditional detector alarms on every path. So each failure is the stated condition failing (E[X_t | past] is not m0), not the proof. A mean drift of 4% is small: it is what α = 0.005 with a half-life of 69 steps (about an hour of one-minute bars) produces, and it is enough. This sharpens E9's finding; E10's forecast-relative monitor is the remedy.

### Q16e. Outside the class: a plug-in baseline (the baseline is estimated)

**Method.** The monitor's own plug-in: τ-hat = 3 times the scaled MAD and m-hat = the mean of min(r², τ-hat²) over a calibration window of 390 or 1440 returns, then five days of monitoring; the returns are i.i.d. throughout, so the null holds exactly and only the baseline is estimated. Three detectors run on the same paths: the plug-in (τ-hat, m-hat); a "τ-hat oracle" that keeps τ-hat but bets against the true mean m(τ-hat) of the law at that level, which is inside the class; and the full oracle (true τ and m0). Search: 37 laws per calibration length (Gaussian; scale mixtures of two normals, 5 weights times 5 scale ratios; Student t, ν = 2.2 to 10; returns rounded to a tick of 0.1 to 0.9 sd) on 6,000 paths, then the worst law of each family re-run on 30,000 fresh paths (`e16b_plugin_search.csv`, `e16b_plugin.csv`). **Reading.** With i.i.d. returns no law found pushes the one-day rate significantly above 5% (the worst, a scale mixture with 10% of returns at 5 times the scale, gives 5.10%, interval 4.86% to 5.36%, with a 390-step calibration), but every law searched gives 40% to 44% within five days against 25% (the worst of each family 41% to 42% on fresh paths), as E14 found; a 1440-step calibration is not significantly above the bound for any law (fresh paths: at most 24.5%, interval 24.1% to 25.0%, at five days; search: at most 25.3% on 6,000 paths). The τ-hat oracle matches the full oracle within noise everywhere (never above 0.59 of the bound on the fresh paths; 0.63 at most in the 6,000-path search), so estimating the truncation level is harmless and the excess comes entirely from m-hat. The deciles of the baseline error m-hat / m(τ-hat) - 1 show where: with a 390-step calibration and q = 1, the one-day rate is 16.0% in the decile where m-hat is most too low (error -29% to -9%) and 7.5% in the decile where it is most too high, but 0.8% to 1.7% in the four middle deciles (4 to 7; 0.8% to 1.1% in deciles 5 to 7, close to the oracle's 0.9%). The shape adversary shows that the plug-in has no distribution-free rate at all: the less noise the monitored law has, the faster a fixed baseline error compounds, up to 32.5% of days within one day (85.8% within five days) at q = 0 with a 390-step calibration, and 16.1% (73.1%) with 1440 steps, while the τ-hat oracle on the same paths never alarms (with Y = 1 at every step its statistic grows by exactly one per step). This is Proposition A.6 (E14) in numbers: a bound of the form C m / A cannot hold for the plug-in, and the failure is the estimated baseline, the condition Theorem B states.

### Q16f. Outside the class: price-level ticks (returns become dependent)

**Method.** The efficient log price is a Gaussian random walk (one sd per step); the observed price is rounded to a tick h, so returns are differences of rounded prices and are dependent (a bid-ask-bounce-like pattern: a move up is often followed by a move back). τ (the protocol rule: 3 times the scaled MAD, with the median of the nonzero absolute returns when more than half are zero) and m0 are the true unconditional values from 1,000 paths of 10,000 steps per tick; 10,000 monitored paths per tick. Since τ and m0 are the true unconditional values, the only condition of Theorem B that can fail is the conditional mean. The control inside the class draws the returns i.i.d. from the marginal law of the price-rounded returns (pooled over the same 1,000 long paths, so the same values with the same frequencies), with the same τ and m0, on 10,000 paths of its own seeds: only the dependence is removed. The older twin rounds each return independently to the same tick; it is inside the class too (with its own exact τ and m0), but it is a different law, with far more zero returns and a much larger B (95% zeros and B = 435 at a tick of 4 sd), so it checks the tick grid, not the values. E[X_t | previous return] / m0 measures the drift of the conditional mean (`e16b_price_ticks.csv`). Bold: the lower end of the interval is above the bound.

**Reading.** Up to a tick of 1.5 sd the conditional mean after an unchanged price or a one-tick move stays within 0.99 to 1.01 of m0, and the rates stay within 1.1 points of the control at five days and well below the bound; at 2 sd (0.98 and 1.03) the five-day rate is 1.9 points above the control (8.9% against 7.0%), still far below the bound. From 3 sd the dependence is strong: after an unchanged price the next X has 0.93 (3 sd), 0.88 (4 sd) and 0.82 (6 sd) of m0, after a one-tick move 1.18, 1.48 and 2.20. At 3 sd the one-day rate is 2.6 times that of the control (2.33% against 0.89%) but stays below the bound; at 4 sd the five-day rate is above it (28.8%, interval 28.0% to 29.7%, against 25%) and at 6 sd both are (17.6% in one day, 66.7% in five). The control, the same values drawn independently with the same τ and m0, stays at or below 0.32 (one day) and 0.57 (five days) of the bound at every tick: at 4 sd it gives 0.90% (0.73% to 1.10%) in one day and 7.4% (6.9% to 7.9%) in five, against 5.28% and 28.8% for rounded prices, and at 6 sd 1.02% and 7.3% against 17.6% and 66.7%. So the excess comes from the dependence, that is from the conditional mean, not from the tails, the discreteness or the size of B (which reaches 149 at 6 sd). The twin stays at or below 0.24 (one day) and 0.56 (five days) of the bound as well. A tick of 4 sd means the price is unchanged in 80% of the steps; this is a very coarse price grid relative to one-step volatility. This agrees in kind with ALT1, where price noise breaks the guarantee for raw returns.

### Reading

Inside the class, Theorem B held in every one of the laws and policies tried, and the strongest adversary found, one that sees the detector's state, uses about half of the bound at one day (0.52) and 0.73 of it at five days. That is 2.7 times what Gaussian data use at one day (0.19) and 1.5 times at five days (0.50), so the bound is not as loose against a worst case as E9's factor of about 4 suggested for natural laws: an adversary inside the class can take that factor down to about 2 at one day. Under every law we tried, the rest of the slack is wealth left in the decrease bets and the small increase bets, which did not use their share of the budget within a day while one draw has to serve all eleven bets on both sides at once; we have not shown that no null law can do better (the only proved limit is 0.98 of the bound at one day, Q16c). For the single bets 0.5 and 0.2 and the decrease bet the same adversary comes within a few hundredths of the bound fraction reached by E11's dynamic programme, so the bound is nearly sharp for these bets at one day or more; for the bet 0.05 the best adversary known reaches only 0.26 of the bound in a day.

Outside the class every failure lines up with the condition that was broken, and each has a control inside the class that stays below the bound (on the same paths for GARCH and the plug-in; for price ticks the same values drawn independently, with the same τ and m0): GARCH clustering breaks the conditional mean condition (a mean drift of about 4% suffices when it persists for an hour; betting against the true conditional mean restores the bound); a plug-in baseline breaks the "true baseline" condition (the excess is entirely the error of m-hat, not of τ-hat, and a law with less noise after calibration makes it as large as 32.5% in one day); price-level ticks break the conditional mean condition once the tick is several times the one-step volatility (the same values drawn independently stay at or below 0.57 of the bound). These are failures of the assumptions, not of the theorem. For practice: the monitor's guarantee is only as good as its baseline and the absence of persistent clustering relative to that baseline, which is why E8 (a confidence-sequence baseline), E10 (a forecast-relative null) and E14 (route B, no baseline) exist.

### Caveats

* A search finds lower bounds on the worst case, never the worst case itself: a law we did not try could do better. The only bound below m / A that is proved is the floor bound of Q16c (0.98 of the bound at one day). The policy families (bold play, an 8-parameter family around it, hold-then-bold) are broad but not exhaustive, and an exact computation over the 11-dimensional state of the default grid was not attempted.
* All rates are Monte Carlo estimates on fresh seeds; the in-sample search values (`train_rate`) are biased upwards, by up to 0.45 points at one day for the 8-parameter policy, and are not reported as results. A few fresh seeds are shared by different families, which makes those comparisons paired, not independent; part b3 (price ticks) reuses the seeds of the plug-in search with a 1440-step calibration, and since the two parts are unrelated this only makes them dependent.
* GARCH uses Gaussian innovations, so that the conditional mean is exact; the map is for A = 7800 and the default grid. The cut points in drift (3.9% to 5.6% at one day, 1.6% to 2.5% at five days) are read off a grid of 64 cells.
* The plug-in part searched four i.i.d. families and one shape adversary that uses only the calibration window; the vectorised plug-in does not extend a calibration window whose median absolute return is zero (the monitor does), so ticks above 0.9 sd were left out there.
* The price-tick model is a Gaussian random walk rounded to a fixed grid, with true unconditional τ and m0; real order books add other effects.
* Everything is synthetic.

## E17. One monitor for 1, 5 and 15 minutes: averaging e-detectors across sampling frequencies

Script `experiments/e17_multifrequency.py` (parts `baselines`, `levels`, `null`, `change`, `real`, `ratematch`, `figures`, each runnable alone); outputs `results/e17_*.csv` and `results/figures/e17_delays.png`. Theory in `docs/theory_multifreq.md`. Code: `src/avmonitor/multifreq.py` (`MultiFrequencyMonitor`, `proved_bound`, `level_for_budget`, `handicap`); tests `tests/test_multifreq.py`. Seeds are fixed in the script. The real-data settings were written into the script's docstring and committed before the real part was run for the first time. Iteration notes, including a design change made after seeing results (γ = 2) and a comparison added after an independent review (`ratematch`, Q17g): `docs/iterations/E17.md`.

**Question.** The monitor bets on one-minute returns. Some volatility changes are easier to see in 5-minute or 15-minute returns: when one-minute prices carry noise (for example from the bid-ask bounce, ALT1), or when returns become autocorrelated, which moves the variance of a block but not the one-minute variance. Instead of choosing one sampling frequency, we can run an e-detector at each frequency and average them (an average of e-values is an e-value: Vovk and Wang 2021). Does the average keep a proved false alarm bound? Does it beat each single frequency? If not, is it at least never much worse than the best one, and does it help under price noise?

**Method.**

* **Theory** (`docs/theory_multifreq.md`). Frequency k sums the one-minute returns of non-overlapping k-minute blocks, clips the squared block return at `τ_k² = (3 × scaled MAD of k-minute returns)²` and runs its own pair of betting detectors (increase and decrease) over blocks, exactly like the one-minute monitor.
  * *Each frequency needs its own null.* The mean of the clipped squared block return, given everything seen up to the start of the block, must stay below the increase baseline (and above the decrease baseline). If one-minute returns are independent with one fixed distribution (this allows fat tails and jumps; prices rounded to a tick give dependent returns and are not covered), the one-minute null implies this for every k, with the true baselines. In general it does not: section 2.1 of the note gives returns that satisfy the one-minute null but whose 5-minute blocks have mean square 17.7 instead of 5.
  * *The obvious proof fails.* A k-minute detector changes only at the end of each block. One minute before a block ends, most of its next bet is already decided by the returns seen so far, so on the one-minute clock it is not a fair bet. The usual proof of `P(false alarm within m minutes) ≤ Σ_k w_k (m / k) / A` for the plain weighted average, checked every minute, therefore fails. Proposition 2 gives a two-minute example in which the expected value of the stopped detector exceeds what the proof needs by 0.484 λ, where λ is the bet size. This shows that the proof fails, not that the bound itself fails; a union bound (Theorem 3) does prove a bound for the plain average, three times larger for balanced weights. Combining e-processes that live on different information flows is a known difficulty (Choe and Ramdas, arXiv:2402.09698).
  * *The fix: a certified average.* Between its block ends, a coarse detector is counted only at the smallest value its wealth can take at the next block end. With `M` its value at the last block end and `ℓ` the smallest possible bet factor (`1 - λ` for an increase bet, `1 - φ` for a decrease bet), this credit is `min(M, ℓ (M + 1))`. At block ends nothing is lost. **Theorem 1:** if every frequency's null holds with the true baselines (for example independent returns, as above), then with each side alarming at 2A, `P(false alarm within m minutes) ≤ Σ_k w_k ⌈m / k⌉ / A`, which is smaller than the one-minute monitor's `m / A`, and the mean time to the first false alarm is at least `(A - κ) / ρ` with `ρ = Σ_k w_k / k` and `κ = Σ_k w_k (1 - 1/k)`. Corollary 4 extends the bound to recalibration after every alarm. Theorem 3 proves bounds for two monitors without certification: `Σ_k w_k ⌊m / k⌋ / A` for the weighted maximum (the same budget as Theorem 1, but no restart result), and three times more than Theorem 1 for the plain average with balanced weights. With the plug-in baselines that the real-data monitor uses, none of these bounds is proved (Q17b shows what happens then).
  * *The price of not knowing the frequency.* If only frequency j sees the change, the average must push that detector to `h_j` times the threshold it would need alone (the handicap). Proposition 3: for any weights the largest handicap is at least the number of frequencies (here 3), the same price as splitting the budget three ways (Bonferroni). Equality holds for "balanced" weights proportional to k.
* **Monitors** (fixed before any run). Every monitor's level A is set so that its proved bound is 5% per 1,440-minute day (Q17a). Each frequency alone; certified averages with **equal** weights (1/3 each), **balanced** weights (proportional to k) and **sqrt** weights (proportional to √k); the **plain average checked every minute** with balanced weights at the certified level, where Theorem 3 proves only 15% (to see whether certification matters in practice); the **weighted maximum** with balanced weights; and the balanced average of **5 and 15 minutes only**. Under price noise also **gap** versions, in which each coarse block leaves out its first one-minute return so that consecutive blocks share no noisy price; under independent noise and an efficient price with independent increments, gap blocks are independent of the past, so Theorem 1 applies exactly to monitors built only from gap blocks (not to the gap versions of the averages, which still contain the one-minute detector). All with c = 3 and the default bet grids; band 0 in the synthetic parts.
* **[SYNTHETIC] laws.** One-minute returns with unit variance in the efficient price: Gaussian; Student t with 3 degrees of freedom (unit variance); jumps (probability 0.005 per minute, size N(0, 8²)); and price noise `r_t = e_t + u_t - u_{t-1}` with Gaussian `e_t` and noise `u_t ~ N(0, γ²)`, γ = 0.5, 1 and 2 (ALT1's model). Under price noise, consecutive one-minute returns are correlated (-γ² / (1 + 2γ²): -0.17, -0.33 and -0.44), so no monitor that uses one-minute returns or plain coarse blocks has a proof there. The true truncation levels and baselines of every law, frequency and block type come from 2 million simulated blocks each (`e17_true_baselines.csv`).
* **False alarms.** 10,000 monitored days of 1,440 minutes per cell, with the true baseline and with the plug-in baseline estimated on the 1,440 minutes before (all block phases of the calibration window are used for the coarse frequencies).
* **Changes** (true baseline, 2,000 paths per cell). The change comes at monitored minute 247, which is not a multiple of 5 or 15, so coarse blocks straddle it. Persistent changes of the standard deviation (×1.25, ×1.5, ×2, ×0.8, ×2/3, ×0.5), watched for 1,440 minutes; bursts (×2 or ×3 lasting 15 or 60 minutes), detected only if the alarm comes before the burst ends plus 15 minutes; and an **autocorrelation jump**: at the change, the lag-one autocorrelation of the efficient returns jumps from 0 to 0.3 while the one-minute variance stays the same, so the variances of blocks move (by factors 1.61 at 5 minutes and 1.78 at 15 minutes, from the closed form for this autocorrelation). For Gaussian returns the one-minute truncated mean does not move; for Student t3 returns it rises by about 4%, because the filter changes the shape of the one-minute distribution (checked by simulation with 2 million draws). The script and the CSV files call this cell "trend"; it is an abrupt change, not a slow one. A path counts as detected if its first alarm comes after the change and in the right direction; a false alarm before the change (at most 1.7% of paths in any cell) or an alarm in the wrong direction is a miss. The delay is counted in minutes from the change.
* **[REAL] five coins.** Binance spot BTC, ETH, XRP, SOL and DOGE one-minute bars, 1 July to 31 December 2025, deseasonalised exactly as in E6 (`e06b_five_coins_monitor.prepare`). Monitors: the three singles, the three certified averages and the balanced maximum, with plain blocks and E6's band 0.25, calibration 1,440 minutes and recalibration after every alarm. Validation exactly as E6 (Q6d, Q6e): the share of up alarms followed by higher robust volatility over the next 1,440 minutes than the one-minute baseline of the calibration window (down alarms: lower), with 95% Wilson intervals and the matched-delay random-time control; and the share of up (down) alarms after which the realised volatility was above (below) an EWMA volatility forecast, against 3,000 random times per coin. Descriptive only: how much of the combined statistic comes from each frequency at the alarm, and the share of alarms with a same-direction one-minute alarm within 60 minutes. After an independent review, a rate-matched comparison of the coarse detectors with the one-minute monitor was added (Q17g; not planned, run after the real results were seen).

**Summary.**

* **The obvious proof fails, and a repaired guarantee is proved.** The standard argument does not cover the plain every-minute average (Proposition 2); a union bound proves three times the budget for it (Theorem 3). The certified average has `P(false alarm within m) ≤ Σ_k w_k ⌈m / k⌉ / A` (Theorem 1) when every frequency's null holds with the true baselines, for example for independent returns. We spend that gain by lowering A until the bound is again 5% per day. With the plug-in baselines used on real data there is no proof.
* **With independent simulated returns, no combination beats the best single frequency (at best it ties), but the good ones stay close to it.** For persistent changes the one-minute detector is the fastest. The equal-weight average is 0% to 5% slower, the sqrt average 4% to 10% and the balanced average 11% to 18%, in line with the handicaps of Proposition 3. After a jump in the lag-one autocorrelation from 0 to 0.3, which the one-minute detector almost never sees (3.8% detected for Gaussian returns, 17.5% for Student t3), the averages detect 95.5% to 97.3% (Gaussian; 83.9% to 89.0% for Student t3) at 1.17 to 1.32 times the 5-minute median delay (Gaussian). **No single frequency handles both short bursts and the autocorrelation jump; every average handles both reasonably well.** Under price noise, where no monitor that uses one-minute returns has a proof, some averages do beat the best single frequency (Q17e).
* **Certification costs little.** The plain average checked every minute, which has only a 15% proved bound at this level, has the same false alarm rates (0.78% against 0.77% for Gaussian returns) and the same delays as the certified one (at most about one point of detection, for decreases under strong noise). The factor 3 in Theorem 3 is a gap in the proof, not in behaviour, in these designs.
* **Price noise.** The one-minute detector is invalid under noise (6.88% and 12.06% per day at γ = 1 and 2, against a 5% target), and every average that contains it inherits part of the excess (balanced 3.09% and 6.50%, against 0.77% for Gaussian returns). The only combination with a proof under noise, the gap average of 5 and 15 minutes (0.54% and 0.52%), detects persistent increases of 25% and 50% better than either proved single frequency at γ = 2 (×1.25: 28.1% against 21.4% and 25.3%; ×1.5: 93.3% against 85.5% and 82.8%) but decreases worse than the 5-minute gap detector alone (×0.5: 47.2% against 56.5%). **γ = 2 was added to the design after the γ = 1 results were seen** (`docs/iterations/E17.md`, iteration 3). At the planned γ = 1 the combination does not help for increases (×1.25: 78.7% against 79.2% for the 5-minute gap detector), and it does not help for the ×3 burst of 60 minutes at either level (γ = 2: 10.9% against 14.8%; γ = 1: 38.2% against 47.9%) or for decreases.
* **Estimated baselines.** The plug-in baseline raises every false alarm rate (to 5.47% for the one-minute detector on Gaussian returns, significantly above 5%; the equal-weight average reaches 5.60%, also significantly above 5%, for Student t3 and jumps). The coarse detectors stay lower (5 minutes 2.45%, 15 minutes 1.66%), and the balanced average stays below 5% on all i.i.d. laws (3.66% to 4.54%).
* **[REAL] On five coins the averages behave like the one-minute monitor.** At alarms, the one-minute detector makes up 98.4% to 99.7% of the combined statistic on average. Alarm rates are 0.65 to 0.68 per day (one-minute monitor 0.68), and the validated shares are about equal or lower by up to 4.6 points (up 78% to 80% against 80%; down 84% to 88% against 88%). The 5-minute and 15-minute detectors alone alarm less often (0.43 and 0.26 per day) and their alarms are confirmed more often (up 90% and 95%, down 95% and 96%), but this is not a comparison at equal alarm rates. An unplanned comparison with E6 suggested that, for up alarms, the 5-minute detector's higher confirmation is not only a rate effect; a rate-matched comparison run after this lead was seen (Q17g) does not support it. With its two levels matched per coin to the 5-minute detector's numbers of up and down alarms, the one-minute monitor's up alarms are confirmed 90.5% of the time against 90.0% (p = 0.88) and its down alarms 96.4% against 94.6% (p = 0.43). Against the 15-minute detector it is as good or better (down alarms followed by volatility below the EWMA forecast: 88.9% against 72.4%, p = 0.0014). So the coarse detectors' higher confirmation in Q17f is explained by their lower alarm rate.

### Q17a. Levels and handicaps

Level A of each monitor for a proved bound of 5% per 1,440-minute day (`results/e17_levels.csv`), and the handicap of each frequency: the factor by which it must exceed its own single-frequency threshold when it alone sees the change. The gap versions have the same levels and handicaps.

| Monitor | Weights on 1, 5, 15 min | A | Proved bound per day | Handicap of 1, 5, 15 min |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 min alone | 1 | 28,800 | 5% | 1.00 |
| 5 min alone | 1 | 5,760 | 5% | 1.00 |
| 15 min alone | 1 | 1,920 | 5% | 1.00 |
| Average, equal | 0.3333, 0.3333, 0.3333 | 12,160 | 5% | 1.27 / 6.33 / 19.00 |
| Average, balanced | 0.0476, 0.2381, 0.7143 | 4,114 | 5% | 3.00 / 3.00 / 3.00 |
| Average, sqrt | 0.1407, 0.3145, 0.5448 | 6,909 | 5% | 1.71 / 3.81 / 6.61 |
| Plain average every minute, balanced | 0.0476, 0.2381, 0.7143 | 4,114 | 15% (Theorem 3) | 3.00 / 3.00 / 3.00 |
| Weighted maximum, balanced | 0.0476, 0.2381, 0.7143 | 4,114 | 5% | 3.00 / 3.00 / 3.00 |
| Average of 5 and 15, balanced | 0.2500, 0.7500 (5 and 15 only) | 2,880 | 5% | 2.00 / 2.00 (5 and 15) |

**Reading.** Equal weights barely handicap the one-minute detector (1.27) but handicap the 15-minute one by 19. Balanced weights spread the price evenly (3 for each), which Proposition 3 shows is the smallest possible worst case. A handicap h adds about log h to the logarithm of the threshold, which is what drives the delay: log 3 = 1.1 against log(2 × 28,800) = 11.0 for the one-minute detector, so we expect the balanced average to be about 10% slower than the best frequency when that frequency carries all the evidence.

### Q17b. False alarms [SYNTHETIC]

Leaving out the first return of each coarse block (gap) barely helps these averages (balanced 5.86%), because the excess comes from the one-minute part. The plain coarse detectors, which have no proof under noise, stay under 5% (5 minutes at most 2.49%). With the true baseline, the three proved gap monitors stay at 0.34% to 0.76%.
* **The plug-in baseline matters more than the combination.** Estimating the baseline roughly triples the one-minute rate (1.96% to 5.47% for Gaussian returns), as E4 and E14 found. In relative terms the coarse detectors suffer even more (15 minutes: 0.39% to 1.66%; a day holds only 96 non-overlapping 15-minute blocks), but they start so low that the balanced average stays under 5% on every i.i.d. law (3.66% to 4.54%). The equal-weight average does not (up to 5.60%).

**Reading.**

* **Bursts belong to the one-minute detector, the autocorrelation jump to the 5-minute detector, and no single frequency does both.** The one-minute detector catches 73.2% of 15-minute ×3 bursts (Gaussian) but only 3.8% of autocorrelation jumps; the 5-minute detector catches 99.2% of the jumps but 0.8% of those bursts. The 15-minute detector is never the best here.
* **The averages do both reasonably well.** With Gaussian returns the balanced average catches 62.7% of the short ×3 bursts and 97.3% of autocorrelation jumps; equal weights 70.3% and 95.5%. On the jump they need 1.17 (balanced) to 1.32 (equal) times the 5-minute median delay. This is the case for averaging: when the right frequency is not known in advance, an average loses a little everywhere instead of failing badly somewhere.
* **Short bursts cost the averages detections.** The handicap raises the threshold, and a burst that ends before the detector crosses it is missed: 13.1% (balanced) against 21.3% for the ×2, 15-minute burst. For bursts, equal weights (small handicap on one minute) are the best compromise; for the autocorrelation jump, balanced weights are.
* With Student t3 returns the one-minute detector sees more of the autocorrelation jump (17.5%), because for this law the change also raises the one-minute truncated mean by about 4%, and the averages see less (83.9% to 89.0%, against 93.8% for the 5-minute detector), but the picture is the same.

* **Moderate noise (γ = 1): the one-minute returns still carry most of the information, but no guarantee.** The one-minute detector is still the fastest single frequency for every change except the autocorrelation jump, but it alarms on 6.88% of null days. Among the proved monitors, the 5-minute gap detector is the best single frequency. The proved 5 and 15 average matches its detection on increases (78.7% against 79.2% at ×1.25; 100% at ×1.5 and ×2, 10 to 25 minutes later), loses on decreases (×0.8: 36.1% against 48.9%) and on the ×3 burst of 60 minutes (38.2% against 47.9%), and wins on the autocorrelation jump (83.5% against 76.3% and 71.2%). Without a proof, some averages beat every single frequency here: the equal-weight average detects 95.9% of ×1.25 changes (median 577 minutes) against 92.1% (600.5) for the one-minute detector (`results/e17_change.csv`).
* **Strong noise (γ = 2, a level added after the γ = 1 results were seen): coarse frequencies win, and the 5 and 15 average helps for the two smaller persistent increases.** The one-minute detector is no longer the best single frequency: the plain 5-minute detector detects more for ×1.25, ×1.5, ×2, ×2/3 and ×0.5 (for example ×0.5: 75.1% against 42.8%) and the plain 15-minute detector for the autocorrelation jump, while the one-minute detector alarms on 12.06% of null days. The proved 5 and 15 average beats both proved singles for ×1.25 (28.1% against 21.4% and 25.3%) and ×1.5 (93.3% against 85.5% and 82.8%), ties at ×2 (100%, 258 against 253 minutes), is worse for the ×3 burst of 60 minutes (10.9% against 14.8%) and is close to the better single on the autocorrelation jump (43.8% against 44.9%). The averages without a proof that contain the one-minute detector beat every single frequency in some cells (balanced: ×1.25 44.1% and ×1.5 97.3% (563), against 37.4% and 93.8% (598) for the plain 5-minute detector), but they alarm on 6.50% of null days. For decreases it is worse than the 5-minute gap detector (×0.8: 1.6% against 4.5%; ×2/3: 13.5% against 21.8%; ×0.5: 47.2% against 56.5%), because the 15-minute detector sees almost no decrease within a day (11.7% at ×0.5) and the average still pays a handicap of 2 on the 5-minute evidence.
* **Gap blocks buy the proof at a cost in power.** Leaving out one return in five makes the 5-minute detector slower (γ = 2, ×1.25: 21.4% against 37.4% with plain blocks). The plain-block 5 and 15 average has no proof but stays at 1.56% and detects more (×1.25: 39.6%; autocorrelation jump 53.2%). Neighbouring plain blocks share one noisy price, but the conditional mean of a block's square moves with the previous block only by the factor `γ⁴ / (k + 2γ²)²` (section 2.1 of the note): 0.020 at 5 minutes and 0.0035 at 15 minutes when γ = 1, 0.09 and 0.03 when γ = 2. This may explain why its false alarm rate stays low; it is not a proof.

**Reading.**

* **On these coins the combination is the one-minute monitor with a small delay.** At alarms, the one-minute detector makes up 98.4% to 99.7% of the combined statistic on average, and 72% to 94% of the averages' alarms have a one-minute alarm in the same direction within 60 minutes before or after. The balanced average alarms a median of 6 to 10 minutes after the matching one-minute alarm (per coin), the equal average 1 to 2 minutes after. Its validation figures are the same as the one-minute monitor's or slightly lower (balanced: up 79% against 80%, down 84% against 88%, EWMA 75% and 77% against 78% and 80%).
* **This fits the synthetic results.** Real one-minute returns on these coins have little of the noise that would favour coarse frequencies: E13 measured lag-one autocorrelations of deseasonalised one-minute returns of -0.016 to +0.027 for BTC, ETH, XRP and SOL and +0.132 for DOGE (`results/e13d_real_crypto_random.csv`), far from the -0.33 of γ = 1. So the situation is like the i.i.d. rows of Q17c, where the average follows the one-minute detector.
* **The coarse detectors alone are more selective, not shown to be better.** The 5-minute and 15-minute alarms are confirmed more often (up 90% and 95%, down 95% and 96%) but come only 0.43 and 0.26 times per day, against 0.68. An unplanned check against E6 suggested that for up alarms this is not only a rate effect: the one-minute monitor at band 0.5 alarms at a similar rate (0.47 to 0.51 per day per coin, `results/e06d_pooled.csv`) and its up alarms are confirmed 79.4% of the time (74.4% to 83.6%), against 90.0% (85.4% to 93.3%) for the 5-minute detector at 0.43 per day; for down alarms the wider band closes the gap (96.7% against 94.6%). The bands differ and alarms are correlated, so this was a lead, not a result. Q17g tests it at matched alarm counts, and the lead does not hold. The 15-minute down alarms beat the EWMA forecast less often (72%) than the one-minute ones (80%).

### Q17g. The coarse detectors at matched alarm counts [REAL, post hoc]

**Why and when.** Not planned. An independent review (round 4, finding M5) pointed out the lead in Q17f: the 5-minute detector's up alarms are confirmed more often than those of the one-minute monitor at a similar alarm rate in E6 (band 0.5). This comparison was added after the real results had been seen, to test that lead. It is reported whichever way it went.

**Method.** For each coin, the one-minute monitor (band 0.25, calibration 1,440 minutes, recalibration after every alarm, as in Q17f) gets separate levels for its increase and decrease sides (`threshold_down` in `MultiFrequencyMonitor`). They are chosen by coordinate-wise bisection on log A, as E6's `match_rule` does for the ratio rule, so that the monitor raises as many up and down alarms as the 5-minute (or 15-minute) detector. Validation as in Q17f, with the HAR forecast added. p-values come from two-proportion z-tests on the pooled counts, coarse detector against matched one-minute monitor. They treat alarms as independent, so they are optimistic. Files: `results/e17_ratematch_levels.csv` (levels and counts per coin), `e17_ratematch_pooled.csv`, `e17_ratematch_summary.csv`, `e17_ratematch_forecast_hits.csv`.

**Matching.** The counts match exactly for three coins against the 5-minute detector (pooled 220 and 172 against 221 and 172) and for two coins against the 15-minute detector (pooled 117 and 117 against 118 and 117); the bisection cannot always hit a count exactly. The levels this needs are far above the one-minute monitor's 28,800: per coin, 4.5 × 10¹⁰ to 2.8 × 10¹⁴ (increase side) and 1.6 × 10⁹ to 5.3 × 10¹² (decrease side) to match the 5-minute detector, and 2.2 × 10²² to 6.2 × 10⁵² and 1.2 × 10¹⁷ to 4.8 × 10²⁴ to match the 15-minute detector. On real data the one-minute statistic grows very fast after a large change, so cutting its alarm count takes many orders of magnitude in the level. (A first run that searched only up to 2.88 × 10⁸ could not reach the targets; see the iteration notes.)

Pooled over the five coins, share in percent with the 95% Wilson interval:

| Monitor | Alarms per day | Up / down | Up confirmed | Down confirmed | EWMA, up | EWMA, down | HAR, up | HAR, down |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 min | 0.43 | 221 / 172 | 90.0% (85.4 to 93.3) | 94.6% (90.1 to 97.1) | 80.5% (74.8 to 85.2) | 87.4% (81.5 to 91.6) | 81.9% (76.3 to 86.4) | 80.2% (73.6 to 85.6) |
| 1 min, matched to 5 min | 0.43 | 220 / 172 | 90.5% (85.8 to 93.7) | 96.4% (92.4 to 98.3) | 81.4% (75.7 to 86.0) | 88.6% (82.9 to 92.6) | 83.6% (78.2 to 87.9) | 82.6% (76.2 to 87.6) |
| p-value | | | 0.88 | 0.43 | 0.83 | 0.74 | 0.63 | 0.57 |
| 15 min | 0.26 | 118 / 117 | 94.9% (89.3 to 97.6) | 95.7% (90.3 to 98.1) | 83.9% (76.2 to 89.4) | 72.4% (63.7 to 79.7) | 82.2% (74.3 to 88.1) | 56.0% (47.0 to 64.7) |
| 1 min, matched to 15 min | 0.25 | 117 / 117 | 97.4% (92.7 to 99.1) | 98.3% (94.0 to 99.5) | 81.2% (73.2 to 87.2) | 88.9% (81.9 to 93.4) | 82.1% (74.1 to 88.0) | 80.3% (72.2 to 86.5) |
| p-value | | | 0.31 | 0.24 | 0.59 | 0.0014 | 0.98 | 0.000067 |

The matched-delay random-time controls are 48% to 56% in every row (`e17_ratematch_pooled.csv`).

**Reading.**

* **The lead does not hold.** At the same numbers of up and down alarms, the one-minute monitor's alarms are confirmed as often as the 5-minute detector's on every measure (differences of 0.4 to 2.4 points, p = 0.43 to 0.88). The 5-minute detector's higher confirmation in Q17f comes from its lower alarm rate, not from the sampling frequency.
* **Against the 15-minute detector the one-minute monitor is as good or better.** The confirmation shares are similar (p = 0.24 and 0.31), but after the 15-minute detector's down alarms the realised volatility is below the forecast less often: 72.4% against 88.9% (EWMA, p = 0.0014) and 56.0% against 80.3% (HAR, p = 0.000067). This difference was not predicted, and the 15-minute comparison was added at the same time as the 5-minute one.
* **The two monitors flag partly different events.** Only 31% of the 5-minute alarms and 10% of the 15-minute alarms have a same-direction alarm of the matched one-minute monitor within 60 minutes (`e17_ratematch_levels.csv`, weighted by alarm counts). Equal precision with different events leaves room for a combination at a matched rate, but this experiment does not test one.

**Answers.** (1) *Does the combination beat each single frequency?* Not in any design with independent returns, and not on the real coins (where, at matched alarm counts, the coarse detectors alone are not better than the one-minute monitor either, Q17g). Under price noise, where no monitor that uses one-minute returns has a proof, some averages do beat every single frequency in some cells (Q17e); among proved monitors, the 5 and 15 gap average beats both proved singles only for persistent increases of 25% and 50% at γ = 2. (2) *Is it never much worse than the best?* With independent returns and equal weights it is 0% to 5% slower than the best frequency on persistent changes and needs 1.32 times the 5-minute delay on the autocorrelation jump (Gaussian); with balanced weights 11% to 18% and 1.17 times. Where one frequency fails badly (the one-minute detector on the autocorrelation jump, the coarse ones on short bursts), every average keeps most of the detection. (3) *Does it help under price noise?* Only partly. Every average that contains the one-minute detector inherits its invalidity. The proved 5 and 15 gap average helps for persistent increases of 25% and 50% at γ = 2 (a level added after seeing γ = 1), not at γ = 1, not for bursts and not for decreases.

**Caveats.**

* The guarantee assumes each frequency's null holds with the true baselines. Real returns cluster in volatility (E9) and may violate the coarse nulls in ways the one-minute null does not (section 2.1 of the note). The plug-in baseline used on real data has no proof for any frequency (Q17b shows how much it adds). A confidence-sequence baseline for each frequency (`docs/theory_multifreq.md`, section 8) is sketched, not implemented.
* Under price noise, only the gap monitors without the one-minute detector are proved, and only for independent noise on an efficient price with independent increments.
* The synthetic designs are i.i.d. apart from the noise and the autocorrelation jump. That jump is one kind of dependence, and an abrupt one; other designs could favour other frequencies.
* Median delays are among detected paths only; when detection shares differ a lot (for example 15 minutes at ×0.8), compare the shares first.
* γ = 2 was added to the design after the γ = 1 results showed the one-minute detector still fastest (`docs/iterations/E17.md`); all other settings were fixed before any run, and the γ = 1 numbers did not change (same seeds).
* On real data, alarms across coins are correlated and the next-day windows of random times overlap, so the pooled intervals and p-values are optimistic (as in E6). The comparison between single frequencies in Q17f is not at equal alarm rates; Q17g is, but it was added after the real results were seen.
* The references were checked through web-search listings only, because the full texts could not be opened from this machine: Vovk and Wang (2021), "E-values: calibration, combination and applications", Annals of Statistics 49(3), 1736 to 1754 (Project Euclid and Royal Holloway listings); Choe and Ramdas, "Combining evidence across filtrations", arXiv:2402.09698 (arXiv listing). We use only their basic points, as stated in the theory note.
